paragraphs: On a very hot evening in July, a young man named Raskolnikov came out of his small attic room on S. Place and started walking slowly toward K. bridge. He seemed unsure and walked carefully.

Raskolnikov had managed not to meet his landlady as he left. His attic was tiny, almost like a closet, at the top of a tall house. The landlady, who gave him his room and meals, lived just below him. He always felt nervous and scared when passing her kitchen because he owed her money and was afraid she might talk to him or ask for payment.

Raskolnikov was not really a coward, but lately he felt tired and irritable. He was so focused on his own problems that he tried to avoid everyone, not just his landlady. He was poor, but didn’t even care about that anymore. He didn’t want to deal with real-life problems, and the idea of talking to his landlady or making excuses made him want to sneak out like a cat.
This evening, as he reached the street, he felt his fears even more strongly.

He thought, “I want to try something big, but I’m scared of small things like this. People are most afraid of taking a new step or saying something new.” He wondered if he was just talking to himself to feel better. He remembered lying in bed for days, thinking of stories like Jack the Giant-killer. He asked himself, “Why am I going there now? Am I really able to do something big? Maybe it’s just a game in my mind.”

The street was very hot and crowded. There were buildings under construction, dust, and bad smells everywhere. Raskolnikov saw many drunk men, even though it was a workday. He was disgusted by it all. Raskolnikov was a handsome young man, tall and slim with dark eyes and hair, but he didn’t notice anything around him. He kept muttering to himself and felt weak because he hadn’t eaten much for two days.

Raskolnikov’s clothes were so old and torn that most people would be embarrassed to wear them, but in this part of town, no one really cared. He didn’t even mind his rags, unless he met someone he knew. Suddenly, a drunk man passing by in a wagon shouted at him about his hat. Raskolnikov grabbed his hat, which was old and beat-up. He felt a strange fear—not shame—because his hat would be easy to remember.

“I knew it,” he muttered. “A silly thing like my hat could ruin everything. People would notice it and remember me. When you want to keep a secret, you shouldn’t stand out. Little things like this can spoil big plans.”

Raskolnikov didn’t have far to go; he knew it was exactly seven hundred and thirty steps from his house. He had counted them before when he was lost in thought. Back then, he thought his plan was just a wild dream, but now he was starting to think he might really try it. He was going for a “practice run,” and felt more and more nervous with each step.

Feeling scared, Raskolnikov reached a big house near the canal. Many people lived there—tailors, cooks, workers, and others. He was happy not to meet any door-keepers and slipped in unseen, using the dark back staircase he already knew. He liked how the darkness made it hard for anyone to notice him.

“If I’m so scared now, what would I feel if I was really going to do it?” he wondered as he reached the fourth floor. Some porters were moving furniture out of a flat there. He knew the German clerk was moving out, so soon only the old woman would live on this floor. “That’s good,” he thought, as he rang the old woman’s bell. The bell made a weak sound. The old woman peeked through the door crack, watching him closely. Seeing other people nearby, she opened the door wider. Raskolnikov stepped inside. The old woman was small, old, and had sharp eyes and nose. Her hair was gray and oily, and she wore a worn-out fur cape, even though it was hot. She coughed and groaned. Raskolnikov looked at her in a strange way, making her suspicious.
“Raskolnikov, a student. I came here a month ago,” he said, trying to be polite.
“I remember you,” the old woman said, still staring at him.
“I’m here for the same thing,” Raskolnikov said, feeling awkward. He wondered if she was always this suspicious.
The old woman waited a little, then pointed to her room and told him to come in.
The small room had yellow walls, flowers in the window, and was bright from the setting sun.

Raskolnikov quickly looked around, trying to remember everything about the room. There was old yellow furniture, a sofa, a table, a dressing table with a mirror, some chairs, and pictures of German girls with birds. In the corner, a lamp burned in front of an icon. Everything was very clean and shiny.
“Lizaveta must clean everything,” Raskolnikov thought. There was no dust anywhere.
“Old widows always keep things clean,” he thought again, glancing at the curtain that covered the door to the old woman’s bedroom. He had never seen inside. The whole flat was just two little rooms.
“What do you want?” the old woman asked sharply, standing in front of him.
“I brought something to pawn,” he said, taking out an old silver watch.
“The time to get your last item back is over. The month was up two days ago,” she said.
“I’ll bring the interest for another month. Please wait a bit,” he replied.
“That’s up to me, whether I wait or sell your things,” she said.
“How much will you give me for the watch, Alyona Ivanovna?” he asked.
“You always bring small things, not worth much. I gave you two roubles for your ring last time, but it wasn’t worth that much,” she said.
“Please give me four roubles for the watch. It was my father’s. I’ll get money soon and will buy it back.”
“A rouble and a half, and pay the interest up front if you want,” she replied.
“A rouble and a half!” Raskolnikov cried.
“Take it or leave it,” she said, handing back the watch. Raskolnikov wanted to leave because he was angry but stayed, remembering he had another reason for coming.
“Fine, take it,” he said, annoyed.
The old woman searched her pocket for keys and went behind the curtain into the other room. Raskolnikov listened carefully. He heard her unlock a drawer.

He guessed, “It must be the top drawer. She keeps the keys on her right side, all together on a steel ring. One key is much bigger—maybe for a special box. That’s good to know.” He thought it was shameful to be thinking like this.
The old woman returned.

“Here: I must take fifteen copecks for the month on a rouble and a half, and twenty copecks for the two roubles you owe me. So you get a rouble and fifteen copecks,” she explained, giving him the money.
“Only a rouble and fifteen copecks?” he said.
“Yes,” she answered.
Raskolnikov did not argue and took the money. He waited, as if he wanted to say or do something else, but wasn’t sure what.
“I might bring you something else soon, Alyona Ivanovna—a silver cigarette box, when I get it back from a friend...” he said, then stopped, feeling embarrassed.
“We’ll talk about it then,” she replied.
“Good-bye. Are you always at home alone? Is your sister here?” he asked, trying to sound casual.
“That’s none of your business,” she said.
“Oh, it’s nothing. You’re very quick to answer. Good day, Alyona Ivanovna,” he said.

Raskolnikov left, feeling even more confused. As he went down the stairs, he stopped a few times, thinking hard. When he reached the street, he cried, “Oh, God, how horrible all this is! Can I really... No, that’s stupid, it’s nonsense!” He felt disgusted with himself and his thoughts. He walked like a drunk person, bumping into others and not caring. Soon he found himself near a tavern. Two drunk men came out, holding each other up. Without thinking, Raskolnikov went down into the tavern. He had never been in one before, but now he was very thirsty and weak from hunger. He sat at a little table in a dark corner, ordered beer, and drank it quickly. He felt better and his mind became clearer.
“It’s all nonsense,” he thought. “There’s nothing to worry about. I just needed food and drink. Now I feel stronger and my head is clear. How silly my worries were!”
Even though he tried to act cheerful, he had a strange feeling that this happiness wasn’t normal either.

There were only a few people in the tavern. Besides the two drunk men, a group of five men and a girl with a concertina had just left, making the room quiet. One man, who looked like a worker, was sitting with some beer. His friend, a big man with a gray beard, was very drunk and had fallen asleep on the bench. Sometimes he would move around, crack his fingers, and sing bits of songs:
“His wife a year he fondly loved
His wife a—a year he—fondly loved.”
Then he would wake up and sing:
“Walking along the crowded row
He met the one he used to know.”

No one else seemed to enjoy his singing. His friend looked at him with suspicion. There was another man in the room who looked like a retired clerk. He sat alone, sipping his drink and watching the others. He also seemed troubled.

Raskolnikov was not used to being around lots of people. Lately, he had been alone almost all the time. But today, he suddenly wanted to be with others. He was tired and sad, and just wanted to rest, even in a dirty tavern.

The tavern owner was in another room, but kept coming down to check on things. He wore dirty clothes and had a greasy face. Two boys helped at the counter, which had old bread, cucumbers, and smelly fish on it. The air was thick with the smell of alcohol, and it was hard to breathe.

Raskolnikov noticed a man sitting nearby who looked interesting. The man was old, with messy clothes and a tired face. He stared at Raskolnikov, hoping to talk. His name was Marmeladov. He looked smart, but also a little crazy and very sad. Finally, Marmeladov spoke up loudly to Raskolnikov.
“Excuse me, sir,” Marmeladov said, “may I talk to you? I can tell you’re educated. My name is Marmeladov. I’m a titular counsellor. Have you ever worked in the service?”
“No, I am a student,” Raskolnikov answered, surprised.
“Ah, a student! I knew it,” Marmeladov said. He moved to sit next to Raskolnikov, bringing his drink, and started talking a lot. He was drunk, but he spoke clearly.

“Sir,” Marmeladov began, “being poor isn’t bad, but begging is. When you beg, people push you away. My wife was beaten by Mr. Lebeziatnikov a month ago. Have you ever had to sleep outside, on a hay barge?”
“No, never. What do you mean?” Raskolnikov asked.
“I just slept on one for five nights,” Marmeladov said. His clothes were covered in hay, and he looked dirty.
People in the tavern started paying attention and laughing quietly. Marmeladov was well-known for talking to strangers when he got drunk.
The innkeeper asked, “Why don’t you work if you have a job?”
Marmeladov answered Raskolnikov, “Why am I not working? My heart hurts because I’m useless. Have you ever begged for money, knowing you wouldn’t get it?”
“Yes, but what do you mean by hopelessly?” Raskolnikov asked.

“I mean, you know for sure no one will help, but you ask anyway. Why would they give me money? They know I can’t pay it back. Mr. Lebeziatnikov says even science says not to feel sorry for people anymore. Still, sometimes I have nowhere else to go.”

“When my daughter got a yellow ticket, I had to ask for help. My daughter, Sonia, has a yellow passport,” Marmeladov explained, looking uneasy. The boys laughed, but Marmeladov didn’t care. “Call me a pig if you want,” he said.

“Yes, I am a pig, but my wife, Katerina Ivanovna, is a lady. She is smart and kind. But she doesn’t understand me. She even pulls my hair sometimes, but I don’t mind. I wish she cared about me more, but I know I am a beast by nature.”

“Sir, I have sold my wife’s stockings for drink. We live in a cold room. She works all day, even though she is sick and coughing blood. We have three children. The more I drink, the more I feel her pain. That’s why I drink — to suffer more,” Marmeladov said, putting his head down.

“You look troubled, young man,” Marmeladov said. “Let me tell you about my wife. She went to a fancy school and once won a gold medal for dancing, but now she is poor and proud. She married her first husband for love, but he gambled and died, leaving her with three kids. I married her when she had nowhere else to go. At first, I stayed away from drink, but after losing my job, I started drinking again. Now we live in a crowded, dirty place owned by Amalia Fyodorovna Lippevechsel. My own daughter, Sonia, had almost no education. She tried to sew shirts for money, but didn’t get paid. The children were hungry. One day Sonia left, and when she came back, she laid thirty roubles on the table. Katerina Ivanovna hugged her and cried. I was drunk, just lying there.”

“After that, some people told bad stories about Sonia, and she had to live somewhere else, at the Kapernaumovs’, who are very poor and all have cleft palates. I tried to get my job back from Ivan Afanasyvitch, and he helped me. When I told my family, everyone was so happy.”

“That was five weeks ago. Katerina Ivanovna and Sonia were so nice to me. They made me coffee, found money for new clothes, and cooked a special dinner. Sonia only visited after dark. Katerina Ivanovna even invited the landlady for coffee. She told everyone how important my job was. When I brought home my first pay, she called me her ‘little poppet’ and even pinched my cheek.”

“Maybe you think this is funny,” Marmeladov said, “but it wasn’t funny to me. I dreamed of making things better for my family. But the very next day, I stole the rest of our money, left home, and lost my job again. Now look at me — I even traded my uniform for these old clothes.”
“This morning I went to see Sonia to ask for money for a drink,” Marmeladov laughed sadly.
“She gave me her last thirty copecks. She just looked at me, didn’t say a word. I took her money for drink! Who could feel sorry for someone like me?” he cried.

Marmeladov stood up and said, “Don’t pity me! I should be punished, not pitied! But I know God will forgive even people like me, and Sonia too. He will call everyone, even the weak and the bad, and forgive us all. Then we will understand everything. Even Katerina Ivanovna will understand.”
Suddenly, Marmeladov said to Raskolnikov, “Let’s go. Take me home to Katerina Ivanovna.”
Raskolnikov helped Marmeladov walk home. Marmeladov was scared, not of being hit, but of Katerina Ivanovna’s sad eyes and the hungry children. He said, “Let her hit me, it helps her feel better.”
They climbed up to a tiny, messy room at the top of the house. The room was filled with old clothes and very little furniture. There was noise and shouting from the other rooms.

Katerina Ivanovna was walking back and forth, looking sick and worried. She didn’t notice them come in. The youngest child, a little girl, was asleep on the floor. A boy was crying in the corner, and an older girl tried to comfort him while watching their mother. Marmeladov dropped to his knees in the doorway, pushing Raskolnikov ahead. Katerina Ivanovna saw her husband and screamed.
“He’s back! The criminal! Where’s the money? Where are your clothes?” she yelled, searching his pockets.
She found nothing, and in anger, she grabbed his hair and dragged him into the room. Marmeladov let her.
“This is a comfort to me, sir,” Marmeladov said as he was pulled by his hair.
The children cried. Katerina Ivanovna shouted, “He’s drunk it all! We’re hungry!” She turned on Raskolnikov, “Have you been drinking with him? Go away!”

Raskolnikov quickly left. Other people from the house peeked in, laughing at the scene. Amalia Lippevechsel, the landlady, yelled for Katerina Ivanovna to leave soon. Quietly, Raskolnikov put some coins on the window for them before leaving.
On the stairs, Raskolnikov thought, “Maybe I shouldn’t have left them the money, but Sonia needs it.” He went home, thinking about how hard Sonia’s life was.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov wondered, “What if people really aren’t so bad, and all these worries are just in my head?”

Raskolnikov woke up late after a bad night of sleep. He did not feel rested and was in a bad mood. He looked around his tiny, messy room and hated it. The room was very small, with old yellow wallpaper peeling off the walls. The ceiling was so low that tall people would bump their heads. There were three old wobbly chairs, a little table with dusty books and papers, and a big, torn sofa where Raskolnikov slept, wrapped in his old coat. He used all his linen as a pillow.

Raskolnikov liked being alone and did not want to see anyone, not even the servant girl, Nastasya, who sometimes cleaned his room. His landlady had stopped sending him food because he had not paid rent, but he did not complain. Nastasya was happy to do less work and only cleaned his room once a week. That morning, she woke him up.
“Get up! It’s past nine. I brought you some tea—are you hungry?” Nastasya asked.
Raskolnikov opened his eyes and saw Nastasya.
“Is that from the landlady?” he asked, sitting up slowly.
“No, it’s from me,” Nastasya replied.
She put a cracked teapot with weak tea and two lumps of sugar in front of him.
Raskolnikov searched his pockets for coins. “Nastasya, please buy me a loaf of bread and some cheap sausage.”
“I’ll get the bread, but wouldn’t you like some cabbage soup instead of sausage? I saved some for you yesterday, but you came home late. It’s good soup.”
After Nastasya brought him the soup, she sat down and started talking. She liked to chat.
“Praskovya Pavlovna (the landlady) wants to tell the police about you,” she said.
Raskolnikov frowned.
“The police? Why?”
“You don’t pay your rent, and you won’t leave the room. That’s why,” said Nastasya.
“That’s too much,” Raskolnikov grumbled. “I’ll talk to her today.”
“She’s silly, but why do you just lie here and do nothing? You used to go teach children. Why not now?”
“I am doing something...” Raskolnikov answered quietly.
“What are you doing?”
“Work...”
“What work?”
“I am thinking,” he said seriously.
Nastasya laughed so hard she almost got sick.
“Have you made any money from thinking?”
“I can’t go out for lessons without boots. And I’m tired of it.”
“Don’t be so picky,” said Nastasya.
“They pay so little. What’s the use?” Raskolnikov said.
“You want to get rich all at once?”
Raskolnikov looked at her strangely.
“Yes, I want a fortune,” he said.
“Don’t be so hasty! Should I get the bread or not?”
“As you please,” said Raskolnikov.
“Oh, I forgot! A letter came for you yesterday,” Nastasya said.
“A letter? From whom?”
“I don’t know. I paid the postman three copecks for it. Will you pay me back?”
“Then bring it! Please!” Raskolnikov cried, suddenly very excited.
Nastasya gave him the letter. It was from his mother, Pulcheria Raskolnikov. He turned pale because he had not received a letter in a long time and felt nervous.
“Nastasya, please leave me alone. Here is your money—now go!” he said.
Raskolnikov waited until Nastasya left. He kissed the letter, looked at his mother’s handwriting, and finally opened it. The letter was long.

The letter said:  
“My dear Rodya,  
It has been two months since I last wrote, and I worry about you every day. You are all Dounia (your sister) and I have. I was sad to hear you left university and lost your job. I could not help you much because my pension is small. The money we sent you before was borrowed from Mr. Vahrushin, a friend of your father’s. Now, thank God, things are better. Dounia has been living with me for six weeks. Her troubles with the Svidrigaïlov family are over, and I will tell you everything.  
When you asked about Dounia’s problems at the Svidrigaïlovs, I could not tell you the truth because you might have come here, and that would have been hard for you. Dounia took a governess job and got a hundred roubles in advance, but this was mostly to send you sixty roubles you needed. At first, Mr. Svidrigaïlov was rude to Dounia, but later we found out he liked her and tried to hide it. Finally, he asked Dounia to run away with him, but she refused. She could not leave right away because of the debt and to protect Marfa Petrovna, his wife.  
One day, Marfa Petrovna heard her husband talking to Dounia in the garden and blamed Dounia for everything. She even slapped Dounia and sent her away in a cart in the rain. We were very sad and people in town gossiped about us. Marfa Petrovna told everyone bad things about Dounia, and we could not go out without being stared at. But later, Mr. Svidrigaïlov showed his wife a letter from Dounia proving she was innocent. The servants also told the truth. Marfa Petrovna was sorry, asked Dounia to forgive her, and went to every house to say Dounia was innocent.  
Now people respect Dounia again, and she was asked to teach in many families, but she said no. Then something wonderful happened—Dounia has a suitor! His name is Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin, a government worker and a distant relative of Marfa Petrovna. He met us, wrote a polite letter, and asked to marry Dounia. He is forty-five but well-off and respectable. Dounia thought about it a long time and prayed, then said yes. He will soon go to Petersburg for work and wants to open a legal office.  
Rodya, this is good for you too. Pyotr Petrovitch said you might help him as a secretary, and Dounia hopes you can become his partner one day. We did not tell him our plans because we want you to feel equal, not like you need charity. After Dounia and Pyotr Petrovitch marry, I think it is better if I live by myself, so I do not get in the way. But the best news is that Dounia and I will come to Petersburg very soon—maybe in a week! We will see you after almost three years. Dounia is very excited. I hope to send you some money before we leave, maybe twenty-five or thirty roubles, but we need to save for travel.  
Please love Dounia as she loves you. You are everything to us. If you are happy, we will be happy. Do you still say your prayers, Rodya? I worry, but I pray for you. Remember when you were little and prayed with me.  
Goodbye, my dear boy. I hug you with all my heart.”
“Yours till death,”
“Pulcheria Raskolnikov.”

As he read the letter, Raskolnikov’s face was wet with tears. When he finished, he looked pale and upset. He lay down and thought for a long time, his heart beating fast. He felt trapped in his little room, so he put on his hat and went outside, not caring if anyone saw him. He walked quickly, talking to himself as he went, and some people thought he was drunk.

Raskolnikov read his mother’s letter and felt upset. He decided right away that he would never allow his sister Dounia to marry Mr. Luzhin. “No, mother, no, Dounia, you can’t trick me!” he thought. He was angry that they made this big decision without asking him. He was sure they thought it was all settled, but he would stop the marriage. He didn’t like Mr. Luzhin at all, even though his mother wrote that Mr. Luzhin was a smart businessman with a good job and money. Dounia said he “seemed kind,” but Raskolnikov did not trust him.

Raskolnikov wondered why his mother wrote about “our most rising generation.” Maybe she wanted him to like Mr. Luzhin. He tried to guess if his mother and Dounia talked openly about the marriage or just kept quiet and understood each other without words. He thought his mother felt bad about letting Dounia marry for his sake. Raskolnikov felt bitter and angry.
Raskolnikov got more upset as he thought about Mr. Luzhin. If he had seen Mr. Luzhin right then, he might have done something terrible.

Raskolnikov thought that Mr. Luzhin acted like a kind man by sending their luggage ahead, but he made Dounia and her mother travel uncomfortably and cheaply. Their mother even had to borrow money to make the trip. Mr. Luzhin seemed selfish, making them pay for everything but a few small things. Raskolnikov was angry that his mother and sister didn’t see this, or maybe they just didn’t want to. He worried that after the wedding, things would only get worse for them. He wondered how his mother would live in Petersburg with so little money. She knitted shawls to earn a little, but it wasn’t enough. Raskolnikov thought she was hoping Mr. Luzhin would help her, but he doubted that would happen.

Raskolnikov wondered how Dounia could agree to marry someone like Mr. Luzhin. He remembered how strong and brave she was, and that she would never do something bad just for money. She could put up with a lot, but he knew she was marrying Mr. Luzhin to help her family, not herself. Dounia would never sell her freedom for nice things, but to make her brother and mother happy, she would sacrifice herself. Raskolnikov realized he was the main reason for her choice. He thought about how sad and hard her life might be with Mr. Luzhin, and he decided he would never allow it. “I won’t have your sacrifice, Dounia, I won’t have it, mother! It shall not be as long as I am alive!”

Suddenly Raskolnikov stopped and thought, “But what can I do to stop the marriage? What right do I have? I am living off their money right now. How can I help them?” He realized his mother and sister were suffering while he did nothing. He worried about what would happen to them in ten years if nothing changed.
Raskolnikov kept asking himself these painful questions. He knew he couldn’t just sit and worry anymore; he had to do something. He needed to make a decision soon.
He suddenly shouted, “Or just give up on life completely! Live quietly and forget about everything!”
Then he remembered what Marmeladov once said: “Every man must have somewhere to turn.”
A new thought came into Raskolnikov’s mind, one he had before but now seemed even stronger and scarier. It felt real this time, and it made his head hurt.

He looked around and wanted to sit down. He saw a bench ahead and hurried to it. On the way, he noticed a young girl walking in front of him. She looked strange. She wore a torn dress and walked unsteadily, waving her arms. She seemed only about fifteen or sixteen, with a pretty face but looking tired and sick. Raskolnikov realized she was very drunk. She sat down heavily on the bench and closed her eyes.

Raskolnikov didn’t sit down but watched her, not sure what to do. The street was almost empty because it was so hot. He noticed a fat, well-dressed man standing nearby, clearly interested in the girl. The man looked annoyed at Raskolnikov for being there. Raskolnikov got angry and decided to confront him.
“Hey! You Svidrigaïlov! What do you want here?” Raskolnikov shouted at the man.
“What do you mean?” the man replied, angry.
“Get away, that’s what I mean,” Raskolnikov said.
“How dare you, you low fellow!” the man answered, raising his cane.
Raskolnikov rushed at him, but just then a policeman grabbed Raskolnikov and stood between them.
“That’s enough, no fighting here. Who are you?” the policeman asked Raskolnikov.
The policeman looked serious but kind.
“You’re just the person I need,” Raskolnikov said. “I’m a student, Raskolnikov. Come, I have something to show you.”
Raskolnikov took the policeman over to the bench.

He explained that the girl was very drunk and looked like someone had tricked her. Her dress was torn and put on wrong, as if someone else had dressed her. The fat man wanted to take her away while she was helpless. Raskolnikov said they needed to help her get home safely.
The policeman quickly understood and looked at the girl with pity.
“Poor thing!” he said, shaking his head. He tried to ask her where she lived, but she just waved her hand sleepily.
Raskolnikov gave the policeman some money. “Call a cab and take her home. But first, we need to know her address!”
The policeman took the money and spoke gently, “Miss, where do you live? I’ll get you a cab and take you home.”
“Go away! They won’t let me alone,” the girl mumbled.
“How sad! Shameful!” the policeman said, feeling sorry for her.
The policeman told Raskolnikov it would be hard to help her if she didn’t say where she lived. He looked at Raskolnikov, surprised that a poor-looking man gave him money.
“Did you meet her far from here?” he asked.
“She was walking in front of me and sat down here,” Raskolnikov answered.
“What a shame,” said the policeman. “She looks like she comes from a good family. There are many poor girls like her now.”
Raskolnikov said the main thing was to keep her safe from the bad man, who was still waiting nearby.
The fat man heard Raskolnikov and looked angry but just walked farther away.
“We can keep her safe if she tells us where to take her,” the policeman said, trying again to get her address.
Suddenly, the girl stood up and walked off, still unsteady. She said, “Oh, shameful wretches, they won’t let me alone!” The fat man followed her at a distance.
“Don’t worry, I won’t let him have her,” the policeman said, and he went after them.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov felt strange and changed his mind.
He shouted, “Hey, come back!”
The policeman turned around.
“Let them go! What does it matter to you?” Raskolnikov said.
The policeman looked at him, confused. Raskolnikov laughed.
The policeman walked after the girl and the man, probably thinking Raskolnikov was crazy.
“He took my money,” Raskolnikov muttered. “Why did I try to help? Do I have that right? Who am I to give away money that isn’t mine?”
Even though he said these things, Raskolnikov felt very sad. He sat on the bench, lost in thought, wishing he could forget everything and start his life again.

“Poor girl,” he thought, looking at the empty spot on the bench. He imagined she would wake up, cry, and get in trouble at home. Maybe she would be thrown out or have to sneak around. He thought about girls like her ending up sick or in trouble, their lives ruined. He wondered if people just accepted that some girls had to suffer so others could be safe.
Suddenly he remembered, “Why did I come out? Oh yes, I was going to see Razumihin after reading the letter. But why did I want to see him?”

Raskolnikov found it odd. Razumihin was his old friend from university, though Raskolnikov didn’t have many friends. He was quiet, proud, and kept to himself. He worked hard and was respected but not liked.

With Razumihin, though, he was friendlier. Razumihin was cheerful, kind, and helpful to everyone. He was tall, thin, and strong, with black hair and a simple way of living. He could handle any trouble and found ways to earn money, even though he was poor. Razumihin had to leave university for a while but was working hard to return. Raskolnikov hadn’t seen him in four months. The last time they met, Raskolnikov avoided him, and Razumihin didn’t want to bother him.

Raskolnikov was thinking about going to see his friend Razumihin to ask for help or work, maybe to get some lessons to teach. But he wondered, “What good would that do? Even if Razumihin helps me and gives me money, what will I do then? That’s not what I want.” He felt it was silly to go to Razumihin now.
Raskolnikov kept wondering why he wanted to go to Razumihin. It seemed like a simple thing, but it bothered him a lot. He felt like it meant something important or scary.
He asked himself, “Can Razumihin really help me fix everything?”
After thinking for a long time, a strange idea popped into his head.
“I’ll go to Razumihin’s,” he said, deciding. “But not now. I’ll go after It happens, when everything will be new again.”
Suddenly, he realized what he was thinking.
“After It? Is It really going to happen?” he cried, jumping up. He started to go home, but the thought of his small, sad room made him feel sick, so he just walked around with no plan.

Raskolnikov felt cold and shaky, even though it was hot outside. He tried to look at things around him to get his mind off his worries, but it didn’t work. He wandered all over the city, looking at gardens, flowers, and people. He counted his money and saw he had thirty copecks. He remembered giving money to the Marmeladovs. He felt hungry, so he went into a tavern, drank a little vodka, and ate a pie. The vodka made him sleepy. He tried to go home, but he was too tired, so he lay down in the grass and fell asleep.

Raskolnikov had a terrible dream. He dreamed he was a little boy, about seven years old, walking with his father in his hometown. They passed a big, noisy tavern where people were singing, shouting, and fighting. Raskolnikov always felt scared of that place. Near the tavern was a graveyard with a church where he used to go with his parents. In the graveyard was the grave of his grandmother and his little brother, who died as a baby. In the dream, he and his father were walking past the tavern, and there was a big crowd. People were happy and singing. In front of the tavern was a big cart, but instead of a strong horse, there was a small, weak brown horse.
A young peasant named Mikolka shouted, “Get in! I’ll take you all in the cart!”
The crowd laughed at Mikolka.
“How can that little horse pull all of us?” they joked.
Mikolka climbed into the cart and grabbed the reins. “She’ll gallop! I’ll make her!” He picked up a whip to hit the horse.
People kept getting into the cart, laughing. They hit the poor horse, but she could barely move. Mikolka got angry and whipped her harder.
Little Raskolnikov cried, “Father, they are beating the poor horse!”
His father tried to pull him away, saying, “They are just drunk, don’t look!” But Raskolnikov broke free and ran to the horse. She was struggling and gasping for breath.
Mikolka yelled, “Beat her to death! I’ll do it!”
Some people in the crowd tried to stop him, but Mikolka didn’t listen.
The horse tried to kick, but she was too weak. Some boys ran up and whipped her even more, even in the eyes. The people in the cart sang and laughed.
Raskolnikov cried and tried to stop them. Someone hit him with a whip, but he didn’t care. He ran to the horse and hugged her.
Mikolka grabbed a heavy stick from the cart and hit the horse hard.
Mikolka hit the horse again and again with the stick. The poor horse tried to pull the cart, but she couldn’t. The crowd kept shouting.
Mikolka picked up an iron bar and hit the horse. The horse fell down and died.
Some young men ran to the horse and hit her, too. Mikolka stood there with the bar, angry.
Little Raskolnikov ran through the crowd, hugged the dead horse, and kissed her. Then he rushed at Mikolka, but his father picked him up and carried him away.
His father said, “Let’s go home.”
Raskolnikov sobbed, “Father! Why did they kill the poor horse?”
His father said, “They are drunk and cruel. It’s not our business.” Raskolnikov felt like he couldn’t breathe, and then he woke up.
Raskolnikov woke up gasping and scared.
“Thank goodness, it was just a dream,” he said, sitting up and breathing hard.
He felt weak and confused, putting his head in his hands.
“Oh God!” he cried. “Could I really do something so horrible—hit someone with an axe and steal? Could I really do it?”
He was shaking with fear.

“Why am I like this?” he wondered. “I know I could never do such a thing. Why do I keep thinking about it? Yesterday, when I tried my experiment, I realized I couldn’t do it. So why am I still thinking about it?”
“No, I can’t do it! Even if my reasons make sense, I just can’t. Why do I still...?”

He stood up and looked around, surprised to be there. He felt lighter, as if a big weight was gone. He felt peaceful for the first time in a long while. “God, show me what to do. I give up this terrible idea,” he prayed.
He crossed the bridge and looked calmly at the river and the sunset. He felt free, like something bad had left his heart.

Later, Raskolnikov remembered that after all his worry, he didn’t go home the shortest way. He wondered why he had walked through the Hay Market, a place he didn’t need to go. He realized that something very important happened there, just when he was in the right mood for it to change his life.

It was about nine o’clock when Raskolnikov walked through the Hay Market. People were packing up their things and going home. Raskolnikov liked this place because no one cared about his old clothes. He saw a huckster and his wife talking with Lizaveta Ivanovna, the younger sister of the old pawnbroker, Alyona Ivanovna. Lizaveta was tall, shy, and afraid of her sister, who was mean to her. Lizaveta was listening to the huckster and his wife very carefully. When Raskolnikov saw her, he felt shocked, though it wasn’t a strange meeting.
The huckster said, “Lizaveta Ivanovna, come tomorrow about seven. They’ll be here too.”
“Tomorrow?” Lizaveta said, thinking about it.
The huckster’s wife said, “You’re so scared of Alyona Ivanovna! She isn’t even your real sister.”
The husband added, “Don’t tell Alyona Ivanovna this time. Just come to us. It will be good for you.”
“Should I come?” asked Lizaveta.
“About seven o’clock tomorrow. You can decide for yourself,” said the huckster.
“And we’ll have tea,” his wife said.
“All right, I’ll come,” Lizaveta said, and walked away slowly.

Raskolnikov had passed by, trying not to be noticed, but he had heard everything. Suddenly, he realized with horror that tomorrow at seven o’clock, Lizaveta would be out, and the old woman, Alyona Ivanovna, would be home alone.
Raskolnikov was only a few steps from home. He went in feeling like everything was already decided for him. He couldn’t think anymore.
He realized that if he had waited years, he wouldn’t find a better moment. Tomorrow at seven o’clock, the old woman would be alone, and no one would know.

Later, Raskolnikov learned why the huckster and his wife wanted Lizaveta (Alyona Ivanovna’s half-sister) to come over. It was nothing special. A poor family was selling women’s clothes and things. Lizaveta often helped sell things for people because she was honest and made fair deals. She was quiet, shy, and always did what people asked.

Lately, Raskolnikov had been feeling superstitious. He saw strange meanings in things that happened around him. Last winter, his friend Pokorev had told him about Alyona Ivanovna, the old pawnbroker, in case he ever wanted to pawn something. Raskolnikov waited a long time before visiting her because he was getting by with teaching jobs. Six weeks ago, he remembered the address and took a small gold ring, a gift from his sister, to Alyona Ivanovna. When he saw her, he disliked her right away, even though he didn’t know much about her. She gave him two roubles. On his way home, he stopped at a tiny tavern for tea and sat thinking deeply. A strange idea wouldn’t leave his mind.

At the next table, a student and a young officer were talking. They had played billiards and were now drinking tea. Raskolnikov heard the student mention Alyona Ivanovna and give the officer her address. This felt odd to Raskolnikov since he had just come from her. The student started telling stories about Alyona Ivanovna.
“She’s great for money,” said the student. “She’s very rich and will take any pledge, even for just a rouble. But she’s a mean old woman.”

The student explained how Alyona Ivanovna was nasty and took away people’s things if they were late with payments. She only gave a little money for valuable items and charged high interest. He also said she had a sister named Lizaveta, whom Alyona often beat and treated like a little child, even though Lizaveta was very tall.

The student and officer talked more about Lizaveta. The student laughed about her, and the officer asked if Lizaveta could do some mending for him. Raskolnikov listened carefully. Lizaveta was younger than Alyona and was her half-sister. She was thirty-five years old, very tall, and not married. She worked all day and night for Alyona, cooking, cleaning, and sewing, but Alyona kept all the money. Lizaveta knew Alyona’s will would leave her nothing but old furniture; all the money would go to a monastery. Lizaveta wore old shoes but was neat and clean. The student thought it funny that Lizaveta was often pregnant.
“But you said she was ugly?” asked the officer.
“She’s very dark and looks strange,” said the student, “but really, she has a kind and gentle face. Many people like her. She’s sweet and always willing to help.”
“You seem to like her yourself,” the officer laughed.

“She’s just odd,” the student replied. “But I’ll tell you what—I could kill that old woman and take her money without feeling bad.” The officer laughed, but Raskolnikov shivered. It was a strange thing to hear.

The student went on, “Think about it. The old woman is mean and does nothing good. She might die soon anyway. With her money, so many people could be helped. If someone killed her and used her money for good, would that be wrong? One bad act for hundreds of good deeds. Her life isn’t worth much; she even hurt Lizaveta’s finger badly.”
The officer said, “She doesn’t deserve to live, but that’s just how things are.”

“But we should fix what’s wrong in nature,” the student argued. “If people never changed things, there would be no great people. Some things, like conscience and duty, can be confusing. Let me ask you—”
“No, let me ask,” the officer interrupted.
“Would you kill the old woman?” the officer asked.
“Of course not! I was just talking. I wouldn’t really do it.”
“Then if you wouldn’t do it, maybe it isn’t right,” said the officer. “Let’s play another game.”

Raskolnikov felt very nervous. He had heard talk like this before, but it was strange to hear it right after thinking about Alyona Ivanovna himself. This talk in the tavern stuck in his mind and made a big difference to him later, almost as if it was a sign.

When Raskolnikov got home, he fell on his sofa and sat still for an hour. It got dark, but he didn’t light a candle. He couldn’t remember what he was thinking. After a while, he felt sick and cold, and was glad to lie down and sleep.
He slept for a long time. Nastasya (the servant) came in at ten the next morning and had trouble waking him. She brought him tea and bread.
“He sleeps so much!” Nastasya said, annoyed.
Raskolnikov got up, his head hurting. He walked around, then lay down again.
“Going to sleep again? Are you sick?” Nastasya asked.
He didn’t answer.
“Want some tea?” she asked.
“Later,” he mumbled, turning to the wall.
Nastasya watched him a moment, then left. She came back at two with soup. The tea was untouched. She shook him, now upset.
“Why are you lying there like a log?” she shouted.
He sat up, then stared at the floor, not speaking.
“Are you sick or not?” she asked again. He didn’t answer. “You should go outside. Will you eat?”
“Later. You can go,” he said weakly.
Nastasya looked at him sadly and left.

After a few minutes, Raskolnikov looked at the tea and soup. He finally took some bread and ate a few spoonfuls, not hungry but just because he had to. His head hurt less. Then he lay down again, but couldn’t sleep. He started daydreaming, imagining he was in Egypt by a cool spring. Suddenly, he heard a clock. He jumped up, worried that he had slept too long and done nothing. He listened at the door and on the stairs. Everything was quiet. He felt nervous and hurried. He had only a few things to prepare. He made a noose from an old shirt and sewed it inside his coat under his arm. This was for carrying an axe secretly. He had planned this before.

Next, he reached under his sofa and pulled out a fake pledge he had made earlier. It was a block of wood wrapped in paper, with a piece of iron to make it heavy. He wrapped it up so it would take a while to open. This was meant to distract Alyona Ivanovna. Just as he finished, he heard someone outside.
“It’s past six.”
“Oh no!”

Raskolnikov grabbed his hat and crept downstairs quietly. He still needed to get the axe from the kitchen. He didn’t trust his knife and had decided to use an axe. He always doubted his plan, but he kept thinking about it.

He thought about the details. Getting the axe was easy, since Nastasya often left the kitchen door open. He could just take it and put it back later. But what if Nastasya came back and noticed it was missing? He would have to wait for her to leave again. Things could go wrong, but he didn’t worry much about these small problems.

Raskolnikov often wondered why most criminals are caught so easily. He decided it was because they lose control and make mistakes, especially right before and after the crime. He believed he would not make those mistakes, because he thought his plan wasn’t really a crime. He trusted his own thinking—but when the time came, things happened differently than he expected.

Right away, his plan started to go wrong. When Raskolnikov went to the kitchen to get the axe, he saw Nastasya was there, hanging up laundry. She watched him as he walked by, so he couldn’t take the axe. He felt defeated.
“Why did I think she wouldn’t be there?” he thought angrily.

He stood in the gateway, not sure what to do. He didn’t want to go outside or back to his room. “What a chance I’ve lost!” he muttered. Then he noticed something shiny under a bench in the porter’s room. No one was around. He tiptoed in and saw it was an axe. He quickly grabbed it, put it in his coat, and left. “When you can’t think of a plan, luck helps,” he thought, feeling better.
He walked calmly, not wanting to look suspicious. Then he remembered he should have bought a cap to wear instead of his old hat, but it was too late.
He checked the time in a shop window. It was ten past seven. He needed to hurry, but he also had to take a longer way to approach the house from the other side.
As he walked, Raskolnikov was not as scared as he thought he would be. His mind wandered to things like fountains and gardens in the city, but soon he remembered what he was about to do.
He thought, “Maybe people going to be executed also notice every little thing around them.” But he tried not to think about it. Now he was close to the house.
As he got to the gate, a big hay wagon came in, hiding him from view. He slipped inside, and nobody saw him. The stairs to Alyona Ivanovna’s room were nearby.

He pressed his hand to his heart, checked the axe, and quietly climbed the stairs. All the doors were closed. Painters were working in a flat on the first floor, but they didn’t notice him. He kept going up.

He reached the fourth floor. The flat across from Alyona’s was empty. The flat below also seemed empty. He wondered if he should leave, but didn’t answer himself. He listened at Alyona Ivanovna’s door. Everything was silent. He checked the staircase, then tried to calm himself. “Am I too pale? Does it show that I’m nervous? Maybe I should wait until my heart stops pounding,” he thought.
But his heart only beat faster. He rang the bell softly, then again, louder.

No answer. He listened at the door. Suddenly he heard someone moving quietly inside, as if listening, just like he was. He made a small noise on purpose, then rang again, calmly. He would always remember this moment. Soon, he heard the latch open.

Raskolnikov knocked on Alyona Ivanovna’s (the old pawnbroker lady) door. She opened it just a little and looked at him with sharp, suspicious eyes. Raskolnikov got nervous. He grabbed the door so she couldn’t shut it.
Alyona Ivanovna didn’t let go of the door handle, so Raskolnikov almost pulled her out into the hallway. She stepped back, scared, and stared at him, unable to speak.
“Good evening, Alyona Ivanovna,” Raskolnikov said, but his voice shook. “I brought you something to pawn. Let’s go inside, where there’s light.”
Raskolnikov walked into the apartment without waiting for her to invite him. Alyona Ivanovna followed, finally able to talk.
“Who is it? What do you want?” she asked.
“It’s me, Raskolnikov. I brought you the pledge I promised,” he said, showing her a small package.
Alyona Ivanovna looked at the pledge, then stared at Raskolnikov suspiciously. He started to feel scared, like she might know what he was thinking.
“Why are you looking at me like that? Take it if you want. If not, I’ll go somewhere else,” he said angrily.
Alyona Ivanovna relaxed a little and looked at the pledge again.
“What is it?” she asked.
“A silver cigarette case,” Raskolnikov replied.
She held out her hand.
“You look pale. Your hands are shaking. Are you sick?” she asked.
“I have a fever,” he answered. “And I haven’t eaten.”
Alyona Ivanovna took the pledge from him.
“What is it?” she asked, checking it again.
“Just look at it. It’s silver,” Raskolnikov insisted.
“It doesn’t look like silver. And why have you tied it up like this?”

Alyona Ivanovna turned to the window and tried to untie the package. While her back was turned, Raskolnikov quietly unbuttoned his coat and took hold of the axe hidden inside. His hands shook so much he was afraid he might drop it.
Alyona Ivanovna got annoyed, “Why did you tie it up so much?” She moved closer to him.
Raskolnikov knew he couldn’t wait any longer. He pulled out the axe and hit Alyona Ivanovna on the head with the blunt side. He felt like he was acting without thinking, like he was in a dream.

The old woman was very short, so the axe hit the top of her head. She cried out softly, then fell to the floor, holding her head. Raskolnikov hit her again and again until she was dead. Her eyes stared wide open.

Raskolnikov put the axe down and searched her pocket for the keys. He was careful not to touch the blood. He ran into her bedroom, a small room full of religious pictures. There was a bed, a chest of drawers, and a box. As he tried the keys on the chest, he suddenly worried that Alyona Ivanovna might still be alive. He ran back, ready to use the axe again, but saw she was really dead. He noticed a string around her neck and tried to pull it off, but it was stuck. With difficulty, he cut it off and took a small purse and two crosses. He put the purse in his pocket and threw the crosses on her body.

Raskolnikov hurried back to the bedroom to open the chest, but the keys wouldn’t fit. Then he remembered the big key probably fit a box under the bed. He found a red box and used the key to open it. Inside were clothes and some hidden things. He wiped his bloody hands on a red coat, thinking the blood wouldn’t show.

When he looked under the clothes, he found a gold watch and other jewelry—probably things people had given to Alyona Ivanovna for money. He stuffed as much as he could into his pockets, but he didn’t have time to take much.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov heard footsteps in the other room. He froze. Then he heard a faint cry, like a moan. He waited, holding his breath. Suddenly, he grabbed the axe and ran out of the bedroom.

In the middle of the room stood Lizaveta (Alyona Ivanovna’s sister), holding a big bundle. She stared at her dead sister, too shocked to even scream. Raskolnikov ran at her with the axe. Lizaveta was so frightened she barely moved. Raskolnikov hit her with the axe, and she fell down dead. He grabbed her bundle, dropped it, and ran to the hallway.
Now Raskolnikov was even more afraid. He wanted to run away. He felt disgusted by what he had done and didn’t even want to go back for more things.

He started to feel foggy, like he was in a dream. He saw a bucket of water in the kitchen and decided to wash the blood off his hands and the axe. He cleaned everything as best he could, then checked his clothes for blood. He thought he should leave right away, but then something scared him even more.
The front door was open about six inches! He realized Alyona Ivanovna hadn’t locked it after he came in. That’s how Lizaveta got in, too.
He quickly closed and latched the door.
“No, I need to get out of here,” he thought.
He opened the door and listened on the stairs.
He waited and listened. He heard people shouting far away, then silence. He was about to leave when he heard someone else coming up the stairs.
Heavy, slow footsteps were coming up. Raskolnikov felt frozen in fear, like in a nightmare.
When the person reached the fourth floor, Raskolnikov slipped back inside the apartment and hooked the door shut. He crouched near the door, holding his breath.
The visitor panted, then rang the bell loudly.
Raskolnikov heard the bell and thought he heard something moving in the room. The visitor rang again and shook the door hard, making the hook rattle. Raskolnikov was scared the door would break.
The visitor shouted, “Are they asleep or murdered? Alyona Ivanovna! Lizaveta! Open the door!”
The man rang and shook the door even harder.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov heard quick steps on the stairs—someone else was coming.
“Good evening, Koch,” the new person said to the first visitor.
Raskolnikov thought the new person sounded young.
“Who are you?” Koch said. “How do you know me?”
“I beat you at billiards the other day,” the young man replied.
“Oh!”
“So they aren’t home? That’s strange. I came on business.”
“Me too,” said Koch.
“I needed money!” the young man complained.
“Why did she ask me to come? She never goes out,” Koch said, annoyed.
“Should we ask the porter where she went?” the young man suggested.
“What?”
“Ask the porter when she’ll be back.”
“Maybe, but she never goes anywhere.”
Koch shook the door handle again.
“Let’s go,” he said.
“Wait!” the young man said. “Do you hear the hook rattling? The door isn’t locked from outside—it’s hooked from inside.”
“So?”
“That means someone is home! If they were all out, the door would be locked with a key, not hooked. They’re inside but not opening the door!”
“That’s true!” Koch said, surprised. He shook the door harder.
“Don’t pull! Something’s wrong. We should get the porter,” the young man said.
“All right,” Koch agreed.
“You wait here. I’ll get the porter,” said the young man.
“Why?”
“Just wait. I’m studying law, so I know something’s wrong!” the young man shouted, running downstairs.
Koch stayed. He rang the bell softly and checked the door handle and keyhole, but the key was on the inside, so he couldn’t see anything.
Raskolnikov held onto the axe, feeling almost crazy. He thought about shouting or fighting when they came in. He just wanted them to hurry up.
Koch got restless and finally left to go downstairs too. The stairs grew quiet.
“What should I do?” Raskolnikov thought.
He unhooked the door and left quietly, closing it behind him. He went down the stairs.
After three flights, he heard a loud voice below. He didn’t know where to hide and almost went back to the apartment.
Suddenly, a man ran out of a flat below, shouting, “Catch him! Mitka! Mitka!” The man’s voice disappeared into the yard.

Right after that, several men started coming up the stairs, talking loudly. Raskolnikov heard the young man’s voice among them. He felt desperate. They were almost upon him—then he saw an open door to an empty apartment where painters had been working. He slipped inside and hid behind a wall just in time as the men ran upstairs.
When they were gone, Raskolnikov tiptoed out and hurried down the stairs.
He saw no one on the stairs or in the gateway. He walked quickly into the street.

Raskolnikov knew the men would soon find the bodies and realize the murderer had just been there. He was afraid to run, so he tried to walk calmly. He wondered if he should throw away the axe or take a cab, but both ideas seemed impossible.
Finally, he reached a busy street and felt a little safer, hidden among the crowd. But he was so tired he could hardly walk. Someone shouted at him for looking strange.
On the canal bank, he noticed there weren’t many people and worried he’d stand out. Even though he could barely walk, he went the long way home to be safe.

By the time he reached his building, he was barely aware of himself. On the stairs, he remembered the axe. He had to put it back without being seen. Luckily, the porter’s room was empty, so he put the axe back under the bench and covered it with wood. He didn’t meet anyone on the way to his room.
At last, in his own room, Raskolnikov fell on the sofa. He didn’t sleep, but lay there, his mind spinning with confused thoughts, unable to think clearly at all.
Raskolnikov lay on his bed for a long time. He was half-awake, half-asleep. He heard loud, sad cries from the street, just like he did every night after two o’clock. The noise woke him up.
“Oh, the drunk men are leaving the taverns. It must be after two o’clock,” Raskolnikov thought. He jumped up from the sofa.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov remembered everything that happened the day before. It all came back to him at once.
He felt cold and scared. His whole body shook, and his teeth chattered. He looked around his room and wondered how he came in the night before without locking the door or even taking off his hat.
Raskolnikov hurried to the window and checked his clothes for any signs of trouble. He was so cold that he took off all his clothes to look for stains. He checked everything three times.
He found some dried blood on the edge of his trousers. He cut off the dirty threads with a knife.

Then he remembered he still had the purse and things he took from the old woman’s box in his pockets! He quickly took everything out and stuffed it into a hole under the wallpaper in the corner. But then he thought, “Is that really hidden well?”
He had only planned to hide money, not small things. So he didn’t have a good hiding place.
Raskolnikov was so tired and cold that he wrapped himself in his old coat and sank into a feverish sleep.
After about five minutes, he woke up again and checked his clothes once more.
“I forgot the loop on the armhole!” he thought. He quickly tore it off, cut it up, and hid the pieces under his pillow.
He looked around the room to make sure he didn’t forget anything. He felt like his mind was getting weaker from the fever.
He noticed the rags he cut off his trousers were still lying on the floor.
Suddenly, he worried that maybe all his clothes had blood on them, but he just couldn’t see it. He remembered the purse had blood, so maybe his pocket did, too.
He turned his pocket inside out and saw blood stains.

“At least I noticed this myself,” he thought, feeling a little better. He tore out the lining of his pocket. Then he saw that his sock was bloody, too. He wondered what to do with all the dirty things.
Raskolnikov stood in the middle of the room, holding the rags and sock.
“Should I burn them? But I have no matches. Maybe I should just throw them away outside,” he thought. But he was too tired and cold. He lay down again.
For hours, he kept thinking he must get up and throw the things away, but he felt too weak to move.
Suddenly, someone knocked on the door loudly.
“Open up! Are you dead or alive in there?” shouted Nastasya (the servant). “It’s past ten!”
A man’s voice said, “Maybe he’s not home.”
Raskolnikov’s heart pounded as he sat up on the sofa.
He got up and unlatch the door. Nastasya and the porter stood there.
The porter handed Raskolnikov a folded paper. “A notice from the office,” he said.
“It’s a summons to the police,” the porter explained.
“To the police? Why?” Raskolnikov asked.
“I don’t know. You’re called, so you must go,” the porter replied.
Nastasya saw Raskolnikov was sick and told him he didn’t have to hurry. She noticed he was holding rags and a sock in his hand.
“Look at what he’s sleeping with! He acts like it’s treasure,” Nastasya joked, then giggled.
Raskolnikov quickly hid the rags under his coat. He wondered if he was going to be arrested. But Nastasya just offered to bring him tea.
“No, I’ll go right away,” Raskolnikov said, trying to stand.

As soon as they left, he checked the rags and sock again. He saw the stains weren’t easy to see because of the dirt. He opened the notice and slowly read it. It was a normal paper asking him to come to the police station at half-past nine.
“Why do I have to go to the police today?” Raskolnikov wondered, very worried.
He started dressing, wondering if he should put on the bloody sock. He put it on, then took it off in disgust, but then put it on again because he had no other socks.
Raskolnikov felt weak and shaky. He was afraid the police would trick him and make him confess everything.
On the stairs, he remembered he left the stolen things in the wall. He thought they might search his room while he was gone, but he was too tired to care and left anyway.
Outside, it was hot and bright. The sunlight hurt his eyes, and he felt dizzy.
The police station was not far away. Raskolnikov walked up the stairs, not wanting to ask anyone for help.
“Maybe I’ll just confess everything,” he thought as he reached the right floor.
The building was busy and hot. The rooms were crowded with people.
Raskolnikov waited, then walked into another room. He showed his notice to a clerk.
“You are a student?” the clerk asked.
“Yes, I used to be,” Raskolnikov answered.
The clerk told him to go into the next room, where the head clerk was.
Raskolnikov handed his paper to the head clerk, who said, “Wait a minute,” and kept working.
Raskolnikov felt a little better, thinking maybe it wasn’t what he feared.
He tried to stay calm and not make any mistakes.
Then an officer came in and sat down. He looked at Raskolnikov and seemed angry that he was so poorly dressed. The officer was the assistant superintendent, Ilya Petrovitch.
“What do you want?” Ilya Petrovitch shouted.
“I got a notice to come here,” Raskolnikov said.
“It’s about money you owe,” the head clerk said, giving Raskolnikov a paper to read.
Raskolnikov felt a huge wave of relief. He wasn’t in trouble for anything else, just for not paying money.
But Ilya Petrovitch was angry. “You were supposed to come at nine, and now it’s twelve!” he shouted.
“The notice just arrived,” Raskolnikov answered, feeling angry too. “And I’m sick with a fever.”
“Don’t shout!” said the officer.
“I’m not shouting. You are,” Raskolnikov replied.
“You don’t pay your debts! You’re a fine one!” Ilya Petrovitch yelled.
But Raskolnikov was just reading the paper. He didn’t understand what it was about.
The head clerk explained, “It’s about money you owe to your landlady. You must promise to pay later and not leave the city.”
“But she is my landlady!” Raskolnikov said.
Raskolnikov felt so happy it was only about money. He didn’t even care what happened next.
Suddenly, Ilya Petrovitch started shouting at a fancy lady, Luise Ivanovna, about trouble at her house the night before.
The more the officer yelled, the more the lady smiled and curtsied, trying to explain what happened. She said a visitor at her house caused a lot of trouble and broke things.
Soon, the real superintendent, Nikodim Fomitch, arrived. He was friendly and tried to calm everyone down.
Ilya Petrovitch told Nikodim Fomitch that Raskolnikov owed money and complained about him.
Nikodim Fomitch said, “Poverty is not a crime. Ilya Petrovitch just gets angry easily.”

Raskolnikov tried to explain that he was poor, sick, and owed money because his landlady trusted him. He said he once promised to marry her daughter, but the girl died. Now his landlady wanted him to pay.
“We don’t need your life story,” Ilya Petrovitch said rudely. “Just sign the paper.”
Nikodim Fomitch thought Ilya was being too harsh, but told Raskolnikov to write.
The head clerk told Raskolnikov to write that he could not pay now but promised to pay later.
“You can hardly hold the pen. Are you ill?” the clerk asked.
“Yes, I’m dizzy. Go on!” Raskolnikov said.
When he was done, Raskolnikov leaned on the table, pressing his head in his hands. For a moment, he wanted to just confess everything. But then he stopped.
He overheard Nikodim Fomitch and Ilya Petrovitch talking about the murders at the old woman’s house. They were trying to figure out what happened and who the killer was.
Raskolnikov tried to leave, but he fainted.
When he woke up, people helped him sit up and gave him water. Nikodim Fomitch asked if he was sick.
The head clerk said Raskolnikov had trouble even holding the pen.
“Have you been ill long?” Ilya Petrovitch asked.
“Since yesterday,” Raskolnikov said.
“Did you go out yesterday?”
“Yes.”
“Even though you were ill?”
“Yes.”
“What time?”
“About seven.”
“Where did you go?”
“Just along the street.”
“Very well, then. We will not keep you,” Ilya Petrovitch said.
Raskolnikov left the police station. As soon as he was outside, he felt better.
“They will search my room now. I know they suspect me,” he thought, hurrying home.
All his old fear came rushing back.

Raskolnikov (the main character) worried, “What if someone searched my room and found the things I hid?” But when he got to his room, it was empty. No one had touched anything, not even Nastasya (the housemaid). He was scared he had left the stolen things in the hiding place.

Quickly, Raskolnikov pulled out all the hidden items and stuffed them into his pockets. There were eight things: two little boxes with jewelry, four small leather cases, a chain, and something else wrapped in paper. He put them in his coat and pants pockets, trying to hide them well. He took the purse too. Then he hurried out, leaving the door open. He felt weak, but he knew he had to hide the evidence before someone came looking for him. He needed to act fast.

He had already decided to throw the stolen things into the canal, hoping the water would hide them forever. But as he walked along the canal, he saw too many people around—women washing clothes, boats, and crowds. He worried someone would see him, or that the boxes would float instead of sinking. Everyone seemed to be watching him, which made him even more nervous.

Then he thought it might be better to go to the big river, the Neva, where there were fewer people and he wouldn’t be noticed as much. He was surprised he hadn’t thought of this sooner and hurried on.

On the way, he wondered if he should go even farther, maybe to the quiet Islands and bury the things under a bush. But as he walked, he saw a quiet courtyard between two big walls. It looked empty and dirty, with rubbish everywhere. There was even a sign that said, “Standing here strictly forbidden.” Raskolnikov thought this would be a good place to hide the stolen things.
He looked around and saw a big stone by the wall. He could hear people walking on the street nearby, but they couldn’t see him unless they came into the yard. He knew he had to hurry.

He bent down, lifted the heavy stone, and put all the stolen things in the hole underneath. The purse was on top. Then he put the stone back, pressed the dirt around it with his foot, and made sure nothing looked strange.

Raskolnikov left the yard and walked into the square. For a moment, he felt a strange joy—he thought no one would ever find the things under the stone, and no one would suspect him. He even laughed a little as he walked, but soon he felt upset again when he remembered the policeman he had talked to before and the girl he had seen a few days ago.
As he walked, Raskolnikov felt like all his thoughts were spinning around one big problem, but he didn’t know what it was.
He got angry at himself and thought, “If it’s started, it’s started. I don’t care about a new life. Why did I lie today? Why did I try to please Ilya Petrovitch? None of that matters!”
Suddenly, he had a simple but confusing thought.

He realized, “If I planned all this, why didn’t I even look inside the purse to see what was in it? I went through so much trouble, but I never checked what I stole. I was ready to throw it all away without looking.”
He told himself it was because he was very sick and tired, and he hoped he would feel better soon. But he was sick of everything.

Raskolnikov kept walking, wanting something to distract him, but he didn’t know what. He started to hate everything and everyone around him. If anyone spoke to him, he felt like he might yell at them.

Suddenly, he found himself near Razumihin’s (his friend’s) house and wondered if he had come there on purpose or by accident. He decided to visit Razumihin anyway because he was too tired to go farther.
He went up to Razumihin’s room.
Razumihin opened the door. He looked surprised to see Raskolnikov, who looked tired and poorly dressed. Razumihin was wearing an old robe and slippers.
“Is it you?” Razumihin said, looking at his friend. “You look worse off than me! Sit down, you must be tired.”
Razumihin noticed Raskolnikov was very sick and tried to feel his pulse, but Raskolnikov pulled away.
“It doesn’t matter,” Raskolnikov said. “I came because I have no lessons to teach... but I don’t really want lessons.”
“You’re not well,” Razumihin said, worried.
“No, I’m not,” said Raskolnikov.
Raskolnikov suddenly didn’t want to see anyone. He felt angry with himself for coming.
“Good-bye,” he said quickly, heading for the door.
“Stop! Wait!” Razumihin called.
“Then why did you come? Are you crazy? You can’t just leave like that!”
“I came because you are the only one who could help. You are kind and smart. But now I see I don’t want any help or sympathy. I want to be alone.”

“You’re acting like a madman,” Razumihin said. Then he started talking about his job. He was translating a book called “Is Woman a Human Being?” and was getting paid for it. He offered Raskolnikov some work and handed him the papers and three roubles.
Raskolnikov took the money and papers without saying anything and left. But soon he came back, put the papers and money on the table, and left again, still silent.
“Are you crazy?” Razumihin shouted. “Why did you come at all?”
“I don’t want... translation,” Raskolnikov muttered as he went down the stairs.
“Then what do you want?” Razumihin called after him, but Raskolnikov didn’t answer.

Out on the street, Raskolnikov wasn’t paying attention and almost got hit by a carriage. The driver whipped him for getting in the way. People laughed and thought he was a pickpocket or pretending to be drunk.
While Raskolnikov stood there, an old woman and a girl gave him twenty copecks, thinking he was a beggar.

He walked a few steps, then looked at the river and the beautiful sky. He remembered how he used to stand there while he was at the university, thinking about big questions. But now, everything felt far away and meaningless. Suddenly, he remembered the coin in his hand and threw it into the water. He felt like he was cutting himself off from everyone.
By the time Raskolnikov got home, it was evening. He had been walking for hours but didn’t remember where he went. He lay down on the sofa, covered himself with his coat, and fell asleep right away.

Raskolnikov woke up to terrible screaming and fighting. He heard his landlady crying and begging not to be beaten on the stairs. He thought Ilya Petrovitch (the assistant policeman) was there, hurting her. He heard people running and shouting in the building. Raskolnikov was terrified and thought they would come for him next.
After a while, everything got quiet. Raskolnikov lay on the sofa, too scared to sleep. Suddenly, Nastasya came in with a candle and some soup.
“You haven’t eaten since yesterday,” she said. “You’re shaking with fever.”
“Nastasya... why was the landlady being beaten?” Raskolnikov asked.
“Who beat the landlady?” Nastasya said, looking at him closely.
“Just now... Ilya Petrovitch was here, beating her on the stairs. Why?”
Nastasya stared at him for a long time without speaking.
Finally, she said softly, “It’s the blood.”
“Blood? What blood?” Raskolnikov asked, scared.
“No one has beaten the landlady,” Nastasya said firmly.
“But I heard it all,” Raskolnikov said quietly. “I wasn’t asleep. I heard everyone run out to the stairs.”
“No one was here. You imagined it. When you’re sick, your mind plays tricks. Will you eat something?” she asked.
“Give me something to drink... Nastasya,” he whispered.
She brought him water, and after one sip, Raskolnikov fell back into a deep sleep.

Raskolnikov was very sick. Sometimes he was awake, sometimes he was confused and didn’t know what was real. He saw people around his bed, talking about him, arguing, and even laughing at him. Sometimes he was alone, and people peeked in to check on him. Nastasya (the servant) was often at his side. There was also another person he knew but couldn’t remember, which made him sad. He felt lost in time. Sometimes he thought he had been sick for a month, sometimes just a day. He knew he had forgotten something important, but he didn’t know what. He tried to get up, but someone always held him down. Then, finally, he woke up completely and knew where he was.
It was ten in the morning. Sunlight came into the room. Nastasya stood beside him with a young man Raskolnikov didn’t know. The landlady peeked in. Raskolnikov sat up.
“Who is this, Nastasya?” he asked.
“He’s himself again!” she said.
“Yes, he is,” the stranger agreed.
“Who are you?” Raskolnikov tried to ask, but just then Razumihin (his friend) came in, ducking through the door because he was tall.
“What a small room!” Razumihin said. “So you’re awake, brother? I just heard from Pashenka (the landlady).”
“He just woke up,” said Nastasya.
Razumihin turned to the stranger. “And who are you?”
“I’m the messenger from the office. I came on business,” the man answered.

Razumihin sat down. “It’s good you’re awake, Rodya (Raskolnikov). You haven’t eaten much for four days. We gave you tea with a spoon. Zossimov, the doctor, saw you twice and said you’ll be fine, just weak from not eating. Now, Mr. Messenger, what do you want?”
The messenger said, “Your mother sent you thirty-five roubles through Mr. Vahrushin. If you can sign for it, you can have the money.”
“Yes, I remember Vahrushin,” Raskolnikov said quietly.
“He can sign it,” Razumihin said, helping Raskolnikov sit up.
But Raskolnikov pushed the pen away. “I don’t want it.”
“You don’t want it?” Razumihin was surprised.
“I don’t want the money,” Raskolnikov repeated.
Razumihin laughed and told the messenger not to worry. He helped Raskolnikov sign the paper.
Finally, Raskolnikov signed. The messenger gave him the money and left.
“Are you hungry?” asked Razumihin.
“Yes,” Raskolnikov said.
Nastasya said there was soup from yesterday.
Razumihin asked her to bring soup and tea.
Raskolnikov felt strange and a little scared, but he stayed quiet to see what would happen.
Nastasya brought soup and said the tea would be ready soon. She brought two spoons, two plates, and set the table nicely.
Razumihin asked for beer too, and Nastasya went to get it.

Razumihin sat by Raskolnikov and started to feed him soup, blowing on each spoonful. Raskolnikov ate eagerly, but Razumihin stopped after a few bites and said he’d check with the doctor before giving more.
Nastasya returned with two bottles of beer.
“And will you have tea?” she asked.
“Yes,” Razumihin said, and told her to bring tea.
Razumihin ate hungrily and told Raskolnikov that Pashenka, the landlady, liked to help him with food. Nastasya brought the tea.

Razumihin poured tea and fed Raskolnikov by spoon, blowing on each one. Raskolnikov felt strong enough to eat by himself, but he pretended to be weak so he could listen and learn what was happening. After a while, he refused more tea and lay back on the pillows, noticing they were clean and soft.

Razumihin started telling Raskolnikov about how he tried to find him after he moved out without leaving an address. He asked people everywhere, finally found the right house, and met all sorts of people: Nikodim Fomitch, Ilya Petrovitch, Mr. Zametov, and of course Pashenka.
Razumihin said he was planning to make trouble for everyone who bothered Raskolnikov, but Pashenka was so nice he changed his mind.

He talked about how Raskolnikov signed an IOU (a note promising to pay money) and had promised to marry Pashenka’s daughter, Natalya, when she was alive. Razumihin said Pashenka was not as simple as she seemed.
Raskolnikov felt bad for signing the IOU and lying that his mother could pay, because his mother was poor.

Razumihin explained that Pashenka sold the IOU to a businessman named Tchebarov, who tried to collect the money. Razumihin stopped him by promising to pay and gave Tchebarov ten roubles to get the IOU back. He handed the torn IOU to Raskolnikov.
Raskolnikov turned to the wall without speaking.
“Sorry if I upset you with all my talking,” Razumihin said.
“Was it you I didn’t recognize when I was sick?” Raskolnikov asked.
“Yes, and you got angry, especially when I brought Zametov.”
“Zametov? Why did you bring him?” Raskolnikov asked quickly.
Razumihin said Zametov wanted to meet Raskolnikov because he’d heard so much about him. Razumihin said he was friends with Zametov now and had even visited Luise Ivanovna with him.
“Did I say anything strange when I was sick?” Raskolnikov asked.
“Of course,” Razumihin said.

Razumihin explained that Raskolnikov talked about many silly things, like a bulldog, earrings, a porter, and his own sock. Zametov had even searched for Raskolnikov’s sock to calm him down. Then Razumihin gave Raskolnikov some of the roubles and said he’d return with an account of what he spent. He told Nastasya to check on Raskolnikov and left.
Nastasya was curious about Razumihin and ran after him to listen.
As soon as they left, Raskolnikov jumped out of bed, anxious to do something, but he couldn’t remember what.
He worried, “Do they know my secret? Are they just pretending? What should I do?”
He searched the room, checking a hole in the wall and the stove, but nothing seemed out of place. He found his sock under the quilt and saw it was dirty.

He got scared, thinking about the police office and Zametov. He wondered if he should escape, but he didn’t have boots. He thought about taking his coat, the money, and the IOU and running far away, maybe even to America. But he was also afraid they would find him.
He drank the rest of the cold beer and soon felt sleepy. He wrapped himself in the quilt and fell into a deep, good sleep.
When he woke up, Razumihin was in the doorway. Raskolnikov sat up.
“You’re awake! Nastasya, bring the parcel!” Razumihin called.
“What time is it?” Raskolnikov asked.
“Almost six o’clock. You slept for over six hours,” Razumihin said.
Razumihin told him not to worry, that rest was good for him. He had been busy moving with his uncle and waiting for Raskolnikov to wake. Then he opened the parcel.

Razumihin took out a new cap, trousers, a waistcoat, boots, and shirts he’d bought for Raskolnikov. He explained the prices and joked about how clever he was at shopping. He wanted Raskolnikov to try them on.
Raskolnikov didn’t want to change clothes, but Razumihin and Nastasya helped him anyway.
Raskolnikov asked, “What money did you use to buy all this?”
“It was your own money, what your mother sent,” Razumihin said.
“I remember now,” Raskolnikov said quietly.
Then, a tall, heavy man came into the room. Raskolnikov thought he looked familiar.

Zossimov was a tall, heavy man with a round, pale face. He wore glasses and had straight, light-colored hair. He was only twenty-seven years old but dressed in neat and stylish clothes. He liked to act relaxed and important at the same time. People thought he was smart at his job, but not very fun to be around.
Razumihin said happily, “I came to see you twice today, brother. Look, he’s awake now!” Zossimov looked at Raskolnikov and asked, “How do you feel?”

Razumihin answered, “He’s still sad. We just changed his shirt, and he almost cried.” Zossimov replied, “That’s normal. You could have waited if he didn’t want to. His pulse is fine. Does your head hurt?” Raskolnikov said quickly, “I’m fine! I feel perfectly well!” He sat up on the sofa, looked at them, but then lay back down and turned to the wall. Zossimov watched him closely.

Zossimov said, “He’s doing all right. Has he eaten?” They told him what Raskolnikov had eaten and asked what was allowed. Zossimov said, “He can have soup and tea. No mushrooms or cucumbers, and better not give him meat either. No more medicine. I’ll check on him tomorrow, maybe even today.” Razumihin said, “Tomorrow evening I’ll take him for a walk to the Yusupov garden and then the Palais de Cristal.” Zossimov suggested not to bother Raskolnikov tomorrow, but said maybe a little walk would be fine.
