Razumihin complained, “Oh, what a bother! I have a house-warming party tonight, just nearby. Couldn’t Raskolnikov come? He could lie on the sofa. Are you coming, Zossimov? Don’t forget, you promised.” Zossimov agreed to come later and asked what the party would be like. Razumihin said, “Just tea, vodka, herrings, and a pie—some friends.” Zossimov asked who would be there. Razumihin listed, “Almost all neighbors, some new friends. My uncle, who just came to Petersburg for business. We only meet every five years.” Zossimov asked about his uncle. Razumihin said, “He used to be a district postmaster and is sixty-five. I like him. Porfiry Petrovitch, the head of the Investigation Department, will also come—you know him.” Zossimov asked if Porfiry was a relative. Razumihin said, “Only a very distant one.” Then he teased Zossimov, asking why he was frowning and if it was because they once argued.

Razumihin said there would also be some students, a teacher, a government clerk, a musician, an officer, and Zametov. Zossimov wondered what he or Raskolnikov could have in common with Zametov. Razumihin said, “If a man is nice, that’s enough for me. Zametov is a good fellow.” Zossimov said, “But he takes bribes.” Razumihin replied, “Maybe, but I still like him. You can’t always find perfect people. I know I’m not perfect either.”

Razumihin explained that Zametov was young, and it’s better to be kind to boys like him. He said he and Zametov really did have something in common. Zossimov asked what. Razumihin said, “It’s about a house-painter. We’re helping him out of trouble. There’s nothing to worry about now, but we’re working on it.”

Zossimov asked, “A painter?” Razumihin explained, “Yes, I told you before about the old pawnbroker woman who was murdered. The painter got mixed up in it.” Zossimov said he read about the murder in the papers.

Suddenly, Nastasya (the maid), who had been listening, said, “Lizaveta was killed too.” Raskolnikov softly repeated, “Lizaveta?” Nastasya explained, “Lizaveta sold old clothes. She used to come here. She even mended a shirt for you.” Raskolnikov turned to the wall and stared at a flower on the wallpaper, not moving.

Zossimov asked about the painter again. Razumihin said, “He was accused of the murder.” Zossimov asked if there was any evidence. Razumihin said, “Not really. It’s just like when they thought Koch and Pestryakov did it. The police work is silly. Pestryakov may come tonight. Rodya, you heard about this before you got sick, the day you fainted at the police office.”

Zossimov looked at Raskolnikov, who didn’t move. Zossimov told Razumihin he was a busybody, but Razumihin insisted, “We’ll help the painter. What’s annoying isn’t just the lies, but that the police believe their own lies. Porfiry is smart, but the police thought Koch and Pestryakov did it just because the door was locked and then found open.”

Zossimov mentioned he knew Koch. Razumihin called Koch a swindler. Then he said what upset him was the old-fashioned way the police worked, and that facts aren’t everything—it matters how you understand them.
Zossimov wanted to hear more about the painter.

Razumihin told the whole story: Three days after the murder, while the police still blamed Koch and Pestryakov, a peasant named Dushkin, who ran a bar near the house, brought a jeweler’s box with gold earrings to the police. Dushkin said a house-painter named Nikolay brought them to him and asked for money. Nikolay said he found the earrings in the street. Dushkin gave him a little money and waited to see if there would be any news, then went to the police when he heard about the murder. Dushkin knew Nikolay because they came from the same place. Nikolay had been working in the murdered woman’s building, painting with another man named Dmitri. Dushkin explained how Nikolay got drunk, left, and when he came back, Dushkin questioned him about the earrings. Nikolay got scared and ran away. After that, Dushkin believed Nikolay must be the murderer.

Zossimov agreed it looked suspicious. Razumihin continued: The police searched for Nikolay, arrested Dushkin, Dmitri, and others. Finally, they found Nikolay in a tavern. He had tried to trade his cross for a drink, and then tried to hang himself in the stable. People stopped him, and he told them to take him to the police, promising to confess everything. At the police station, they asked him many questions. He said he found the earrings in the street, but then changed his story, saying he found them in the flat where he was painting with Dmitri. He explained he and Dmitri had been fooling around, playfully fighting, then Dmitri ran outside. When Nikolay went back to get his things, he stepped on the box with the earrings near the door.

Raskolnikov suddenly sat up, looking scared, and asked, “Behind the door? Lying behind the door?” Razumihin asked what was wrong, but Raskolnikov said, “Nothing,” and turned back to the wall. Everyone went quiet.
Razumihin said Raskolnikov must have woken from a dream. Zossimov told Razumihin to go on with the story.

Razumihin explained that after finding the earrings, Nikolay took them to Dushkin, lied about where he found them, and then went drinking. He still said he knew nothing about the murder. When asked why he tried to hang himself, he said he was scared of being blamed.

Razumihin said now the police were sure Nikolay was the murderer, but he thought that was wrong. Zossimov said the earrings were important evidence. Razumihin argued that Nikolay’s answers sounded honest; he really did just find the box.

Zossimov pointed out that Nikolay had lied at first. Razumihin said there were many witnesses who saw Nikolay and Dmitri fighting and laughing at the time of the murder, like kids, right in front of everyone. The bodies upstairs were still warm. If they had just done something so terrible, would they really be playing and laughing? It didn’t fit at all.
Zossimov agreed it was strange, but not impossible. Razumihin insisted that if the police only look at the earrings and ignore the playful fighting and the witnesses, they’re making a big mistake.

Zossimov asked if it was proved the earrings belonged to the old woman. Razumihin said yes, Koch recognized the jewel-case and the owner proved it. Zossimov asked if anyone saw Nikolay when Koch and Pestryakov were going upstairs. Razumihin said no, and that was the worst part for Nikolay.

Zossimov said the only defense was that they were fighting and laughing, which was helpful but not perfect. He asked how Razumihin explained everything. Razumihin said, “It’s clear: the real murderer dropped the earrings. The murderer was hiding upstairs when Koch and Pestryakov knocked, then escaped when it was safe. He must have dropped the earrings behind the door while waiting to leave. That’s how I think it happened.”
Zossimov said it sounded too perfect, like a story. Razumihin asked why, but before they could argue more, the door opened and someone new came in.

A man named Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin walked into the small, messy room. He looked around with a frown, surprised at how shabby it was. He stared at Raskolnikov, who was lying on an old sofa, looking sick and tired. Luzhin also looked at Razumihin, who sat nearby and stared back. For a minute, no one spoke. Then Luzhin turned to Zossimov, the doctor, and asked, “Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a student, or used to be a student?” Razumihin quickly answered, “Here he is on the sofa! What do you want?” Luzhin seemed a bit bothered by this, but finally sat down when Razumihin offered him a chair and told Nastasya (the maid) to make room.

Razumihin explained, “Rodya (that’s Raskolnikov) has been very sick, but now he’s getting better. I’m his friend and used to be a student too. This is his doctor. Please, say what you came to say.” Luzhin asked if he would bother the patient, but Zossimov said it was fine. Luzhin said, “Your mother started a letter to you when I was nearby. I waited a few days before coming, thinking you would have heard the news.” Suddenly, Raskolnikov sat up and said, “So you’re the fiancé? I know, and that’s enough!” Luzhin was a little upset but didn’t argue.

Raskolnikov looked hard at Luzhin, noticing his new, fancy clothes. Luzhin wore a neat jacket, new trousers, and a bright tie. He held gloves in his hand and had a fresh haircut. He looked younger than he really was. Raskolnikov lay back and stared at the ceiling, not impressed. Luzhin acted like he didn’t notice.

Luzhin said, “I’m sorry to see you ill. If I had known, I would have come sooner. I’ve been busy with work, but your mother and sister will arrive soon. I found them a place to stay nearby.” Raskolnikov asked, “Where?” Luzhin answered, “In Bakaleyev’s house.” Razumihin explained it wasn’t a nice place, but it was cheap. Luzhin said it was only for a short time, and that he would get a better flat later. He mentioned he was staying with a friend named Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov.

Luzhin said he liked meeting young people to learn new ideas. Razumihin and Zossimov talked with him about how people and the country were changing. Luzhin said, “I think people are more practical now and have better ideas.” Razumihin didn’t agree and said, “Practicality is hard to find. People talk about good ideas but don’t always act on them.” Luzhin disagreed and said, “Things are changing for the better. People care more about themselves now, and that helps everyone.” Raskolnikov whispered, “He just learned all that to show off!” Luzhin kept talking about progress and science. Razumihin finally said he was tired of these kinds of speeches and wanted to know what kind of person Luzhin was. Luzhin got a bit offended, but decided to leave soon.
Luzhin said to Raskolnikov, “I hope when you are better, we can get to know each other. I hope you get well soon.” Raskolnikov didn’t reply. Luzhin stood up to go.

Then Zossimov and Razumihin started talking about the murder of the old pawnbroker lady. They said the police were questioning everyone who had left items with her. Razumihin thought the murderer was new to crime and just got lucky escaping. Luzhin joined in, asking about the case. He said he was surprised that crime was increasing, not just among poor people, but even among people with good jobs. He wondered why this was happening.

Razumihin explained that people wanted easy money and didn’t want to work hard for it. Raskolnikov suddenly said, “That fits your theory!” Luzhin was confused. Raskolnikov explained, “If everyone only cares about themselves, then people will think it’s okay to do anything—even bad things.” Luzhin argued back that his ideas didn’t mean people should hurt others.

Suddenly, Raskolnikov asked Luzhin angrily, “Is it true you told my sister you liked that she was poor so you could control her?” Luzhin got red and said that was not true and blamed Raskolnikov’s mother for misunderstanding. Raskolnikov sat up and said in a loud voice, “If you ever talk about my mother again, I’ll throw you down the stairs!” Luzhin got very upset and said, “I see how it is. I tried to be kind, but I won’t forget this.” Raskolnikov shouted, “I am not ill!” Luzhin replied, “So much the worse…” and left the room, looking insulted.

Razumihin shook his head and said, “How could you do that?” But Raskolnikov yelled, “Leave me alone! I want to be alone!” Zossimov told Razumihin they should go and not upset Raskolnikov more. They left the room, talking on the stairs about how Raskolnikov seemed troubled by something in his mind. Razumihin thought maybe it was because of Luzhin and the news about his sister’s engagement.
Now Raskolnikov was alone with Nastasya. She asked if he wanted tea. He said, “Later! I’m sleepy! Leave me.” He turned to the wall, and Nastasya left him alone.

As soon as Nastasya (the servant) left, Raskolnikov quietly got up and locked the door. He opened the parcel Razumihin (his friend) had brought and began to get dressed. Strangely, he felt calm and sure of himself, even though he knew he was still weak. He put the money from the table—twenty-five roubles—and some change in his pocket. Then he quietly left his room and went outside, making sure Nastasya didn’t hear him.

The sun was setting, and the air was hot and dusty. Raskolnikov felt dizzy, but he walked quickly, not caring where he was going. He only thought, “Today, everything must end. I can’t go on like this.” He didn’t want to think about how, just that something had to change.

He walked toward the Hay Market, as he often did. He saw a young man playing a barrel organ and a girl singing beside him, hoping for some coins. Raskolnikov gave the girl a five-copeck piece. She stopped singing, thanked him, and moved on.
Raskolnikov asked a man nearby if he liked street music. The man looked surprised and walked away, not answering.

Raskolnikov reached the corner where he remembered the huckster and his wife talking with Lizaveta (the murdered woman). They weren’t there. He stopped and asked a young man in a red shirt if he knew the man who kept a booth there. The young man didn’t really answer, just joked and talked about a tavern nearby.
Raskolnikov walked into a crowd of peasants, wanting to talk to someone, but they ignored him. So he took a turn into another street.

He walked past many buildings with bars and eating-houses. There were lots of women, some sitting, some standing, some talking. A drunk soldier wandered by, and a beggar was arguing. Raskolnikov stood with the women, who looked tired and hurt.
He listened to the music and singing coming from one bar. He thought about going inside and wondered if he should get drunk.

A young woman from the group invited him in. He noticed she was pretty and told her so. She smiled and called him nice-looking. Another woman teased him for being so thin, and a tipsy man joked about the women.

The first girl called after him, asking for six copecks for a drink. Raskolnikov gave her fifteen copecks. She told him her name was Duclida. Another woman scolded her for asking, saying she would be too embarrassed.
Raskolnikov thought about how people would rather live any kind of life than die, even in the worst place. “How true that is!” he thought.
He went into a restaurant called the Palais de Cristal, remembering Razumihin had just talked about it. He asked the waiter for tea and newspapers from the last five days.
Raskolnikov read through the newspapers, looking for news about the murder. Suddenly, Zametov (the police clerk) sat down beside him, looking cheerful.
Zametov was surprised to see Raskolnikov, since he’d heard Raskolnikov was very sick. He said he’d even visited him.
Raskolnikov said he knew Zametov had visited. He joked about Razumihin and some of their friends.
Raskolnikov teased Zametov about drinking champagne and having fun. Zametov laughed and said they had just been celebrating.
Raskolnikov laughed too and made fun of Zametov “profiting by everything.” He mentioned the case of the old woman who was murdered.
Zametov was surprised and asked how Raskolnikov knew about that.
Raskolnikov said, “Maybe I know more than you do.”
Zametov told Raskolnikov he still seemed sick and shouldn’t be out.
Zametov noticed Raskolnikov was reading the newspapers and asked if it was about the fires. Raskolnikov replied mysteriously that he wasn’t reading about fires.
Raskolnikov asked if Zametov wanted to know what he was reading. Zametov said he didn’t care, but Raskolnikov kept teasing.
Raskolnikov finally said he was looking for news about the murder of the old pawnbroker woman—the same one Zametov had talked about at the police office.
Zametov said it was none of his business if Raskolnikov read about it.
Raskolnikov whispered about the old woman, reminding Zametov of when he fainted at the police office.
Zametov was almost alarmed, asking what Raskolnikov meant.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov started laughing hard, remembering the moment he had hidden behind the door with the axe.
Zametov said, “You are either mad, or…” and stopped, surprised by his own idea.
Raskolnikov pressed him, wanting to know what he meant.
Zametov got angry and said it was all nonsense.
After a long silence, Zametov told Raskolnikov to drink his tea. Raskolnikov remembered to sip his tea and eat some bread.
Then Zametov talked about a gang of people who made fake money. Raskolnikov said they were foolish, not real criminals, and explained how easily they were caught.
Zametov said it was possible for someone’s hands to tremble from fear.
They talked about whether either of them could do such a thing. Zametov said he couldn’t, and asked Raskolnikov if he could.
Raskolnikov described how he would have changed the fake notes, making it very difficult for anyone to catch him.
Zametov laughed and said it was easy to talk, but in real life even desperate people made mistakes—like the murderer of the old woman, whose hands shook and who failed to steal much.
Raskolnikov asked why, if it was so clear, they hadn’t caught the murderer yet.
He teased Zametov about how the police only look for people who suddenly start spending money, saying even a child could fool them.
Zametov said most criminals do start spending, but Raskolnikov wouldn’t be so obvious.
Raskolnikov noticed Zametov seemed to really want to know how he would act if he were the murderer. Zametov admitted he did.
Raskolnikov whispered how he would have hidden the money and jewels under a big stone and left it there for years so no one could ever find it.
Zametov called Raskolnikov a madman, scared by how serious he was.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov said, “And what if it was I who murdered the old woman and Lizaveta?” Then he realized what he’d said.
Zametov turned white, shocked.
Raskolnikov asked if Zametov believed him. Zametov quickly said he didn’t.
Raskolnikov teased him, saying that must mean Zametov believed it a little before.

Raskolnikov got up, shouted for the waiter, and paid for his tea and vodka. He showed Zametov his money, asking where it came from, knowing Zametov had checked with his landlady about his money before.
He left the restaurant, shaking from excitement and exhaustion.
Zametov sat thinking for a long time, his mind changed by what Raskolnikov had said.

As Raskolnikov left, he bumped into Razumihin on the steps. Razumihin was very surprised and angry, saying he had been searching everywhere for Raskolnikov, even the garret, and almost blamed Nastasya for his disappearance.
Raskolnikov quietly said he just wanted to be alone, that he was tired of everyone.
Razumihin was upset, saying Raskolnikov was too sick to be alone and demanded to know what he had been doing at the Palais de Cristal.
Raskolnikov tried to leave, but Razumihin grabbed his shoulder and threatened to carry him home if he didn’t listen.
Raskolnikov told Razumihin that his kindness was making things worse and begged to be left alone.

After this, Razumihin let go and said, “Well, go to hell then.” But then he invited Raskolnikov to his housewarming party, offering tea and a place to rest. He said Zossimov (the doctor) would be there too.
Raskolnikov refused.
Razumihin insisted that Raskolnikov would change his mind and come, reminding him of the address.
Again, Raskolnikov said he would not come and walked away.
Razumihin yelled after him, saying he would refuse to know him if he didn’t come, and asked if Zametov was in the restaurant.
Raskolnikov said yes and that he had talked to Zametov. He didn’t tell Razumihin more, just walked away.
Raskolnikov turned the corner and walked on, while Razumihin watched him leave, worried he might hurt himself. Razumihin tried to follow, but lost him in the crowd and went back to talk to Zametov.

Raskolnikov walked to a bridge, feeling very weak. He leaned on the rail, looking at the sunset and the canal water. Suddenly, he saw a tall woman with red eyes and a scarf on her head. Without saying anything, she climbed over the railing and jumped into the canal.
People shouted, “A woman is drowning!” and crowded around. A policeman ran down, jumped into the water, and pulled her out. She soon coughed and sat up, wet and silent.
Someone in the crowd said the woman had tried to hurt herself before. Her neighbor explained she had left her daughter to watch the woman, but trouble happened again.
The crowd broke up. Raskolnikov watched, feeling nothing but disgust. He decided, “This isn’t the way,” and thought about going to the police.
He started walking toward the police office, feeling empty and tired. He didn’t want to think anymore.

Instead of going straight, he turned down a side street and, without planning, found himself standing at the gate of the house where the murders happened. He went inside and walked up to the fourth floor. The apartment was being redone, with workers putting up new wallpaper. Raskolnikov was annoyed to see the place changed. He listened to the workers talk about clothes and fashion books.
Raskolnikov walked into another room, remembering where all the furniture had been. He rang the doorbell several times, feeling the same fear as before, but also a strange satisfaction.
One worker asked him what he wanted. Raskolnikov said he was looking for a flat to rent, but also asked about the blood from the murder.
The worker was confused and asked who he was. Raskolnikov told him to come to the police station and he’d explain.
The workers finished their jobs and left, locking up. Raskolnikov followed them outside.
Outside, some people stood by the entrance: porters, a peasant woman, a man in a long coat, and others. Raskolnikov asked if the police office was open. The porter said yes.
Raskolnikov stood quietly, lost in thought. The workers told the others that Raskolnikov had asked about blood and the murder, and even rang the doorbell a lot.
The porter asked who he was. Raskolnikov explained he was Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a former student, and where he lived.
They asked what he wanted at the flat. He said he was just looking at it.
One man said to take him to the police station. Raskolnikov said, “Come along,” but no one really moved.
The porter and others called him a rogue and told him to get along. One grabbed Raskolnikov by the shoulder and pushed him into the street.
Raskolnikov looked back at them, then walked away quietly.

He stood at the crossroads, unsure if he should go to the police or not. Suddenly, he saw a crowd down the street and heard shouting. He walked toward it, knowing he would soon go to the police and that everything would be decided.

A fancy carriage stopped in the street. Two gray horses stood still. The coachman stood nearby, looking worried. People crowded around, and a policeman pointed a lantern at something near the carriage wheels. Everyone was talking loudly. The coachman kept saying, “What a misfortune! Good Lord, what a misfortune!”
Raskolnikov pushed through the people. He saw a man lying on the ground, covered in blood. The man wore old clothes and looked very hurt. His face was bleeding and crushed. He wasn’t moving.

The coachman tried to explain, saying, “I wasn’t going fast! I shouted three times for him to move! But he was drunk and fell under the horses. I tried to stop, but it was too late. The horses got scared and ran over him.”
The police just wanted to get the injured man to a hospital or police station. No one knew who the man was.

Raskolnikov got closer and saw the man’s face in the lantern light. He suddenly shouted, “I know him! It’s Marmeladov, a retired government clerk. He lives nearby in Kozel’s house. Quick, get a doctor! I’ll pay!” He showed money to the policeman.
The police were glad to know who the man was. Raskolnikov gave them his own name and address and begged them to carry Marmeladov to his home, just a few houses away.

“He has a family—a wife and children!” Raskolnikov said. “He’ll get help faster at home than at the hospital. Please hurry!” He secretly gave the policeman some money, and people helped carry Marmeladov.
They carried Marmeladov to Kozel’s house, with Raskolnikov holding his head and showing the way.
“This way! Be careful with his head. I’ll pay you all!” Raskolnikov kept saying.

Inside, Katerina Ivanovna, Marmeladov’s wife, was walking around her small room, talking to her daughter Polenka, who was helping her little brother get ready for bed. Lida, the youngest, waited her turn. The family was poor; the children wore rags, and the air was full of smoke, making Katerina Ivanovna cough a lot.

Katerina Ivanovna told Polenka stories about her happier life before marrying Marmeladov, and complained about how their life had gotten so hard. Suddenly, she heard a noise and saw people carrying someone into her room.
“Where do we put him?” the policeman asked.
“On the sofa, head this way,” Raskolnikov said.
Someone in the hallway shouted, “Run over! Drunk!”
Katerina Ivanovna turned pale and could barely breathe. The children were scared and Lida ran to Polenka, shaking.
Raskolnikov rushed to calm Katerina Ivanovna. “Don’t be scared. He was run over, but he’ll wake up. I brought him here, and I’ll pay for everything!”
Katerina Ivanovna hurried to her husband.
She didn’t faint; instead, she put a pillow under Marmeladov’s head and tried to help. She was shaking but stayed strong.
Raskolnikov sent someone to get a doctor who lived nearby.
“A doctor is coming,” Raskolnikov told Katerina Ivanovna. “Don’t worry, I’ll pay. Give me water and a towel, quick.” He started washing the blood from Marmeladov’s face.
Katerina Ivanovna brought water but was so weak she almost dropped it. Raskolnikov found a towel and helped clean Marmeladov.
Katerina Ivanovna was having trouble breathing, and Raskolnikov wondered if he had made a mistake bringing Marmeladov home instead of the hospital.
“Polenka,” Katerina Ivanovna said, “run to Sonia and tell her father was run over. If she’s not home, leave a message.”
The little boy said, “Run your fastest!” then sat quietly again.
Soon the room was crowded with people. Only one policeman stayed to keep order. The other people who lived in the building peeked in.
Katerina Ivanovna shouted at everyone, “Let him die in peace! This isn’t a show! Take off your hats! Show respect!” Her cough stopped her, but people listened and moved back.
Outside, some said Marmeladov should be taken to the hospital instead.
Katerina Ivanovna ran to the door to yell at them, but met Madame Lippevechsel, the landlady, who came to see what was happening.
“Your husband has been trampled! Take him to the hospital! I am the landlady!” Madame Lippevechsel said.
Katerina Ivanovna argued with her, calling her “Amalia Ludwigovna,” and saying she would tell the Governor-General if she didn’t let Marmeladov die in peace.
As Katerina Ivanovna was talking, Marmeladov woke up and groaned. He looked around, confused, and saw Raskolnikov and his family. Katerina Ivanovna cried and tried to help him.
“His chest is crushed! He’s bleeding so much!” she cried, trying to take off his shirt.
Marmeladov recognized his wife and whispered, “A priest.”
Katerina Ivanovna leaned against the window sadly.
Marmeladov kept asking for a priest.
“Someone went to get one,” Katerina Ivanovna told him.
Marmeladov looked at little Lida, who was scared and shaking.
“Barefoot, barefoot!” he said, looking at Lida’s bare feet.
“Be quiet, you know why she has no shoes,” Katerina Ivanovna snapped.
Just then, the doctor arrived.
The doctor, a little old man, checked Marmeladov and saw his chest was badly hurt and his ribs were broken. The policeman explained what happened.
The doctor told Raskolnikov quietly, “It’s amazing he woke up.”
“Will he be all right?” Raskolnikov asked.
“No, he will die in five or ten minutes,” the doctor said. “I can try to bleed him, but it won’t help.”
Right then, the priest came in to give Marmeladov his last prayers. The doctor waited.

Everyone stepped back as the priest prayed with Marmeladov. Katerina Ivanovna knelt with her children and made them pray, too. Little Lida shook with fear, but the boy prayed quietly. More people peeked in, and a candle lit up the room.
Polenka came back, breathless, saying, “She’s coming, I saw her outside!” meaning Sonia.
Sonia, Marmeladov’s older daughter, came in. She looked out of place in her bright, old dress. She was thin, scared, and looked at her father on the bed.
The priest finished. Katerina Ivanovna went to her husband. The priest tried to comfort her, but she asked, “What am I supposed to do with the children?”
The priest said, “God is merciful; ask Him for help.”
“He’s merciful, but not to us,” Katerina Ivanovna said.
The priest suggested maybe the people who caused the accident would give her money.
“No! Why should they pay? He got drunk and ran under the horses! He only brought us misery. Thank God he’s dying—one less to feed!” Katerina Ivanovna cried, very upset.
The priest reminded her to forgive.
Katerina Ivanovna was busy caring for Marmeladov and said she had already forgiven a lot.
Suddenly, she coughed so hard there was blood on her handkerchief. The priest saw and was silent.
Marmeladov tried to say something to Katerina Ivanovna, but she said, “Be quiet, I know what you want to say!”
Just then, Marmeladov saw Sonia standing in the corner.
“Who’s that?” he asked, trying to sit up and see her.
“Lie down!” Katerina Ivanovna told him.

Marmeladov finally recognized Sonia and was very sad to see her dressed so poorly. He tried to reach for her, but fell off the sofa. They picked him up, but he was dying. Sonia hugged him, and he died in her arms.
Katerina Ivanovna cried, “He got what he wanted. What will I do now? How will I bury him or feed the children?”

Raskolnikov went to her and said, “Your husband told me all about your family. He loved you all very much. Please let me help you. Here is some money. I’ll come again to visit.” He gave her twenty roubles.
Raskolnikov left, but in the crowd met Nikodim Fomitch, a police official.
“Is that you?” Nikodim Fomitch asked.
“He’s dead,” said Raskolnikov. “The doctor and priest did all they could. Please be kind to his wife; she is very sick.”
“But you’re covered in blood,” Nikodim Fomitch noticed.
“Yes, I am,” Raskolnikov answered, then walked away.
Raskolnikov walked outside, feeling tired but strangely alive. On the stairs, the priest passed him. Then he heard someone calling, “Wait! Wait!” It was Polenka.
She stopped on the steps, smiling at him, happy to give him a message.
“What’s your name? Where do you live?” she asked, a little out of breath.
Raskolnikov put his hands on her shoulders and looked at her kindly.
“Who sent you?”
“Sonia sent me,” Polenka said, smiling.
“Mother told me to run fast, too,” Polenka added.
“Do you love Sonia?”
“I love her more than anyone,” Polenka answered seriously.
“And will you love me?”
Polenka hugged Raskolnikov and cried softly on his shoulder.
“I’m sorry for father,” she said. “It’s nothing but troubles now.”
“Did your father love you?”
“He loved Lida most because she is little and sick. But he taught us to read and even grammar. Mother liked that, even though she didn’t say it. She wants me to learn French soon.”
“Do you know your prayers?”
“Of course! I say prayers by myself, but Kolya and Lida say them aloud with mother. We pray for Sonia, and for our second father, since our first father died.”
“Polenka, my name is Rodion. Pray for me, too.”
“I’ll pray for you all my life,” Polenka promised, hugging him again.
Raskolnikov told her where he lived and promised to visit. She left, happy. It was late at night when he walked outside. Soon he was standing on a bridge, thinking.
“Enough!” Raskolnikov said to himself. “Real life matters. I want to live! I feel strong now. I will try my best!”
He felt weak but hopeful. He thought, “I can be strong. I want to visit Razumihin and let him win his bet. I need strength in life.”
He remembered he asked Polenka to pray for him and smiled to himself.
Raskolnikov found Razumihin’s place. There was a party going on, and Razumihin, his friend, came out to meet him, happy but a little drunk.
“I just came to say you’ve won your bet. I’m too tired to come in. I’ll see you tomorrow!” Raskolnikov said.
“I’ll walk you home,” Razumihin said.
“What about your guests?” Raskolnikov asked.
Razumihin said the guests wouldn’t miss him, and he wanted to get some fresh air. He went to get Zossimov, the doctor.
Zossimov checked on Raskolnikov and said, “Go to bed and take this medicine.”
Raskolnikov took the medicine.
“Good you’re taking him home,” Zossimov told Razumihin. “He’s better than before.”
As they walked, Razumihin told Raskolnikov that Zossimov wondered if Raskolnikov was mad, but Razumihin said he wasn’t.

Razumihin explained that Zametov, a clerk, had told Zossimov about a strange conversation with Raskolnikov. People wondered if Raskolnikov was acting strangely, but Razumihin said it was just because he was sick.
Razumihin talked a lot, saying Raskolnikov’s talk had confused Zametov, but that was over now.
Raskolnikov said, “I just saw a man die. I gave all my money to his family. I was hugged by a little girl. I saw Sonia in a bright feather. I’m tired—help me walk.”
“What’s wrong?” Razumihin asked.
“I’m dizzy and sad. Look, there’s a light in my room!”
They reached the stairs and saw a light coming from Raskolnikov’s room.
“Maybe it’s Nastasya,” Razumihin guessed.
“She’s never in my room this late, but never mind. Good-bye!”
“I’m coming with you!” Razumihin said.
“Let’s shake hands now, before we go in,” Raskolnikov said.
“Nothing’s wrong—come with me. You’ll see,” Raskolnikov said.
When they got to the door, they heard voices inside.
Raskolnikov opened the door and was shocked.
His mother and sister were sitting on his sofa, waiting for him. He had forgotten they were coming, even though he was told that day. They had been worried and crying, asking Nastasya about him.
When Raskolnikov came in, his mother and sister ran to hug him. But he felt so overwhelmed that he fainted.
Razumihin rushed in, picked up Raskolnikov, and put him on the sofa.
“Don’t worry, he just fainted. He’ll be fine!” Razumihin told the mother and sister, trying to calm them.
He even pulled Dounia, Raskolnikov’s sister, over to show her that Raskolnikov was waking up. The family was very grateful to Razumihin, who had helped Raskolnikov so much while he was sick.

Raskolnikov sat up on the sofa. He held his mother, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, and his sister, Avdotya Romanovna (Dounia), by the hand and looked at both of them. He looked so upset that his mother began to cry, and Dounia’s hand shook.
Raskolnikov said, “Go home with Razumihin. Good-bye till tomorrow. Is it long since you arrived?”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna answered, “This evening, Rodya. The train was late. But I won’t leave you! I want to stay here with you tonight.”
“Don’t make it harder for me,” Raskolnikov said, sounding annoyed.
Razumihin quickly said, “I’ll stay with him! I won’t leave him for a second.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna tried to thank Razumihin, but Raskolnikov interrupted.
“I can’t have it! Enough, go away... I can’t stand it!” he said.
Dounia whispered, “Come, Mama, let’s go out for a minute. We’re upsetting him.”
“Can’t I look at him after three years?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried.
Raskolnikov stopped them again. “Wait. Have you seen Luzhin?”
“No, Rodya, but he knows we’re here. We heard Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin visited you today,” his mother said.
“Yes, he was here. Dounia, I told Luzhin I’d throw him out and told him to go away.”
“Rodya, what are you saying!” his mother said, but stopped, looking at Dounia.
Dounia and Pulcheria Alexandrovna had already heard about the argument with Luzhin from Nastasya, but didn’t know all the details.
“Dounia,” Raskolnikov said, “I don’t want you to marry Luzhin. Tomorrow, you must refuse him. Write him a letter. I’ll read it in the morning.”
“Good heavens!” cried Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
“Brother, be careful what you say,” said Dounia, but then she spoke gently, “Maybe you’re too tired to talk now.”
“You think I’m not myself? No, I mean it. You want to marry Luzhin for my sake, but I won’t let you do it. Write the letter before tomorrow.”
“I can’t do that!” Dounia said, upset. “Why should you decide?”
Their mother tried to calm them. “Dounia, be quiet, tomorrow... Let’s go.”
Razumihin said, “He’s talking nonsense now. Tomorrow he’ll be better. But today he really did drive Luzhin away, and Luzhin got mad.”
“Then it’s true?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried.
“Good-bye till tomorrow, brother,” Dounia said kindly. “Let’s go, mother.”
Raskolnikov tried again. “Sister, I am not ill in the head. This marriage is wrong. I may be bad, but you mustn’t be. I’d rather not have a sister than see you marry Luzhin. It’s me or him! Go now.”
“You’re out of your mind!” Razumihin shouted, but Raskolnikov just lay down, exhausted, and turned away. Dounia glanced at Razumihin. He noticed her look and was surprised.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was overwhelmed.
“I won’t go,” she whispered to Razumihin. “I’ll stay somewhere here—please take Dounia home.”

Razumihin whispered back, “You’ll spoil everything. Come out to the stairs anyway. Nastasya, bring a light! He almost fought with the doctor and me earlier! If you upset him now, he might run away or hurt himself.”
“What do you mean?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked.
“And Dounia can’t be left alone in those rooms. Luzhin should have found you better lodgings... But never mind me, I’ve had a bit to drink.”
“I’ll ask the landlady here if we can stay,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna insisted. “I can’t leave Rodya.”

They stood on the stairs. Razumihin, very excited, held both women’s hands and tried to convince them to leave. He squeezed their hands hard and kept talking, sometimes forgetting his manners. Even though he acted strangely, Pulcheria Alexandrovna trusted him because she was worried about her son. Dounia was also worried but remembered what Nastasya had said about Razumihin and decided not to be scared of him.

“You can’t stay with the landlady,” Razumihin said. “If you stay, you’ll upset Raskolnikov more. Here’s what I’ll do: Nastasya will stay with him. I’ll take you home. Then I’ll come back and tell you how he is. After that, I’ll get Dr. Zossimov to come. You’ll hear from me and the doctor. If there’s anything wrong, I’ll bring you back myself. The landlady is impossible—she’s jealous about Dounia. So, do you trust me?”
“Let’s go, mother,” said Dounia. “He’ll do what he promised. He’s already helped Rodya.”
Razumihin was overjoyed. “You understand me, because you’re an angel! Nastasya, go stay with Raskolnikov. I’ll be back soon.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna still worried, but let Razumihin help her and Dounia down the stairs.

As they walked, Razumihin said, “You think I’m drunk, but it’s just seeing you that made me act this way. I’ll pour water on my head to wake up! I care about you both. I’m Rodya’s friend, so I’m your friend too. Zossimov was afraid Rodya might go mad, so he shouldn’t be upset.”
“What did you say?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked.
“Did the doctor really say that?” Dounia asked, worried.

“Yes, but it’s not true. The doctor gave him medicine, and your visit will help. In an hour, Zossimov will tell you himself. I got this way arguing at a party. They talk nonsense! I almost fought with them. My uncle is still there.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna started to say something, but Razumihin got even more excited.

Razumihin said loudly, “I don’t mind if people talk nonsense. That’s how people learn! If you make mistakes, you find the truth. It’s better to be wrong in your own way than right in someone else’s. We are still learning, like in school. We use other people’s ideas too much. Am I right?”
“Oh, mercy, I don’t know,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said.
“Yes, but I don’t agree with everything,” said Dounia, but then cried out because Razumihin squeezed her hand too hard.
“You are both so good,” Razumihin cried. He dropped to his knees to kiss their hands, right there on the street.
“Stop, please, what are you doing?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said.
“Get up!” Dounia said, laughing but also upset.

Razumihin got up. “I’m just a fool, but I had to show respect. Here are your lodgings. Rodya was right to send Luzhin away. How dare he put you here! And you’re his fiancée? Well, your fiancé is a scoundrel.”
“Excuse me, Mr. Razumihin, you’re forgetting yourself,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said.

“Sorry, I forgot myself,” Razumihin said quickly. “But you can’t be mad at me for being honest. Luzhin is not good enough for you. He’s not clever, he’s a fool and a miser. I respect my friends, but not Luzhin. Anyway, lock yourselves in tonight. I’ll be back soon with news, and later with Zossimov.”
“Dounia, what will happen now?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked, worried.
“Don’t worry, mother,” Dounia said, taking off her hat. “God sent Razumihin to help us, even if he’s a bit silly. We can trust him. He’s done so much for Rodya.”
“I don’t know if he’ll really come. I didn’t want to leave Rodya... And our meeting was so different from what I hoped. He seemed so unhappy.”
Tears came to her eyes.
“No, mother. You were crying, so you didn’t see. He’s just very sick.”

“Oh, that illness! What will happen? And how he talked to you, Dounia!” her mother said, watching Dounia closely, but feeling a little better because Dounia defended her brother. “I hope he’ll feel better tomorrow.”

“He’ll say the same thing tomorrow, I’m sure,” Dounia answered. She kissed her mother, who hugged her back. Then Pulcheria Alexandrovna waited anxiously for Razumihin to return, while Dounia paced the room, thinking.

Razumihin’s crush on Dounia was obvious, even if it was silly. Dounia was very beautiful—tall, strong, and graceful, with dark hair and kind eyes. She looked serious, but her smile was wonderful. She loved her brother and was upset by his harsh words, which made Razumihin like her even more.

Razumihin had been right when he said the landlady, Praskovya Pavlovna, would be jealous of Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia because of him. Pulcheria Alexandrovna, though older, still looked kind and pretty. She was gentle but had strong beliefs she would never break.
Twenty minutes later, there were two quiet knocks at the door. Razumihin had come back.
“I won’t come in, I’m in a hurry,” he said. “Raskolnikov is sleeping well. Nastasya is with him. Now I’ll get Zossimov. You should go to bed; you’re tired.”
He ran off again.
“What a helpful young man!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, very happy.
“He seems wonderful!” Dounia said, and started walking around the room again.

About an hour later, they heard a knock. Razumihin returned with Dr. Zossimov. Zossimov didn’t want to come at first, but he became pleased when he saw how much they respected him. He only stayed ten minutes but made Pulcheria Alexandrovna feel much better. He said Raskolnikov was getting better, but his sickness was partly from being poor and partly from worries and ideas. When Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked if Raskolnikov was insane, Zossimov smiled and said maybe he had some fixed idea, but family would help him recover, as long as nothing new upset him. He left, pleased with himself.
“We’ll talk tomorrow; go to bed now!” Razumihin said, following Zossimov out. “I’ll come early with news.”
“Avdotya Romanovna is really pretty,” Zossimov said as they walked outside.
“You said what?” Razumihin shouted and grabbed Zossimov by the collar, shaking him. “Don’t you dare!”
“Let me go, you drunken fool,” Zossimov said, then laughed loudly. Razumihin stood thinking.
“I’m an idiot,” Razumihin said, “but you are too.”
“No, not like you. I’m not thinking anything foolish,” Zossimov replied.
They walked in silence until they reached Raskolnikov’s house. Then Razumihin spoke, worried.

“Listen, Zossimov, you’re a good doctor, but you’re lazy and spoil yourself. You’ll be staying in the landlady’s flat tonight. (It took work to convince her!) I’ll be in the kitchen. You can get to know her. Don’t get the wrong idea—it’s not what you think.”
“But I don’t think that way!” Zossimov said.
“She’s shy, but she likes you. Help me out. I’ll repay you.”
Zossimov laughed even more.
“You really like her! But what should I do?”

“Just talk to her. You’re a doctor, maybe you can help her with something. She has a piano. I play a song for her sometimes, and she likes it. You can talk about anything, she just likes someone to sit with her. But don’t talk of love—she’s too shy. Just act like you care.”
“But did you promise her anything? Like marriage?”
“No, nothing of the sort! She’s not like that. Someone tried that before.”
“Then just stop seeing her.”
“I can’t just stop!”
“Why not?”
“I don’t know! There’s something about her.”
“Then why did you make her like you?”

“Maybe I liked her too, at first. But she doesn’t care if it’s you or me, as long as someone is there. You could even teach her math—she’d just sigh and be happy. She just wants company. It’s comfortable.”
“But what do I want with her?” asked Zossimov.

“You are made for each other! There’s something nice about being with her—like being safe and cozy. Anyway, sometimes I check on Raskolnikov at night. You can too. But if you see anything wrong, wake me up. It will be fine, though.”

Razumihin woke up at eight in the morning, feeling worried and confused. He remembered everything that happened yesterday and knew things were very different now. He felt embarrassed about dreams he had, and decided to focus on what he needed to do today.

Razumihin’s worst memory from yesterday was how badly he had behaved. He was drunk and had said mean things about Avdotya Romanovna’s fiancé, Luzhin, even though he didn’t really know him. He felt ashamed, thinking, “Why did I judge them? What right did I have?” He even remembered making a silly comment about the landlady being jealous of Avdotya Romanovna and felt so embarrassed he hit the stove with his fist and hurt his hand.
Razumihin thought, “I can’t take back what I did. The only thing I can do is go see them and help, but say nothing and not ask for forgiveness, because it’s all ruined now.”

Even though he felt bad, Razumihin made sure to dress as neatly as he could. He brushed his clothes and made sure he was clean, because he didn’t want to upset anyone, especially since they needed his help.
He washed up carefully, using soap from Nastasya. He thought about shaving, but decided not to, thinking that the ladies might think he did it only to look good for them.
While Razumihin was talking to himself, Zossimov, the doctor, came in. Zossimov had slept in the landlady’s sitting room.
Zossimov wanted to check on Raskolnikov before leaving. Razumihin told him that Raskolnikov was sleeping. Zossimov said not to wake him and that he would come back around eleven.
Zossimov wondered if Raskolnikov would go visit his family or if they would come to him.
Razumihin guessed that Raskolnikov’s mother and sister were coming and would talk about family matters. He offered to leave, saying Zossimov, as the doctor, had more right to be there.
Zossimov replied that he would not stay long, as he had many things to do.
Razumihin worriedly told Zossimov that yesterday, when he was drunk, he had told Raskolnikov and the ladies that the doctor was afraid Raskolnikov might go mad.
Zossimov said, “You told the ladies that, too.”
Razumihin felt bad and asked if Zossimov really thought Raskolnikov was going mad.

Zossimov said it was nonsense. He explained that Raskolnikov was very sick and upset, and all the things that had happened to him could have caused his illness. Zossimov also said that Zametov talked too much last night.
Razumihin and Zossimov talked a bit more, and Zossimov asked Razumihin to tell Raskolnikov’s mother and sister to be careful with him today.
Razumihin said he thought they would be fine.
Zossimov wondered why Raskolnikov was so against Luzhin, since Luzhin had money and Dounia didn’t seem to dislike him.
Razumihin got annoyed and told Zossimov to ask them himself.
Zossimov laughed at Razumihin and left, thanking the landlady for letting him stay the night.

At nine o’clock, Razumihin arrived at the ladies’ lodgings. Pulcheria Alexandrovna (Raskolnikov’s mother) was very happy to see him and almost kissed his hands. He was embarrassed, but Avdotya Romanovna (Dounia) looked grateful and friendly, which made Razumihin feel even more nervous.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna was glad to hear Raskolnikov was still asleep because she had something important to discuss. The ladies invited Razumihin to breakfast. The waiter brought tea, but everything was messy and dirty, making the ladies feel ashamed. Razumihin tried to complain about the lodgings but remembered Luzhin and stopped. He was glad when Pulcheria Alexandrovna started asking questions.

For forty-five minutes, Razumihin answered their questions. He told them about Raskolnikov’s life over the past year and about his illness, but he left out some things, like the police station incident. The ladies listened closely and wanted to know even more.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked, “Tell me, what is Raskolnikov like now? What does he like and dislike? What are his hopes and dreams?”
Dounia said, “Mother, how can he answer all that at once?”

Razumihin explained that Raskolnikov was serious, proud, and sometimes gloomy. He said Raskolnikov had a kind heart, but didn’t like to show his feelings. Sometimes he was cold and didn’t want to talk. He thought Raskolnikov’s family being here would help him get better.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna hoped this was true.

Razumihin looked at Dounia, noticing she was walking around with her arms folded, listening carefully. She was wearing a plain dress and a scarf, and their things looked poor, but she still looked proud and strong. This made Razumihin even more nervous.
Dounia said she was glad Razumihin spoke honestly about her brother and thought he needed a woman’s care.
Razumihin said, “He loves no one and maybe never will.”
Then he blurted out, “You are a lot like your brother, Avdotya Romanovna!” He felt embarrassed, but Dounia laughed.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna said that Raskolnikov was always unpredictable, even as a child. She remembered when he wanted to marry his landlady’s sick and poor daughter, even though everyone begged him not to.

Razumihin said he had heard about the marriage that didn’t happen because the girl died. He explained that the girl was not pretty and was sick but must have had good qualities, and Raskolnikov wouldn’t have cared about money.
Dounia said she was sure the girl was good.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna admitted she was almost glad the girl died, because she didn’t know who would have suffered more. She then asked Razumihin about what happened yesterday with Luzhin, looking worried.
Razumihin told them everything, blaming Raskolnikov for being rude to Luzhin on purpose, not just because he was ill.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was surprised Razumihin spoke so politely about Luzhin this morning.
She asked, “So this is your opinion of Pyotr Petrovitch?”
Razumihin said he respected her choice and only spoke badly of Luzhin last night because he was drunk and out of his mind. He felt ashamed about it now.
With no support from Dounia, Pulcheria Alexandrovna nervously said there was something that worried her a lot.

She explained that early that morning they received a note from Luzhin. He hadn’t met them at the station and said he would visit that evening at eight o’clock. In the note, Luzhin requested that Raskolnikov not be there when he came, because Raskolnikov had insulted him.

Razumihin read Luzhin’s letter. Luzhin said he couldn’t come that morning, would visit at eight o’clock, and would leave if Raskolnikov was present. He also mentioned seeing Raskolnikov give money to a poor girl after her father died, which surprised him.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was upset and asked Razumihin, “What should I do? How can I ask Rodya not to come? He’ll come on purpose if he finds out!”
Razumihin said calmly, “Do what Dounia thinks is best.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna said Dounia insisted Raskolnikov must be there at eight, but didn’t explain why. She was also confused about Raskolnikov giving money to the dead man’s daughter.
Dounia reminded her mother how much sacrifice it took for them to send Raskolnikov money.
Razumihin said Raskolnikov was not himself yesterday and mentioned something about a dead man and a girl, but Razumihin hadn’t understood.
Dounia said, “The best thing is for us to go to him ourselves. It’s getting late!”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna hurried to get ready, worried that Raskolnikov would think they were angry with him for coming late.
As the ladies got dressed, Razumihin noticed their clothes were old and had holes, but they still looked proud. He was happy to escort them.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, “I never thought I’d be afraid to see my own son, my darling Rodya! I’m afraid, Dmitri Prokofitch.”
Dounia kissed her mother and told her to have faith in Rodya.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna said she did have faith, but hadn’t slept all night.
They went outside.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna said she had dreamed of Marfa Petrovna, who was now dead, and asked if it was a good sign.
Razumihin asked, “Who is Marfa Petrovna?”
Dounia said, “Later, mother, he doesn’t know who she is.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna apologized and said she felt Razumihin was almost like family. She noticed his hurt hand and asked about it.
Razumihin was happy and said he bruised it.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna worried she might annoy Raskolnikov with her feelings and asked Razumihin how she should act.
Razumihin said, “Don’t ask him too many questions or about his health if he frowns. He doesn’t like that.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna said it was hard to be a mother, and they reached the stairs to Raskolnikov’s home.
Dounia told her mother not to worry so much and that Raskolnikov should be happy to see her.
Razumihin offered to check if Raskolnikov was awake.
As they reached the landlady’s door, they saw it was open a crack and a pair of black eyes watched them. When they noticed, the door slammed shut, making Pulcheria Alexandrovna jump.
“He is much better!” said Zossimov happily as everyone came in.

Zossimov had arrived a little earlier and was sitting on the sofa. Raskolnikov sat across from him, dressed and looking much cleaner than before. The small room quickly filled up with people. Nastasya (the maid) also came in to listen.
Raskolnikov really did look better than yesterday, but he was still pale and looked tired and sad. He seemed like someone who had been badly hurt. He didn’t talk much and moved around restlessly.

When his mother, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, and his sister, Dounia (Avdotya Romanovna), walked in, Raskolnikov’s face brightened for a second, but then looked even more full of pain. Zossimov, the young doctor, watched him closely. He noticed Raskolnikov wasn’t happy to see his family, but was determined to get through the visit. Zossimov was surprised how well Raskolnikov was able to hide his feelings, since yesterday he had been upset by even the smallest thing.
“Yes, I’m almost well now,” Raskolnikov said, as he kissed his mother and sister. Pulcheria Alexandrovna looked very happy. “This time I mean it,” he added to Razumihin, shaking his hand.

Zossimov was glad the ladies had arrived, because talking to Raskolnikov alone was hard. “If you keep getting better, you’ll be just as you were before soon,” he said. “But you need to keep busy and set a goal for yourself. That will help you recover.”
“Maybe you’re right,” Raskolnikov replied quietly.
Zossimov went on, “I think you got sick after leaving the university and having nothing to do. You need to work and have a purpose.”
“Yes, yes. I’ll hurry back to the university. Then everything will be fine,” Raskolnikov said, but he looked like he was making fun of the idea.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna thanked Zossimov for visiting them the night before.
“You saw them last night?” Raskolnikov asked, surprised. “You didn’t sleep after your trip?”
“Oh, Rodya, we’re used to staying up late. It was only until two o’clock,” said his mother.
Raskolnikov frowned. “I don’t know how to thank you, Zossimov. I don’t understand why you pay me so much attention. It makes me feel uneasy.”
Zossimov laughed. “Don’t be upset. You’re my first patient, and doctors care a lot about their first patients.”
Raskolnikov pointed at Razumihin. “I can’t say anything about him, even though I’ve only given him trouble.”
“What nonsense!” Razumihin shouted. “Why are you being so sentimental?”
Dounia watched her brother carefully, noticing something odd in his manner.
“Mother, I just realized how worried you must have been yesterday, waiting for me,” Raskolnikov said, as if reciting something.
He held out his hand to Dounia with a real smile. Dounia was happy and squeezed his hand. Pulcheria Alexandrovna’s face glowed with joy to see her children making up.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna quickly said, “Oh, Rodya, you have no idea how unhappy Dounia and I were yesterday! We came straight from the train to see you, and Nastasya told us you had a fever and ran away from the doctor. We were terrified! I even thought of that poor Lieutenant Potanchikov who had a fever and fell in a well. We almost went to find Pyotr Petrovitch for help, because we were all alone.”
“Yes, how annoying,” Raskolnikov replied, distracted.
“I only just woke up and wanted to visit you,” he explained, “but my clothes were dirty. I forgot to ask Nastasya to wash out the blood.”
“Blood? What blood?” his mother asked, afraid.
“It’s nothing. I helped carry a man who got run over,” Raskolnikov said. “A clerk.”
“But if you were delirious, how do you remember everything?” Razumihin asked.
“I remember every detail, but I don’t know why I did what I did,” Raskolnikov said.
Zossimov explained, “That happens sometimes, like in a dream.”
“So what happened with the man who was run over?” Razumihin asked.

“I got blood on me helping him,” Raskolnikov said. “Mother, I did something bad yesterday. I gave all the money you sent me to his poor widow and her children for the funeral. I know you needed the money. I shouldn’t have done it without asking. Please forgive me.”
“That’s all right, Rodya, I know you only do good things,” said his mother.
“Don’t be too sure,” Raskolnikov said, forcing a smile.
The room went quiet and everyone felt awkward.
Suddenly, Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, “Rodya, Marfa Petrovna is dead.”
“Who?”
“Marfa Petrovna Svidrigaïlov! I wrote to you about her.”
“Oh, yes. How did she die?”
“Very suddenly, the same day I sent you the letter. They say her husband beat her badly.”
“Were they really on such bad terms?” Raskolnikov asked Dounia.
“No, he was usually patient with her for years, but suddenly lost his temper,” Dounia replied.
“So he can’t have been that awful if he was patient for so long. Are you defending him?” Raskolnikov asked.
“No, I still think he’s terrible!” Dounia said, shivering.
“After the beating, she had dinner, then went to take her usual bath. She suddenly had a stroke and died,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna finished.
“Did he beat her badly?” someone asked.
“That doesn’t matter,” Dounia replied.
Raskolnikov asked, “Are you all afraid of me?”
“Yes, it’s true,” Dounia said, looking at him. “Mother was crossing herself coming up the stairs.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna said quickly, “Don’t be upset, Rodya! I was just nervous. I was so happy to see you. I’m still happy now.”
“Hush, mother,” he said, not meeting her eyes but squeezing her hand. “We’ll have time to talk.”
Suddenly, Raskolnikov felt very strange and cold inside. He realized he had just told a big lie: he would never be able to talk freely about everything.
He got up and walked to the door, but Razumihin grabbed his arm. Raskolnikov sat down again, and everyone looked at him, confused.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov shouted, “Why is everyone so quiet? Let’s talk! Say something!”
“Thank God, I was afraid you’d get sick again,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said, crossing herself.
“What’s wrong, Rodya?” Dounia asked.
“Oh, nothing! I just remembered something,” he said, laughing.
“Well, if you remembered something, that’s all right,” Zossimov said, and stood up. “I have to go, but I’ll visit again.”
“What a good man,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said.
Raskolnikov suddenly became lively. “He is good and smart. So is Razumihin. Do you like him, Dounia?” He laughed for no reason.
“Very much,” Dounia said.
“What a pig you are!” Razumihin said, blushing. Pulcheria Alexandrovna smiled, and Raskolnikov laughed loudly.
“Don’t leave, Razumihin,” Raskolnikov said. “Zossimov is gone, so stay. What time is it? That’s a nice watch, Dounia.”
“It was a present from Marfa Petrovna,” Dounia said.
“And very expensive,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna added.
“I like big watches,” Dounia said.
“I thought it was from Luzhin,” Raskolnikov said.
“No, he hasn’t given Dounia any presents yet,” his mother replied.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov said, “Remember, mother, I once wanted to get married?”
“Yes, my dear,” said his mother, looking at Dounia and Razumihin.
“She was always sick and wanted to help the poor. I don’t know why I liked her. Maybe because she was weak,” Raskolnikov said, lost in thought.
“It wasn’t just a spring dream,” Dounia said warmly.
Raskolnikov looked at her, but didn’t answer. He kissed his mother, then sat down quietly.
“You still love her?” his mother asked.
“Her? Now? No, that’s all over. Everything here feels far away. Even you seem far away now,” he said, biting his nails and falling silent.
“What a sad place you live in, Rodya!” his mother said suddenly. “It’s like a tomb. I’m sure your room made you so sad.”
“My room? Maybe it did,” he said, laughing strangely. “You said something funny just now, mother.”
Raskolnikov was starting to feel he couldn’t stand this awkward family visit anymore. But he remembered there was something important he needed to talk about.
“Dounia,” he said seriously, “I’m sorry for yesterday, but I still mean what I said: if you marry Luzhin, I can’t think of you as my sister anymore. If I’m bad, you don’t have to be. One is enough.”
“Rodya, don’t call yourself bad!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried. “You said the same yesterday.”

Dounia answered, “You think I’m marrying just to help someone else, but I’m not. I’m marrying for my sake, because life is hard for me. Of course, I want to help my family, but that’s not the main reason.”
“I’m marrying Pyotr Petrovitch because he’s better than the other choices I have. I will do what he expects and I’m not tricking him. Why are you smiling?” Dounia asked, blushing.
“You’re lying, sister,” Raskolnikov said. “You can’t respect Luzhin. You’re marrying for money. At least you can blush for it.”
“I am not lying!” Dounia cried. “I wouldn’t marry him if I didn’t respect him. If I ruin anyone, it’s only myself. I’m not committing a crime. Why do you look so pale, Rodya?”
“You’ve made him faint!” his mother exclaimed.
“No, I’m fine,” Raskolnikov said quickly. “You said you would prove today that you can respect Luzhin. How?”
“Mother, show Rodya Pyotr Petrovitch’s letter,” Dounia said.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna handed Raskolnikov the letter. He looked at Dounia, surprised, then read it twice.
“What surprises me,” Raskolnikov said, “is that Luzhin is a businessman, but he writes such a clumsy letter.”
“They all write like that,” Razumihin said.
“That’s just court language,” Razumihin added.
“Pyotr Petrovitch is proud he made his own way,” Dounia said.

“If he’s proud, that’s fine,” Raskolnikov replied. “But in the letter, he says, ‘blame yourselves,’ and threatens to leave if I come. He’s really saying he’ll abandon you if you don’t do what he wants. If one of us wrote that, you’d be angry.”
“No, you’re right,” Dounia said. “He just isn’t good at writing.”

“But there’s something else,” Raskolnikov said. “He lies about me. I gave money to a poor widow, not her daughter, and not for any trick. He wants to make us fight. He’s smart, but that’s not enough. I don’t think he values you, Dounia. I’m telling you because I want the best for you.”
Dounia didn’t answer. She had already made up her mind.
“So what will you do, Rodya?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked.
“Luzhin says you can’t come tonight or he’ll leave. Will you come?”
“That’s for you and Dounia to decide. I’ll do what you think is best.”
“Rodya, I want you to be there,” Dounia said. “Will you come?”
“Yes.”
“Razumihin, will you come at eight o’clock too?” Dounia asked.
“That’s right, Dounia,” said Pulcheria Alexandrovna. “I feel better now. Let Luzhin be angry if he wants!”

Just then, the door opened quietly, and a young girl came in, looking shy and scared. Everyone stared at her, surprised. At first, Raskolnikov didn’t know who she was. Then he realized it was Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov (sometimes called Sonia). He had met her yesterday, but she looked very different now. Today, Sonia wore a plain old dress and an old hat, and she carried a little umbrella. She looked very young, almost like a child, and very nervous. She was so shy that she almost turned to leave. Raskolnikov was surprised and felt sorry for her. He quickly asked her to stay and sit down. Razumihin, who was sitting near the door, stood up so Sonia could come in. At first, Raskolnikov showed her the sofa, but then he decided it was too personal and gave her Razumihin’s chair instead.

Sonia sat down, still shaking and looking nervously at Raskolnikov’s mother, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, and his sister, Dounia (her full name is Avdotya Romanovna). Sonia was so scared to sit near them that she stood up again and quickly spoke to Raskolnikov. “I... I have come for just a minute. I’m sorry to bother you,” she said softly. “I come from Katerina Ivanovna. She had no one else to send. She asks you... to come to the church in the morning... and after... to come to our house... to honor us...” Sonia was so nervous she couldn’t finish.

“I will try, of course,” Raskolnikov said, also sounding unsure. He asked Sonia to sit down and said he wanted to talk to her for a moment. Sonia sat down again, still very nervous. Raskolnikov blushed and seemed upset, but then he introduced her: “Mother, this is Sofya Semyonovna Marmeladov, the daughter of Mr. Marmeladov, who was run over yesterday—the man I just told you about.” Pulcheria Alexandrovna looked at Sonia, and Dounia stared at her too, trying to understand her. Sonia tried to look up but was even more embarrassed.

Raskolnikov quickly asked Sonia if the police had bothered their family after Mr. Marmeladov died. Sonia said, “No, everything was clear, so the police left us alone. Only the other people who live with us are upset because the body has stayed there too long. It’s hot, so today they will take it to the cemetery chapel until tomorrow. At first, Katerina Ivanovna didn’t want to, but now she agrees it is needed.” Sonia then asked Raskolnikov again to come to the church service and to the funeral lunch. Raskolnikov was surprised she wanted to have a lunch, but Sonia explained, “It will be simple. We counted the money to make sure there was enough, and Katerina Ivanovna really wanted it. It makes her feel better.” She thanked Raskolnikov for helping them with money the day before, saying that without him, they wouldn’t have been able to afford the funeral. Sonia tried hard not to cry.

While they talked, Raskolnikov watched Sonia closely. She was thin and pale, with a small face and sharp chin. She wasn’t pretty, but her blue eyes were kind and clear, and she looked very young, almost like a child. Her childish way of moving made her seem even younger.

Raskolnikov tried to keep the conversation going and asked Sonia why she was looking around his poor room. Sonia replied quietly, “You gave us everything yesterday,” and looked down again, embarrassed. Dounia and Pulcheria Alexandrovna both looked at Sonia kindly.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna stood up and said, “Rodya, let’s have dinner together. Dounia and I will go now. You should take a walk and rest before seeing us again.” Raskolnikov agreed, saying he had something else to do first. Razumihin was surprised and asked if they wouldn’t have dinner together. Raskolnikov said he would come, then asked Razumihin to stay a minute. Pulcheria Alexandrovna invited Razumihin to dinner too, and Dounia added, “Please do.” Razumihin was very happy. Everyone felt a bit awkward as they said goodbye. Pulcheria Alexandrovna tried to say goodbye to Sonia, but it didn’t quite work, and she hurried out. Dounia gave Sonia a polite bow; Sonia quickly curtsied, looking even more uncomfortable.
In the hallway, Raskolnikov called to Dounia, “Give me your hand.” Dounia laughed and gave him her hand again, and Raskolnikov squeezed it warmly. Dounia left, feeling happy.

Raskolnikov turned to Sonia and said, “God give peace to the dead, but the living must go on.” Sonia looked surprised at how bright he suddenly seemed. For a moment, he remembered everything about Sonia’s father.

Outside, Pulcheria Alexandrovna told Dounia she felt better after leaving Raskolnikov’s room, even though she never expected to feel that way. Dounia said Raskolnikov was still very sick and that they needed to be patient with him.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna worried aloud about what would happen if Pyotr Petrovitch (Dounia’s fiancé) broke off their engagement. Dounia said, “He wouldn’t be worth much if he did.” Pulcheria Alexandrovna was also worried about Sonia. She said she felt from the moment Sonia walked in that she was the cause of trouble. Dounia disagreed and said Sonia was a good girl, and all the rumors were nonsense. Pulcheria Alexandrovna hoped she was right, and Dounia called Pyotr Petrovitch a slanderer. They walked on in silence.

Back in the room, Raskolnikov pulled Razumihin to the window to talk. Sonia got ready to leave, but Raskolnikov stopped her, saying he wanted to talk a little more and that there were no secrets. He asked Razumihin about Porfiry Petrovitch, who is in charge of the murder case they had talked about. Raskolnikov explained that he had pawned a ring and his father’s watch at the old pawnbroker’s place and was worried about what to do. He didn’t want to lose the watch because it was special to his family. Razumihin said not to go to the police but to talk to Porfiry directly, and he was very excited about it. They decided to go right away, with Razumihin saying Porfiry would be glad to meet Raskolnikov. Raskolnikov introduced Sonia to Razumihin, saying he was a good friend.

Sonia, still embarrassed, gave her address to Raskolnikov when he asked. They all left together. Razumihin asked Raskolnikov if he locked his door, and Raskolnikov laughed, saying he never locked it and was glad not to need to. Outside, Raskolnikov asked Sonia how she found him. Sonia said he had given his address to Polenka, her little sister, yesterday. Sonia explained how she found his room, and then hurried away, glad to be alone. She thought about everything that had happened and remembered that Raskolnikov might visit her soon. She felt nervous and kept saying to herself, “Not today, please, not today!” She was so lost in thought, she didn’t notice a man following her.

This man had listened when Sonia asked about Raskolnikov and watched all three of them, especially Raskolnikov. He waited until Sonia left, then started following her. He was about fifty, tall and strong, with nice clothes and a cane. He had blond hair and a beard, blue eyes, and looked younger than his age.

When Sonia reached her house, the man followed her inside. She noticed him only when they were on the stairs. She went to her door and rang the bell at No. 9, which said “Kapernaumov, Tailor” in chalk. The man was surprised and rang the next door, No. 8.

He told Sonia, “You live at Kapernaumov’s? He fixed a waistcoat for me. I’m staying nearby. How strange!” Sonia looked at him but didn’t say anything. He said cheerfully, “We’re neighbors! I just came to town. Goodbye for now.” Sonia slipped inside, feeling uneasy.

On the way to Porfiry’s, Razumihin was very excited, saying over and over, “That’s great, brother, I’m glad!” Raskolnikov wondered what Razumihin was so happy about. Razumihin asked if Raskolnikov had pawned things at the old woman’s and when he had done it. Raskolnikov said it was two or three days before her death and that he wasn’t planning to get the things back now because he had little money left.

Razumihin said that explained why Raskolnikov kept talking about rings and chains in his fever. Raskolnikov realized everyone must have heard about it. Razumihin said Porfiry Petrovitch was very smart and really wanted to meet Raskolnikov. Raskolnikov asked why, and Razumihin explained he had talked about him, and Porfiry was interested because Raskolnikov was a law student. Razumihin apologized for anything silly he might have said while drunk.

Raskolnikov joked, “What, do they think I’m crazy?” Razumihin said not to worry. Raskolnikov got annoyed and told Razumihin to stop apologizing. They walked in silence. Raskolnikov felt nervous about meeting Porfiry and wondered if he knew Raskolnikov had visited the old woman’s flat yesterday.

Suddenly, Raskolnikov teased Razumihin, saying he seemed excited today, almost like a boy with a crush. Razumihin denied it, but Raskolnikov kept joking and said he would tell their mother about Razumihin’s blushing and neat appearance. Razumihin called him a pig, and they both laughed as they went into Porfiry Petrovitch’s apartment. Razumihin whispered, “Not a word here or I’ll... brain you!”

Raskolnikov walked into the room, trying hard not to laugh out loud. Razumihin came behind him, looking embarrassed and red-faced, with a grumpy expression. Raskolnikov bowed to Porfiry Petrovitch (the police investigator), who stood in the middle of the room. Raskolnikov tried to introduce himself, but when he looked at Razumihin, he started laughing again. Razumihin looked even angrier, which made the whole scene funny.
“Fool! You fiend,” Razumihin shouted, waving his arm and knocking over a little table with a tea-glass on it. Things fell and broke.
“Gentlemen, why break the furniture? That costs money!” said Porfiry Petrovitch, jokingly.

Raskolnikov kept laughing, but tried to stop and look serious. Razumihin felt bad about breaking the glass and went to look out the window, scowling. Porfiry Petrovitch laughed too, waiting for someone to explain what was going on. Zametov (another policeman) had been sitting in the corner, but stood up when Raskolnikov and Razumihin came in. Zametov looked surprised to see Raskolnikov.
Raskolnikov, pretending to be shy, said, “Excuse me, my name is Raskolnikov.”
“Very nice to meet you,” said Porfiry Petrovitch. “But why won’t your friend even say good morning?” He nodded at Razumihin.
“I don’t know why he’s mad,” said Raskolnikov. “I only told him he was like Romeo as we walked here.”
“Pig!” Razumihin grumbled, still looking away.
Porfiry Petrovitch laughed. “He must have a good reason to be so upset.”

Razumihin suddenly laughed too and came over to Porfiry. “Never mind! We’re all being silly. Let’s get to business. This is my friend Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov. He’s heard of you and wants to meet you. He also has a little matter to discuss. Oh, Zametov, what are you doing here? Have you met before?”
“Yes, we met at your rooms yesterday,” said Zametov.
“So I didn’t need to introduce you!” said Razumihin. “Porfiry, where’s your tobacco?”
Porfiry Petrovitch wore a dressing-gown and slippers. He was about thirty-five, short and stout, with a round head and face, and short hair. His face looked kind, but his eyes seemed serious.

Porfiry Petrovitch asked Raskolnikov to sit on the sofa and waited for him to explain his business. Raskolnikov explained clearly why he had come, and even had time to look at Porfiry, who didn’t take his eyes off Raskolnikov. Razumihin listened closely.
Porfiry Petrovitch said, “You have to give information to the police that your things were at the pawnbroker’s, and you want to get them back. Or you can write to me.”
Raskolnikov, pretending to be embarrassed, said, “The problem is I don’t have any money right now. I just wanted to say the things are mine, and I’ll get them back later.”
“That’s fine,” said Porfiry Petrovitch coldly. “Just write to me and say those things are yours.”
“On a plain piece of paper?” Raskolnikov asked.
“Yes, any paper,” said Porfiry Petrovitch, looking at him oddly, maybe even winking.
Raskolnikov thought, “He knows something!”
He said, “Sorry to trouble you. These things aren’t worth much, but they mean a lot to me because of who gave them to me.”
“That’s why you were worried when I said Porfiry was asking about the pledges,” Razumihin said.
Raskolnikov gave Razumihin an angry look, but stopped himself.
“Are you making fun of me?” he said. “These things may look like trash, but my mother would be very sad if the watch was lost. You know how mothers are.”
“No, I didn’t mean that!” said Razumihin quickly.
“Your mother is here with you?” Porfiry asked.
“Yes,” said Raskolnikov.
“When did she arrive?”
“Last night.”
Porfiry said calmly, “Your things wouldn’t have been lost anyway. I’ve been expecting you.”
“Expecting him? How did you know he had things there?” Razumihin asked.
Porfiry told Raskolnikov, “Your ring and watch were wrapped together, and your name and the date were written on the paper.”
Raskolnikov forced a smile and said, “You must have a good memory to remember all the pledges.”
“We know about everyone who had pledges. You’re the only one who hasn’t come forward,” said Porfiry.
“I haven’t been very well,” said Raskolnikov.
“I heard that too. You look pale,” said Porfiry.
Raskolnikov snapped, “No, I’m fine!” but inside he was upset and angry.
“Not well! He was delirious yesterday!” Razumihin said. “He ran off and was gone all day.”
“Really? You don’t say!” said Porfiry.
“Nonsense! Don’t believe it!” Raskolnikov said, but Porfiry didn’t notice.
“Then why did you go out if you weren’t well? Why sneak away?” Razumihin asked.
“I was tired of them,” said Raskolnikov. “I went to get new lodgings and took money with me. Zametov saw it. Was I sensible or delirious yesterday, Zametov?”
“You talked sensibly, but were very irritable,” said Zametov.
Porfiry added, “Nikodim Fomitch told me he saw you late last night at a man’s house who had been run over.”
Razumihin said, “You gave your last penny to the widow. If you wanted to help, you could have kept some money for yourself!”
“Maybe I found a treasure!” said Raskolnikov. Then he turned to Porfiry, “Sorry for wasting your time with all this.”
“Not at all! You’re very interesting to me,” said Porfiry.
“Could we have some tea?” Razumihin asked.
“Great idea! Maybe something to eat too?” said Porfiry.
Porfiry went out to order tea.

Raskolnikov was very upset and angry inside. He thought the others were trying to catch him, and wondered if they knew his secret. He worried about how they talked and looked at him, and tried to figure out if it was just his imagination.
Porfiry came back, acting more cheerful.
“Yesterday’s party left my head spinning,” he joked to Razumihin.
Razumihin said, “Rodya, yesterday we argued about whether crime is just because society is unfair. What do you think?”
“That’s a common question,” Raskolnikov said.
“It wasn’t quite like that,” said Porfiry.
“Yes, they say crime only happens because something is wrong in society,” said Razumihin.
“You’re wrong,” said Porfiry, laughing.
Razumihin argued excitedly that people aren’t just shaped by their surroundings, and that human nature is important too. He said it was silly to think that fixing society would make crime disappear.
