“He’s getting carried away!” laughed Porfiry. “But environment does matter in crime.”
“So, if a man does something terrible, is it because of his environment?” asked Razumihin.
“Maybe, yes,” said Porfiry.
Razumihin got frustrated, but everyone laughed.
“He likes to joke,” Razumihin said about Porfiry. “He even tricked us before by pretending he was getting married.”
Porfiry said, “By the way, Raskolnikov, I read your article about crime in a magazine.”
“My article? I wrote something months ago, but I sent it to another magazine.”
Porfiry explained that the magazines were joined and his article was published.
“You might even get paid for it!” said Porfiry.
“I’ll look for it in the reading-room!” said Razumihin.
“How did you know it was mine? I only signed it with an initial,” asked Raskolnikov.
“The editor told me,” said Porfiry. “I was interested.”
“I wrote about what criminals feel before and after a crime,” said Raskolnikov.
“Yes, but at the end you suggested that some special people have the right to break the law,” said Porfiry.
“What? A right to crime? Not because of the environment?” Razumihin asked.
“No, not because of that,” said Porfiry. “In his article, Raskolnikov says there are ‘ordinary’ people who must obey the law, and ‘extraordinary’ people who can break it.”
“That can’t be right,” said Razumihin, confused.

Raskolnikov replied, “It’s not exactly like that, but close. I think that some extraordinary people have an inner right to break the law if it’s for something very important, like helping all of humanity. If great leaders like Napoleon had to break old laws to do something good, they had the right to do it. But that doesn’t mean they can do anything they want. Most people are ordinary and follow the rules, but a few are extraordinary and move the world forward. There are not many of these people, but they exist.”
“Do you believe in the New Jerusalem?” Porfiry asked.
“I do,” said Raskolnikov.
“And do you believe in God?”
“I do,” Raskolnikov answered.
“Do you believe Lazarus rose from the dead?”
“Yes, I do. Why are you asking?”
Porfiry said, “But some extraordinary people do succeed in life, right?”
“Yes, some do,” said Raskolnikov.
“And then they might punish others?”
“If they think it’s needed, yes,” said Raskolnikov.
Porfiry asked, “But how do you tell extraordinary people apart from ordinary ones? Shouldn’t they wear a special uniform, so others know?”
“Oh, people often make mistakes about which group they belong to!” said Raskolnikov.
“But only ordinary people make that mistake,” he said. “Real extraordinary people are rare and often unnoticed. People who pretend get put back in their place, so don’t worry.”
“How many extraordinary people are there?” asked Porfiry. “It would be scary if there were a lot.”
“Don’t worry, there are very few,” said Raskolnikov. “Maybe one in a thousand, or even less. A true genius is one in a million.”
“Are you two joking?” Razumihin asked. “Rodya, are you serious?”
Raskolnikov didn’t reply. Razumihin thought Porfiry was being rude.
Razumihin said, “If you really believe this, Rodya, the scary part is that you say it’s okay to kill for a good reason.”
“It is more scary than the law,” Porfiry agreed.
“You must be exaggerating. I’ll read your article. I don’t believe it,” said Razumihin.
“It’s not all in the article,” said Raskolnikov. “Just a hint.”
Porfiry said, “Sorry to ask more, but what if someone young thinks he’s a Napoleon and tries to get money for a big idea by stealing or worse?”
“That can happen,” said Raskolnikov calmly. “Foolish people, especially young ones, might fall for that.”
“Well then?”
“That’s not my fault,” said Raskolnikov. “Society has prisons and police. Just catch the criminal.”
“And if we catch him?”
“He gets punished.”
“But what about his conscience?” asked Porfiry.
“Why do you care?” said Raskolnikov.
“Just out of humanity.”
“If he has a conscience, he’ll suffer. That’s his punishment too.”
“But what about real geniuses?” Razumihin asked. “Shouldn’t they feel sorry for their crimes?”
“Great men always have sadness,” Raskolnikov said softly.
He stood up, looking serious. Everyone else stood too.
Porfiry said, “One last question. When you wrote your article, did you think of yourself as extraordinary?”
“Maybe,” Raskolnikov answered coldly.
“If you were in trouble, would you steal or murder for a good cause?” asked Porfiry, winking.
“If I did, I wouldn’t tell you,” said Raskolnikov.
“I don’t think I’m a Napoleon or anyone like that, so I can’t answer,” he said.
“In Russia, everyone thinks they’re a Napoleon,” said Porfiry.
“Maybe a future Napoleon killed Alyona Ivanovna last week?” said Zametov.
Raskolnikov stared at Porfiry. Razumihin looked angry. It was silent. Raskolnikov turned to go.
“Are you leaving already?” said Porfiry politely. “Don’t worry about your things. Come see me tomorrow at eleven o’clock. Maybe you can help us.”
“Do you want to question me formally?” asked Raskolnikov.
“No, not now. I talk to everyone who had pledges. You’re the last. By the way,” he added, “when you went upstairs to the pawnbroker’s, it was after seven, right?”
“Yes,” said Raskolnikov, wishing he hadn’t.
“Did you see any painters in a flat with an open door on the second floor? It’s important.”
“Painters? No, I didn’t see them. But on the fourth floor, some men were moving a sofa and squeezed me against the wall. But no painters, and no open flat that I remember.”
“Wait!” Razumihin cried. “The painters were there on the day of the murder, but Raskolnikov was there three days before. Why are you asking?”
“Oh, I mixed it up!” said Porfiry, slapping his forehead. “Sorry, I’m confused. It would help us if someone saw the painters at that time.”
Porfiry walked them to the door very politely.
Outside, Raskolnikov and Razumihin walked in silence, feeling gloomy. Raskolnikov took a deep breath.

Razumihin was very confused. He kept saying, “I don’t believe it, I can’t believe it!” as he and Raskolnikov walked to Bakaleyev’s house, where Pulcheria Alexandrovna (Raskolnikov’s mother) and Dounia (his sister) were waiting. Razumihin kept stopping to argue because they were finally talking honestly about Raskolnikov’s troubles.

Raskolnikov just smiled and said, “Don’t believe it, then! You never notice anything, but I pay attention to every word.” Razumihin replied, “You’re too suspicious. Yes, Porfiry and Zametov did act strange, but why? If they really suspected you, they’d hide it. But they were bold and careless.” Raskolnikov explained, “If they had any proof, they’d try to trick me and search my room. But they have nothing real, just guesses. Maybe Porfiry wanted to scare me by pretending he knew more.”

Razumihin agreed but was angry. “It’s insulting! They only suspect you because you are a poor student, sick, lonely, and you fainted at the police station. That’s all! If I were you, I’d just laugh at them. Don’t let it get you down.”

Raskolnikov, still upset, said, “But now I have to talk to them again tomorrow. I’m annoyed I even spoke to Zametov yesterday.” Razumihin decided, “Then I’ll talk to Porfiry myself and find out what’s going on!”

Suddenly Razumihin stopped Raskolnikov and argued about the police’s questions. He said, “You think their question about the painters was a trap. But if you had done it, would you have said you saw the painters?” Raskolnikov replied, “Yes, I would have. Only silly people deny everything. Smarter people admit what can’t be denied and try to explain it away. Porfiry probably expected me to say I saw the painters to sound truthful, then he’d catch me on a small detail.” They talked more about how clever people can get caught in simple ways.
Raskolnikov laughed, surprised at how openly he was talking. Suddenly, he felt nervous as they reached Bakaleyev’s house.

Raskolnikov suddenly said, “Go in without me. I’ll be back soon.” When Razumihin tried to come along, Raskolnikov got upset and shouted at him. Razumihin watched Raskolnikov hurry away, then promised himself he would get answers from Porfiry today. He went inside to calm Pulcheria Alexandrovna.

When Raskolnikov got home, he was sweaty and out of breath. He went straight to his room and checked the hiding place in the corner where he had put some things. He searched carefully but found nothing. He worried that something might have slipped out and could be found as proof against him.
Raskolnikov stood lost in thought, then left his room, confused.

Suddenly, he heard someone call, “Here he is!” The porter pointed him out to a short man in a long coat, who looked a bit like a woman and had a wrinkled, unhappy face. The man stared at Raskolnikov, then walked away without a word.

Raskolnikov asked the porter what happened. The porter said, “That man asked if a student named Raskolnikov lived here. I pointed you out, and he left.” Raskolnikov ran after the stranger and followed him, finally walking beside him.

Raskolnikov asked, “Were you looking for me?” The man said nothing. Then, suddenly, he looked at Raskolnikov and said quietly, “Murderer!” Raskolnikov felt cold and scared. He asked, “Who is a murderer?” The man replied, “You are a murderer,” and walked away, leaving Raskolnikov standing in shock.
Raskolnikov slowly walked home, feeling weak and chilled. He lay on his sofa, exhausted and not really thinking, just seeing random memories and pictures in his mind.

He heard Razumihin and Nastasya whispering not to wake him. After a while, Raskolnikov opened his eyes and started to worry again about the strange man and whether someone had seen what he did. He thought about Nikolay finding the jewel box, and how even tiny clues could become big problems. He felt weak and angry with himself for what he had done.

He started thinking about his mother and Dounia and felt like he couldn’t be near them. Then he remembered Lizaveta, the other woman hurt because she came in at the wrong time, and Sonia, who was always gentle and kind. He felt sorry for them.

Raskolnikov lost track of time and suddenly found himself outside in the evening, not remembering how he got there. He saw the same strange man again and followed him into a building. Raskolnikov found himself in the old woman’s apartment, just like the night of the crime. Everything was quiet and strange. He saw a cloak hanging and behind it, the old woman was sitting, laughing silently. Suddenly, there were people everywhere, watching him. He tried to run but couldn’t move. He woke up screaming—it was just a nightmare.
But as he woke up, his door opened and a man he didn’t know stood there, staring at him.
Raskolnikov pretended to be asleep, wondering if he was still dreaming. He peeked and saw the man come in, sit down, and wait without saying a word. The man was older, with a full, light beard.
After a while, Raskolnikov sat up and asked, “What do you want?”
The man smiled and said, “I knew you were only pretending to sleep. My name is Arkady Ivanovitch Svidrigaïlov. Nice to meet you.”

Raskolnikov wondered if he was dreaming. He looked at the man who had just come in. It was Svidrigaïlov (a man who once tried to bother Raskolnikov’s sister, Avdotya Romanovna). Raskolnikov couldn’t believe it was really him.

Svidrigaïlov said he had come for two reasons. First, he wanted to meet Raskolnikov because he had heard a lot about him. Second, he hoped Raskolnikov would help him talk to Avdotya Romanovna. Svidrigaïlov thought Raskolnikov could help because Avdotya Romanovna did not like him.
Raskolnikov stopped him and said he would not help. He also said that no one in his family liked Svidrigaïlov and wanted nothing to do with him. Raskolnikov told Svidrigaïlov to leave.

Svidrigaïlov laughed and said he had hoped to trick Raskolnikov, but it did not work. He kept talking about things that happened between him, Marfa Petrovna (his late wife), and Avdotya Romanovna. Raskolnikov rudely asked if Svidrigaïlov had something to do with Marfa Petrovna’s death. Svidrigaïlov said no, that she died of sickness after eating and bathing, and that doctors agreed. Still, he wondered if he had upset her too much.

Raskolnikov laughed at Svidrigaïlov for worrying. Svidrigaïlov said he only hit Marfa Petrovna twice in seven years, and that she was not really upset. He said some people even like being insulted, though Raskolnikov thought this was strange.

Raskolnikov thought about leaving but stayed, curious. He asked if Svidrigaïlov liked fighting. Svidrigaïlov said no, and explained more about his life with Marfa Petrovna. He talked about people in town and how he was once in debt, but Marfa Petrovna helped him pay it off. She was older than him and loved him, but she also kept the document showing he owed her money, just in case.

Raskolnikov asked if the document was the only thing keeping Svidrigaïlov there. Svidrigaïlov said no, he just didn’t want to leave. Marfa Petrovna even wanted him to travel, but he didn’t like traveling. He said it made him sad, and he preferred to stay home. He also mentioned hearing about someone flying in a balloon, but didn’t want to go himself.

Svidrigaïlov explained that Marfa Petrovna eventually gave him back the document and gave him some money too. He managed the estate well and read books, but she worried he would study too much. Raskolnikov asked if Svidrigaïlov missed Marfa Petrovna. Svidrigaïlov said maybe, then suddenly asked if Raskolnikov believed in ghosts.

Raskolnikov was surprised, but Svidrigaïlov said he had seen Marfa Petrovna three times after she died: once after her funeral, once at a train station, and once in his room. Svidrigaïlov said she just talked about small things, like winding the clock or her dress, and then left. Raskolnikov wondered if Svidrigaïlov was telling the truth. Svidrigaïlov said he almost never lied. He told another story about seeing the ghost of a servant named Filka.

Raskolnikov said Svidrigaïlov should see a doctor. Svidrigaïlov replied that he felt strong and that just because only sick people see ghosts doesn’t mean ghosts aren’t real. He said maybe ghosts are part of another world, and when people get sick, they get closer to that world.

Raskolnikov said he didn’t believe in life after death. Svidrigaïlov wondered if maybe the afterlife was just a small, spider-filled room, instead of something big and wonderful. Raskolnikov was shocked by this idea.
Svidrigaïlov pointed out that just a little while ago they were strangers and now were talking about deep things. He said maybe they were alike.
Raskolnikov, annoyed, asked Svidrigaïlov to explain why he had come, since he wanted to leave.
Svidrigaïlov asked about Avdotya Romanovna’s marriage to Mr. Luzhin (Pyotr Petrovitch). Raskolnikov told him not to talk about his sister, but Svidrigaïlov said he came to talk about her.

Svidrigaïlov said he thought Mr. Luzhin was not a good match for Avdotya Romanovna. He believed she was marrying him for her family and would be happier if the marriage was stopped. Svidrigaïlov said he wanted to help.
Svidrigaïlov admitted he no longer loved Avdotya Romanovna but had once been impressed by her.
He realized he didn’t really want to marry her anymore, but had thought about it when he came to Petersburg.

Svidrigaïlov said he was planning a trip and wanted to settle things before he left. He had left his children with an aunt, and they were fine. He wanted to give Avdotya Romanovna ten thousand roubles to help her break off the marriage with Mr. Luzhin. He wanted to apologize for his past actions and help her.

Raskolnikov was shocked and called Svidrigaïlov crazy for making such an offer. Svidrigaïlov explained he had no bad intentions and didn’t need the money anyway. He just wanted to do something good for Avdotya Romanovna after causing her trouble. He said if Raskolnikov didn’t tell her about the offer, he would try to see her himself.
Raskolnikov asked if Svidrigaïlov would leave Avdotya Romanovna alone if he passed on the message. Svidrigaïlov said he would still like to see her, but wasn’t sure.
Svidrigaïlov stood up and got ready to go. He said he didn’t mean to bother Raskolnikov and added that he had seen him earlier that morning.
Raskolnikov was uneasy and asked where Svidrigaïlov saw him. Svidrigaïlov said it was by chance, and that Raskolnikov reminded him of himself.
Raskolnikov asked about Svidrigaïlov’s upcoming trip. Svidrigaïlov replied that maybe he would travel, or maybe get married instead, because people were trying to find him a new wife.

Svidrigaïlov then remembered something else: he told Raskolnikov that Marfa Petrovna had left Avdotya Romanovna three thousand roubles in her will. Avdotya Romanovna would get the money in a few weeks.
Raskolnikov asked if this was true, and Svidrigaïlov said yes. Then, Svidrigaïlov said goodbye and left. On his way out, he ran into Razumihin in the doorway.
It was almost eight o’clock. Raskolnikov and Razumihin hurried down the street, trying to reach Bakaleyev’s before Luzhin got there.
“Who was that man?” Razumihin asked as they walked.

“That was Svidrigaïlov,” said Raskolnikov. “He’s the landowner where my sister, Dounia, used to work as a governess. He bothered her so much that his wife, Marfa Petrovna, sent Dounia away. Later, Marfa Petrovna apologized. She just died. Svidrigaïlov came here right after her funeral. He’s strange and I’m worried about what he wants. We have to protect Dounia from him.”
“Protect her? What could he do?” asked Razumihin. “But don’t worry, Rodya, we’ll keep her safe. Do you know where he’s staying?”
“No, I didn’t ask,” said Raskolnikov.
“That’s too bad. I’ll find out,” said Razumihin.
“Did you see him?” Raskolnikov asked.
“Yes, I saw him well,” said Razumihin.
“You’re sure?” asked Raskolnikov.
“Yes, I remember his face,” said Razumihin.
They walked in silence for a while.
“Maybe I just imagined him,” Raskolnikov muttered.
“What do you mean?” Razumihin asked.
“Maybe I’m really going mad and seeing things,” Raskolnikov said quietly.
“Come on, you’re just upset,” said Razumihin. “But what did Svidrigaïlov want?”

Raskolnikov didn’t answer, so Razumihin started telling his own story. He explained how he went to see Porfiry and Zametov. He tried to talk, but things didn’t go well. He argued with Porfiry, got angry, and left. At first, he was worried about messing things up, but then he decided they shouldn’t care about what Porfiry and Zametov think. “Let’s just laugh at them!” Razumihin said.
Raskolnikov agreed, but wondered what Razumihin would think if he ever found out the truth.

They reached Bakaleyev’s and saw Luzhin in the hallway. All three entered together. Pulcheria Alexandrovna (Raskolnikov’s mother) greeted Luzhin, and Dounia welcomed her brother. They all sat at the table for tea. Dounia and Luzhin sat opposite each other; Razumihin and Raskolnikov sat near Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
For a moment, no one spoke. Luzhin blew his nose loudly and looked important, but also a little annoyed.

Luzhin asked Pulcheria Alexandrovna if they had a good trip. Dounia said she was fine, but her mother was tired. Luzhin talked about how long Russian train rides were. Pulcheria Alexandrovna thanked Razumihin for helping them when they arrived and introduced him to Luzhin.
Luzhin barely nodded to Razumihin and went quiet. Everyone was silent again. Pulcheria Alexandrovna started talking about Marfa Petrovna’s death.

Luzhin said he already knew, and that Svidrigaïlov had come to Petersburg right after the funeral. Dounia was worried to hear this. Luzhin said he was trying to find out where Svidrigaïlov was staying.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna said she was scared of Svidrigaïlov and even thought he caused Marfa Petrovna’s death.

Luzhin explained some bad things he had heard about Svidrigaïlov. He said Marfa Petrovna once helped Svidrigaïlov avoid being sent to Siberia for a terrible crime. He said Svidrigaïlov was not a good man.

Dounia asked if Luzhin really had proof of all this. Luzhin told a story about a girl who had died and how people said Svidrigaïlov was cruel. Dounia remembered hearing that a servant named Philip had hanged himself, and some people blamed Svidrigaïlov.
Luzhin said Dounia seemed to defend Svidrigaïlov, but he still wanted to help protect her and her mother. He thought Svidrigaïlov would get into trouble again soon.
Dounia asked Luzhin to stop talking about Svidrigaïlov because it made her sad.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov said, “He just came to see me.”

Everyone was surprised. Raskolnikov explained that Svidrigaïlov visited while he was asleep and wanted to meet Dounia to make her a proposal. He also said Marfa Petrovna left Dounia three thousand roubles in her will.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna thanked God for the money. Luzhin said it was true. Dounia asked Raskolnikov what else Svidrigaïlov wanted. Raskolnikov said he would tell her later.
Luzhin looked at his watch and got ready to leave. Dounia stopped him. She said he wanted to talk with her and her mother, so he sat down again.
Luzhin said he couldn’t speak openly with Raskolnikov there, and complained that his request for a private meeting had been ignored.
Dounia said it was her idea for her brother to be present. She wanted everything out in the open and said if Raskolnikov had insulted Luzhin, he would apologize.

Luzhin grew more upset. He said some insults can’t be forgiven. Dounia insisted they had to solve everything now. She said if Luzhin and Raskolnikov couldn’t be friends, she would have to choose between them. She wanted to know who really cared for her.
Luzhin got angry and said Dounia shouldn’t talk like that, as if he was less important than her brother. Dounia said she had always valued her family, but now had to be sure who mattered most.

Luzhin said that loving a husband should come before loving a brother. Then he told Pulcheria Alexandrovna that Raskolnikov had insulted him by making fun of something Luzhin said about marrying a poor girl. He wanted to know how she wrote about it in her letter.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna couldn’t remember exactly what she wrote, but said she and Dounia didn’t think Luzhin’s words were so bad, otherwise they wouldn’t have come.
Luzhin said Raskolnikov must have exaggerated, and blamed Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna got braver and said Luzhin had also written something untrue about Raskolnikov.
Luzhin denied it. Raskolnikov said Luzhin wrote that he gave money to a girl he didn’t know, to make trouble between him and his family. He called this mean and false.
Luzhin said he only answered questions about Raskolnikov, and asked Raskolnikov to prove he was wrong.
Raskolnikov said the girl Luzhin was talking about was better than Luzhin himself, and that he had already let her sit with his mother and Dounia.
Everyone was shocked. Luzhin said this showed why he and Dounia couldn’t get along, and he decided to leave. He asked not to have such meetings again.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was a little hurt and said Luzhin acted like he was in charge, but that they needed kindness since they came to Petersburg for him.
Luzhin said things were different now that Dounia had money from Marfa Petrovna. Dounia said it sounded like Luzhin expected them to be helpless.
Luzhin said he would leave, and hoped they enjoyed talking about Svidrigaïlov’s proposal.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna was shocked. Razumihin fidgeted in his chair.
Raskolnikov asked Dounia if she was ashamed. Dounia said she was and told Luzhin to leave.
Luzhin was surprised and couldn’t believe Dounia was sending him away.
Luzhin warned that if he left, he would never come back.
“Good!” said Dounia, standing up. Luzhin got angry and said he could protest.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna told him he had no right to speak to Dounia that way and told him to leave.
Luzhin complained about the money he had spent, but Raskolnikov just laughed. Pulcheria Alexandrovna got angry and said he had not paid for their trunk, so he had no real expenses.
Dounia begged her mother to stop. She told Luzhin to please go.
Luzhin, still angry, said he had helped Dounia’s reputation after people had gossiped about her and that he deserved thanks. He said maybe he had been foolish to do so.
Razumihin jumped up angrily and Dounia called Luzhin mean and spiteful. Raskolnikov held Razumihin back and quietly told Luzhin to leave the room.
Luzhin glared at Raskolnikov, then turned and left in a fury, blaming Raskolnikov for everything. Even as he went downstairs, he still hoped he might get Dounia back one day.

Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin had never believed Dounia (Avdotya Romanovna) and her mother could leave him. He was very proud and thought he was smarter than everyone else. He loved looking at himself in the mirror and cared most about his money, which made him feel important.

When Luzhin told Dounia he was marrying her even though people gossiped about her, he really thought he was being generous. But he knew the rumors were not true, and everyone already liked Dounia. Still, he thought he was heroic for choosing her, and he wanted everyone to thank him. When Luzhin left, he felt hurt and angry that no one admired him.

Luzhin needed Dounia. He had always dreamed of marrying a poor girl who would be grateful to him and look up to him. He thought Dounia was perfect—she was smart, good, and proud. He wanted her to think he was her hero. He also hoped that marrying her would help him be more important in society. Luzhin was planning to start a new business in Petersburg and thought a good wife would help. Now, everything was ruined. He was upset and wanted to fix things the next day. He blamed Raskolnikov for the breakup, but he was more worried about Svidrigaïlov. Luzhin had a lot to think about.
“It was my fault!” Dounia told her mother, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, hugging her. “I thought about his money, but I didn’t know he was a bad man. If I had known, nothing would have tempted me!”
“God has saved us!” whispered Pulcheria Alexandrovna, still not believing it.

Soon they all felt better and even laughed. Dounia still looked worried sometimes, remembering what happened. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was surprised that she felt happy, since she had thought breaking up with Luzhin would be terrible. Razumihin was very happy and excited, hoping now he could help the family more. Raskolnikov, though, just sat quietly. Even though he wanted Luzhin gone, he now seemed the least interested. Dounia thought maybe her brother was still angry.
Dounia went to Raskolnikov. “What did Svidrigaïlov say to you?”
“Yes, tell us!” said Pulcheria Alexandrovna.
Raskolnikov said, “He wants to give you ten thousand roubles, and he wants to see you when I am there.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna cried, “See her? Never! And how dare he offer her money!”
Raskolnikov told them what Svidrigaïlov had said, but he left out the strange story about Marfa Petrovna’s ghost.
“What did you tell him?” asked Dounia.

“At first I said I wouldn’t give you his message,” Raskolnikov answered. “Then he said he would try to see you anyway. He said he doesn’t love you anymore and doesn’t want you to marry Luzhin. He talked a lot but it didn’t make much sense.”
“What do you think about him, Rodya?” Dounia asked.

“I really don’t understand him,” said Raskolnikov. “He says he wants to give you money, but also says he isn’t rich. He says he is leaving, then forgets and talks about marrying someone else. I think he has a secret plan, and maybe it’s not good. He acted very strange—maybe he is pretending, or maybe he is really upset after Marfa Petrovna died.”

“God bless her soul,” Pulcheria Alexandrovna said. “We would be lost without her three thousand roubles! Rodya, this morning we only had three roubles left, and Dounia and I were thinking of pawning her watch so we wouldn’t have to borrow from Luzhin.”
Dounia looked worried after hearing about Svidrigaïlov’s offer.
“He must have a terrible plan,” she whispered, shivering.
Raskolnikov saw how scared she was.
“I think I’ll have to see him again,” he told Dounia.
“We’ll watch him! I’ll keep an eye on him!” Razumihin said bravely. “Rodya told me to take care of you, Avdotya Romanovna. Will you let me?”
Dounia smiled and shook Razumihin’s hand, but she still looked worried. Pulcheria Alexandrovna looked at her carefully, but holding the three thousand roubles made her feel better.
Fifteen minutes later, everyone was talking happily. Even Raskolnikov listened. Razumihin was full of ideas.

“Why should you leave?” Razumihin said. “You’re all together now and need each other. Let’s work together! I have an uncle who wants to lend me money, and with some of your money, we can start a business. We can be partners!”
Razumihin explained his plan: He wanted to start a publishing company because he knew how to work with books and believed they could make money by translating and publishing good stories.
“Why miss this chance?” Razumihin said. “We have the money and the skills. We’ll work hard, learn, and publish good books. I know the business well, and we’ll start small and grow.”
Dounia’s eyes sparkled.
“I like your idea, Dmitri Prokofitch!” she said.
“I don’t really know about this,” said Pulcheria Alexandrovna, “but maybe it’s good. We should stay here for now.” She looked at Raskolnikov.
“What do you think, brother?” Dounia asked.
“I think it’s a good idea,” Raskolnikov replied. “It’s too soon for a big business, but we can start with a few books. Razumihin knows what he’s doing. We’ll talk more later.”

“Great!” Razumihin cheered. “There’s an apartment in this building you could rent—three rooms, not too expensive. I can pawn your watch tomorrow and bring the money. You can all live together, and Rodya can stay with you. But where are you going, Rodya?”
“Are you leaving already?” Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked, surprised.
“Now, at this moment?” said Razumihin.
Dounia stared at her brother in disbelief. Raskolnikov was holding his cap, ready to go.
“You act like it’s the last time we’ll see each other,” he said, trying to smile. “Maybe it is...”
“What’s wrong?” cried his mother.
“Where are you going, Rodya?” asked Dounia.
“I just... have to go,” he said, sounding unsure, but his face was serious.

“I wanted to tell you, Mother and Dounia, that it would be better if we didn’t see each other for a while. I feel sick and unhappy. I’ll come back when I can. Please leave me alone for now. If you love me, let me go. Good-bye!”
“Oh no!” Pulcheria Alexandrovna and Dounia were very scared. Even Razumihin was worried.
“Rodya, please make up with us! Let’s be together again!” said his mother.
Raskolnikov walked slowly to the door. Dounia ran after him.
“Brother, what are you doing to Mother?” she whispered, upset.
He looked at her sadly.
“It’s okay. I’ll come... I’m coming,” he mumbled, and left.
“He’s so selfish!” cried Dounia.
“He’s not heartless—just sick. He’s not himself! You’re the one being hard!” Razumihin whispered, squeezing her hand. “I’ll be back soon,” he shouted to the worried mother, and ran after Raskolnikov.
Raskolnikov was waiting for Razumihin in the hallway.
“I knew you’d follow me,” Raskolnikov said. “Go back to them—stay with them always. Maybe I’ll come back... if I can. Good-bye.”
He walked away without saying more.
“Where are you going? Why are you acting like this?” Razumihin called after him.
Raskolnikov stopped again.
“Don’t ask me anything. I have nothing to say. Don’t come to see me. Stay with them. Do you understand?”
They stood quietly in the dark hallway, looking at each other. Razumihin felt something strange pass between them, something scary. He turned pale.
“Do you understand now?” Raskolnikov said, his face twitching. “Go back to them,” he said, then quickly left.
After that, Razumihin went back to the ladies. He comforted them, promised that Rodya just needed rest, and said he would take care of them like a son and a brother from now on.

Raskolnikov walked to the old green house by the canal where Sonia lived. He asked the porter for directions to Kapernaumov the tailor, and found the dark, narrow staircase. He climbed to the second floor and walked along a dark hallway. Suddenly, a door opened near him and he grabbed it.
“Who is there?” a woman asked nervously.
“It’s me. I’ve come to see you,” Raskolnikov said, stepping inside.
Sonia stood by a candle on a broken chair. When she saw Raskolnikov, she was surprised and didn’t know what to say.
“Which is your room? This way?” Raskolnikov asked, trying not to look at her, and walked in.

Sonia followed him, carrying the candle. She set it down and stood in front of him, looking very upset and scared. She was pale, and tears filled her eyes. Raskolnikov sat on a chair and looked around the room.
The room was big but very low. There was hardly any furniture, just a bed, a table, and a few chairs. The walls were old and dirty. It was clear Sonia was very poor.
Sonia watched Raskolnikov nervously as he looked around.
“I’m late... It’s eleven, isn’t it?” he asked, not looking up.
“Yes, it is,” Sonia answered quietly. “I heard the clock.”
“I’ve come to you for the last time,” Raskolnikov said sadly, even though it was his first visit. “I might not see you again.”
“Are you going away?”
“I don’t know... maybe tomorrow.”
“So you won’t come to Katerina Ivanovna tomorrow?” Sonia’s voice shook.
“I don’t know. I’ll see in the morning. But that’s not why I came. I want to say something...”
Raskolnikov noticed Sonia was still standing. “Why are you standing? Sit down,” he said gently.
Sonia sat. Raskolnikov looked at her kindly. “You’re so thin. Your hand is like a shadow,” he said, taking her hand. Sonia smiled a little.
“I’ve always been like that,” she said.
“Even when you lived at home?”
“Yes.”
Raskolnikov looked away and changed the subject.
“You rent this room from the Kapernaumovs?”
“Yes.”
“Do they live next door?”
“Yes, with their children.”
“I’d be afraid to sleep here at night,” Raskolnikov said.
“They’re good people,” Sonia answered. “All the furniture is theirs. The children come to see me.”
“They all stammer, don’t they?”
“Yes. The father stammers and is lame. The mother can’t speak well. They have seven children. Only the oldest stammers; the others are just sick. But how do you know about them?”
“Your father told me. He told me about you and how Katerina Ivanovna knelt by your bed.”
Sonia looked embarrassed.
“I thought I saw my father today,” she whispered.
“Who?”
“Father. I was walking outside and I thought I saw him ahead of me. I wanted to go to Katerina Ivanovna....”
“You were walking in the streets?”
“Yes,” she whispered, looking down.
“Did Katerina Ivanovna ever beat you?”
“No! Never!” Sonia said, upset.
“You love her, then?”
“Of course! You don’t understand. She’s like a child... her mind isn’t well because she’s so sad. She used to be smart and kind. You just don’t know!”
Sonia was upset and wrung her hands. She looked very sad, but also wanted to defend Katerina Ivanovna.
“Beat me? Never! And even if she did, what does it matter? She’s so unhappy. She thinks everyone should be good, but people aren’t. She just doesn’t see it.”
“And what will happen to you?” Raskolnikov asked.
“Will they stay with you?” he asked. “You took care of them before. Your father used to come to you for money. What now?”
“I don’t know,” Sonia said sadly.
“Will they stay here?”
“I don’t know. They owe rent, and the landlady wants them to leave. Katerina Ivanovna says she won’t stay another minute.”
“How is she so bold? Does she count on you?”

“No! We’re like one family. What else could she do? She has so much hope, she wants to start a new life in her old town, open a school, and take me with her. But she’s sick, always working, always worried. Today we tried to buy shoes for Polenka and Lida, but didn’t have enough money. In the shop she cried because she couldn’t pay. It was so sad.”
“Now I understand why you live like this,” Raskolnikov said bitterly.
“Aren’t you sorry for them?” Sonia asked. “I know you gave your last coin, even if you didn’t see everything. I’ve made her cry too, only last week. I can be cruel!”
“You were cruel?”

“Yes. I went to see them, and father asked me to read to him, but I said no because I wanted to show Katerina Ivanovna some collars I bought from Lizaveta. Katerina Ivanovna liked them and wanted them so much, but I didn’t want to give them to her. She was so sad, not because of the collars, but because I refused her. I wish I could take it back.”
“Did you know Lizaveta, the pedlar?”
“Yes. Did you?”
“Katerina Ivanovna is very ill. She will soon die,” Raskolnikov said.
“No, no, no!” Sonia cried and grabbed his hands.
“It might be better if she did,” Raskolnikov said.
“No! Not better at all!” Sonia said, upset.
“And the children? Will you take care of them?”
“I don’t know,” Sonia cried, holding her head.
“What if you get sick and go to the hospital? What will happen to them?” Raskolnikov asked.
“How can you say that? That can’t happen!”

“You’re not safe from it,” Raskolnikov said. “If you get sick, Katerina Ivanovna and the children will be left alone. She’ll beg and the children will cry. She’ll get taken to the hospital and die. Then what?”
“God won’t let that happen!” Sonia cried.
Sonia looked at him, begging for help.
Raskolnikov got up and walked around the room. Sonia hung her head, very sad.
“Can’t you save any money?” he asked.
“No,” Sonia whispered.
“Have you tried?” he asked.
“Yes,” Sonia said softly.
“You don’t get money every day?” Raskolnikov asked.
Sonia blushed.
“No,” she whispered.
“It will be the same with Polenka, won’t it?” he said suddenly.
“No, never! God wouldn’t let it happen!” Sonia cried.
“He lets others come to it.”
“No, God will protect her!” Sonia said.
“Maybe there is no God,” Raskolnikov said, laughing.
Sonia looked at him, shocked and hurt. She hid her face and cried.
“You say Katerina Ivanovna’s mind is unhinged—your mind is, too,” Raskolnikov said.
Five minutes passed. Raskolnikov walked around, then went to Sonia. He put his hands on her shoulders, looked into her tearful face, then suddenly knelt and kissed her foot. Sonia drew back, scared.
“What are you doing?” she whispered, feeling afraid.
Raskolnikov stood up.

“I didn’t bow to you, but to all people who suffer,” he said wildly, then turned to the window. “Listen, I told a rude man today that he wasn’t worth your little finger, and that I honored my sister by letting her sit beside you.”
“You said that? And in front of them?” Sonia cried, frightened. “Sit with me? An honor? But I’m... dishonored. Why did you say that?”

“It wasn’t for your shame, but because you suffer so much. But you are a great sinner, too. You’ve thrown yourself away for nothing. Isn’t it awful, living in this way, hating it, and not helping anyone? Why do you do it? Wouldn’t it be better to jump in the canal and end it?”
“But what would happen to them?” Sonia asked quietly.
“Do you pray to God a lot, Sonia?” he asked.
“What would I be without God?” she whispered quickly, squeezing his hand.
“What does God do for you?” he asked.
“Be quiet! Don’t ask! You don’t deserve to know!” Sonia cried.
“He does everything,” she whispered.
There was a book on the chest of drawers. Raskolnikov picked it up. It was the New Testament, old and worn.
“Where did you get this?” he asked.
“It was brought to me,” Sonia answered quietly.
“Who brought it?”
“Lizaveta. I asked her for it.”
“Where is the story of Lazarus?” he asked.
“Find it and read it to me, Sonia.”
“You’re not looking in the right place... It’s in the fourth gospel,” Sonia said.
“Find it and read it,” Raskolnikov said, sitting down.
Sonia hesitated, but took the book.
“Haven’t you read it?” she asked.
“Long ago. Read!” he said.
“You go to church often?”
“N-no,” Sonia whispered.
“Will you go to your father’s funeral tomorrow?”
“Yes, and I went to church last week for Lizaveta. She was killed with an axe.”
“Were you friends with Lizaveta?”
“Yes. She was kind. We read and talked together. She will see God,” Sonia said.
“Read!” Raskolnikov said impatiently.
“Why? You don’t believe...” Sonia whispered.
“Read! I want to hear. You used to read to Lizaveta.”
Sonia opened the book, hands shaking. She tried to start but her voice broke.
“Now a certain man was sick named Lazarus of Bethany...” she managed to read, but stopped, her voice trembling.
Raskolnikov saw how hard it was for her, but insisted. Sonia struggled, but continued reading the story of Lazarus, how Jesus raised him from the dead.
She read how Martha and Mary were sad for their brother Lazarus.
Martha went to Jesus.
She said, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
“But I know God will do whatever you ask,” she read.
Jesus said, “Your brother will rise again.”
Martha said, “I know he will rise at the last day.”
Jesus said, “I am the resurrection and the life. Anyone who believes in me, even if he dies, will live.”
“She said to Him—” Sonia read, then stopped to take a breath.
“Yes, Lord, I believe that You are the Christ, the Son of God who was to come into the world.”
Sonia read how Mary fell at Jesus’ feet and cried, “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”
Jesus saw her crying and was troubled.
He asked, “Where have you laid him?”
“Jesus wept.”
The people saw how much Jesus loved Lazarus.
Some wondered why Jesus hadn’t saved him.
Sonia’s voice grew stronger as she read how Jesus came to the grave.
Jesus said, “Take away the stone.” Martha said, “But he’s been dead four days.”
Jesus said, “Did I not tell you that if you believe, you will see the glory of God?”
They took away the stone. Jesus prayed and then called out, “Lazarus, come out!”
“And he that was dead came forth,” Sonia read.
Jesus told them to unwrap Lazarus and let him go.
Many of the people believed in Jesus.
Sonia finished reading, closed the book, and stood up, shaking.
“I came to talk to you,” Raskolnikov said, getting up and going to Sonia. She looked at him. He looked serious and determined.
“I left my family today—my mother and sister. I won’t see them again.”
“Why?” Sonia asked, shocked.
“I only have you now,” he said. “Let’s go together. We are both cursed—let’s go our way together.”
“Go where?” Sonia asked, stepping back.
“I don’t know. But it’s the same path for both of us.”
Sonia didn’t understand, but knew Raskolnikov was deeply unhappy.
“No one else will understand, but you do. I came to you because I need you.”
“I don’t understand,” Sonia said softly.
“You’ll understand later. Haven’t you done the same? You gave up your own life for others. But you can’t go on alone—you’ll go mad. We must go together!”
“What for? Why?” Sonia cried.

“Because you can’t stay like this! You have to face the truth, not just hope God will fix everything. What if you get sent to the hospital tomorrow? What about the children? Polenka could end up on the streets, begging like other children. Children are meant to be loved—they are our future.”
“What can I do? What can I do?” Sonia wept, wringing her hands.

“Break what must be broken and accept the suffering. That’s all. Freedom and power, that’s the goal! Remember my words. If I don’t come tomorrow, you’ll hear everything. If I come, I’ll tell you who killed Lizaveta. Goodbye.”
Sonia was terrified.
“Do you know who killed her?” she asked, shocked.
“I know and I’ll tell you—only you. I chose you long ago. Goodbye. Don’t shake hands. Tomorrow!”
Raskolnikov left. Sonia stared after him, thinking he was out of his mind. But she felt dizzy, too.
“How does he know who killed Lizaveta? What did he mean? He must be so unhappy. He left his family—why? What did he want from me? He kissed my foot and said he can’t live without me... Oh, heavens!”
Sonia spent the night feverish and dreaming. She woke up crying, thought of Polenka, Katerina Ivanovna, Lizaveta, the gospel, and Raskolnikov with his pale face, weeping.

Next door was an empty room. Sonia was used to it being unoccupied. But all that time, Svidrigaïlov had been standing in the empty room, listening at the door. He found the conversation interesting and decided to bring a chair next time, so he could listen more comfortably.

The next morning at eleven o’clock, Raskolnikov (a young student) went to the police office to see Porfiry Petrovitch (the detective). He had to wait a long time and thought maybe they were watching him or would arrest him right away. But nobody seemed to care. Raskolnikov started to think maybe the strange man from yesterday hadn’t told the police anything after all, and maybe he was just imagining things because he was nervous. He felt scared but tried to act calm and ready before being called in to see Porfiry Petrovitch.

Raskolnikov found Porfiry Petrovitch alone in his office. The room looked official and had a sofa, a big desk, and some chairs. Porfiry greeted him in a friendly way, but Raskolnikov noticed he seemed a little awkward, like he was hiding something.
“Ah, my dear fellow! Here you are in our office,” Porfiry said, holding out his hands. “Come, sit down, old man… or maybe you don’t like those names? Please, sit here on the sofa.”
Raskolnikov sat down and watched Porfiry closely, trying to figure out what he was up to. They both looked at each other and quickly looked away.
“I brought you this paper about the watch,” Raskolnikov said, handing it over. “Is it okay or should I write it again?”
“Yes, yes, it’s fine,” Porfiry answered quickly, looking at the paper and then putting it on the desk.
Raskolnikov started to ask, “I think you said yesterday you wanted to ask me questions about the old woman who was murdered?” But inside, he was very nervous and worried he might say too much.
“No hurry, no hurry,” Porfiry said, walking around the room, sometimes looking at Raskolnikov and sometimes away.
“We have plenty of time. Do you smoke? Here, have a cigarette!” Porfiry said, talking about his office and repairs, trying to make small talk.
Porfiry kept repeating, “A capital thing, a capital thing,” and suddenly stared at Raskolnikov.

Raskolnikov decided to challenge him. “Tell me, isn’t it a rule for detectives to start talking about silly things first before asking important questions, so the person they’re questioning isn’t ready when the real question comes?”

“Yes, yes… Do you really think that’s why I was talking about my office?” Porfiry replied, winking and laughing. He laughed so hard he turned red, and Raskolnikov tried to laugh too, but soon stopped and stared at Porfiry with hate.

Raskolnikov stood up and said seriously, “Porfiry Petrovitch, you wanted to ask me questions. I’m here. Ask them now or let me go. I have to go to a funeral. I’m sick of all this. If you want to question me, do it the proper way.”

“Good heavens! What do you mean? What should I ask?” Porfiry said, acting surprised and making Raskolnikov sit down again. Porfiry tried to act friendly and said he was nervous and laughed a lot because of his nerves.
Porfiry started talking about how hard it is for smart people to talk to each other and how awkward things can be. He asked Raskolnikov to put down his cap and relax.
Raskolnikov listened quietly and wondered if Porfiry was only pretending to be silly to distract him.

Porfiry kept talking about his health, how he wanted to exercise more, and how confusing police questions could be. He said sometimes it’s better to just have a friendly chat, and that detectives can’t always follow the rules exactly.
As Porfiry talked and walked around, Raskolnikov noticed he sometimes stopped near the door, like he was listening for something.

Suddenly, Porfiry looked at Raskolnikov and said, “You’re right to laugh at our detective rules. If I thought someone was a criminal, why would I arrest him right away? Sometimes it’s better to watch and wait, let him walk around, and see what he does.”

Porfiry explained that every crime is special. Sometimes, if the suspect is left alone but knows he’s being watched, he’ll get so nervous that he’ll make a mistake or even confess. “It’s like a butterfly flying around a candle—he’ll keep coming back until he gets caught,” Porfiry said.
Raskolnikov stared at Porfiry, pale and silent.
Raskolnikov thought, “Porfiry is trying to scare me on purpose. He wants me to panic, but I won’t let him win. He has no proof.”
He decided not to say anything and hoped Porfiry would say too much if he stayed quiet.

Porfiry kept talking, saying that young men like Raskolnikov trust their brains too much. He said even clever people can make mistakes when they’re nervous or sick. “At the most important moment, their true feelings show. Their faces give them away!” Porfiry said, then noticed Raskolnikov looked very pale and asked if he wanted the window open.
“No, don’t worry,” Raskolnikov said and laughed suddenly.
Porfiry laughed too. Raskolnikov stood up, still shaking.

“Porfiry Petrovitch,” Raskolnikov said loudly, even though he was scared, “I see you really suspect me of murdering the old woman and her sister. If you want to arrest me, do it. But don’t make fun of me!”
“I won’t allow it!” he shouted, banging the table.
“Good heavens! What’s wrong?” Porfiry said, pretending to be scared. “Sit down, please!”
Porfiry rushed to open the window and brought Raskolnikov some water, telling him he was ill and needed to calm down.
Raskolnikov watched Porfiry, not sure what to believe, but he didn’t drink the water.
Porfiry made him take a sip, saying, “You had a little attack! You must take care of yourself.”
Porfiry started talking about Razumihin (Raskolnikov’s friend) visiting him, but Raskolnikov said, “No, he didn’t come from me, but I knew he went to see you.”

Porfiry then said he knew everything about Raskolnikov, how he went to the old woman’s flat at night and asked about blood. He said he understood that Raskolnikov was upset and just wanted answers, but he was making himself and Razumihin sick with worry.
Raskolnikov was shocked that Porfiry knew about the flat.
Porfiry said he once saw a man who thought he was a murderer just because he felt guilty. He told Raskolnikov he should see a doctor and stop doing strange things like ringing bells at night.
“I wasn’t sick. I knew what I was doing!” Raskolnikov shouted, trying to figure out Porfiry’s game.
“If you really were guilty, wouldn’t you say you were sick? But you keep insisting you were not,” Porfiry said slyly.
Porfiry pointed out that Raskolnikov talked too much and didn’t hide things like a guilty person would.
“You keep lying,” Raskolnikov said. “You’re trying to show you know everything I do, but you’re just trying to scare me. I don’t believe you!”
Porfiry laughed and said, “You’re hard to trick! But I like you and want the best for you.”
He told Raskolnikov to think of his mother and sister, who were now in town, and not to upset them.
Raskolnikov got angry and asked, “How do you know about them? Are you spying on me?”
Porfiry said he learned things from Raskolnikov himself and from Razumihin, and explained that if he really suspected Raskolnikov, he would have arrested him already.
Raskolnikov was startled.
“You’re lying,” he said. “You weren’t talking like this before. I know you’re not telling the truth.”

Porfiry replied, “But I gave you every chance to defend yourself! I even talked about sickness and delirium to help you. But if you were really sick, why would you think about just those things and not others?”
Raskolnikov stood up and demanded, “Tell me now, am I free from suspicion or not?”
Porfiry said, “Why do you want to know so much? Why are you so uneasy? You’re like a child who wants to play with matches!”
“Don’t make fun of me! I can’t stand it!” Raskolnikov yelled, banging the table again.
“Be quiet! They’ll hear!” Porfiry whispered, now looking serious and stern for a moment.
“Arrest me or search me if you must, but don’t play with me!” Raskolnikov whispered back angrily.
“Don’t worry about the rules,” Porfiry said, smiling slyly. “I invited you here as a friend.”
“I don’t want your friendship!” Raskolnikov shouted, grabbing his cap to leave. “What will you do if you really want to arrest me?”
As Raskolnikov tried to leave, Porfiry stopped him and said, “Don’t you want to see my little surprise?”
“What surprise?” Raskolnikov asked, now worried.
“It’s sitting behind that door!” Porfiry said, pointing to a locked door. “I locked him in so he wouldn’t escape.”
“What is it? Where?” Raskolnikov asked, going to the door, but it was locked.
“Here’s the key!” Porfiry said.
“You’re lying!” Raskolnikov shouted, rushing at Porfiry, who backed away calmly.
“You’re trying to trick me into giving myself away!” Raskolnikov yelled.
“You couldn’t give yourself away any more, you’re so angry,” Porfiry said. “If you shout, I’ll call the clerks.”
“You have no proof! You just want to make me mad so I’ll confess! Where are your witnesses?”
Porfiry listened at the door as a noise came from behind it.
“Ah, they’re coming!” Raskolnikov shouted. “Bring your witnesses, your deputies—I'm ready!”
But just then, something strange happened, something neither Raskolnikov nor Porfiry expected.

Raskolnikov remembered the scene very clearly. There was a lot of noise outside the door, and suddenly it opened a little. Porfiry Petrovitch (the police detective) shouted, “What is it? I gave orders…” but nobody answered at first. It sounded like people were pushing someone at the door.

Suddenly, after a quick struggle, a pale young man came into the room. He looked strange and scared, like he was about to be punished. He was dressed like a worker and looked very serious. A guard tried to hold him back, but the young man shook him off. Many people crowded into the doorway, watching.
Porfiry Petrovitch was annoyed. “Why have you brought him so soon?” he muttered. But the young man, Nikolay (a workman), suddenly knelt down.
“What’s the matter?” asked Porfiry, surprised.
“I am guilty! I am the murderer,” Nikolay said, out of breath but loud enough for everyone to hear.
Everyone froze in shock, even the guard. For a moment there was silence.
“What is it?” Porfiry asked, finally recovering.
“I... am the murderer,” Nikolay said again.
“Who did you kill?” Porfiry asked, very confused.
Nikolay was quiet for a second, then said, “Alyona Ivanovna and her sister Lizaveta Ivanovna. I killed them with an axe. Darkness came over me.” He was still on his knees.
Porfiry thought for a moment, then waved the other people away and closed the door. He looked at Raskolnikov (who was standing in the corner), then back at Nikolay, and rushed to Nikolay.
“You’re in too much of a hurry!” Porfiry shouted. “Did you really kill them?”
“I am the murderer. I want to give evidence,” said Nikolay.
“What did you kill them with?”
“An axe. I had it ready.”
“Did you do it alone?”
“Yes, alone. Mitka is not guilty,” Nikolay said.
“Why did you run downstairs with Mitka? The porters saw you both!” Porfiry asked.
“It was to trick them,” Nikolay replied quickly, like he had prepared the answer.
“It’s not his own tale,” Porfiry muttered to himself and then looked at Raskolnikov again.

Porfiry turned to Raskolnikov. “My dear Rodion Romanovitch (that’s Raskolnikov's full name), you must go now. It’s no good for you to stay. Goodbye!” He took Raskolnikov by the arm and showed him to the door.
“I suppose you didn’t expect it?” Raskolnikov asked, trying to act calm.
“You didn’t expect it either! Look, your hand is shaking!” Porfiry laughed nervously.
“You are shaking too, Porfiry Petrovitch!” said Raskolnikov.
“Yes, I am. I didn’t expect it,” said Porfiry. He wanted Raskolnikov to leave quickly.
“And your little surprise, aren’t you going to show it to me?” Raskolnikov asked.
“You are funny! Goodbye, till we meet!” said Porfiry.
“That’s in God’s hands,” Porfiry added with a strange smile.

As Raskolnikov walked through the office, he noticed many people looking at him, including the two porters from the house. But as soon as he started down the stairs, Porfiry ran after him, out of breath.
“One word, Rodion Romanovitch. I still have some questions for you, so we will meet again, right?” Porfiry said, smiling.
“Forgive me for losing my temper earlier,” Raskolnikov said, trying to sound brave.
“Don’t mention it! We may see a lot of each other, if God wills it,” Porfiry replied.
“And get to know each other very well?” asked Raskolnikov.
“Yes, very well,” Porfiry agreed, looking closely at him. “Now you’re going to a birthday party?”
“To a funeral.”
“Oh yes, the funeral! Take care and get well.”
“I don’t know what to wish you,” said Raskolnikov as he started down the stairs. “Your job is a funny one.”
“Why funny?” Porfiry asked, stopping.
“Because you must have bothered poor Nikolay until he confessed, and now you’ll keep questioning him, saying, ‘You are lying! You’re not the murderer!’ It’s a funny business!”
“You noticed I said it wasn’t his own story?” Porfiry laughed.
“Of course I noticed!”
“You are very quick! You notice everything,” Porfiry said. “That’s like the writer Gogol.”
“I look forward to meeting you again,” Porfiry said.
“So do I,” Raskolnikov replied.

Raskolnikov walked home, feeling confused. When he got home, he sat on the sofa for a while, thinking. He couldn’t understand Nikolay’s confession. It was strange and amazing. But he knew it was real, and soon people would find out it wasn’t true. Then they would come after him again. Until then, he was safe and had to do something for himself.

He thought about what had happened with Porfiry and shivered with fear. He knew Porfiry was clever and had almost caught him, but there were no real facts yet. Maybe he was safe for now. He wondered what surprise Porfiry had planned, and if it would have happened if Nikolay had not burst in.

At least for today, Raskolnikov felt a little safe. He felt almost happy and wanted to hurry to Katerina Ivanovna’s house. He would miss the funeral, but he could still go to the dinner and see Sonia.
As he was about to leave, the door opened slowly by itself. Raskolnikov jumped back. A man from the day before, who worked underground, came in. He looked sad and sighed deeply.
“What do you want?” Raskolnikov asked, very scared. The man didn’t answer, but bowed down and touched the floor with his finger.
“I have sinned,” the man said softly.
“How?” asked Raskolnikov.
“By evil thoughts,” the man answered.

The man explained that when Raskolnikov had asked the porters to go to the police station about the blood, he got angry that they let Raskolnikov leave. He was upset and couldn’t sleep, so he came yesterday to ask about Raskolnikov.
“Who came?” Raskolnikov asked, trying to remember.
“I did. I wronged you,” the man replied.
“Then you come from that house?” asked Raskolnikov.
The man said he was at the gate with the others and that he had worked in that house for years. He was most upset about what happened.

Raskolnikov realized the man couldn’t tell Porfiry anything important, just about Raskolnikov asking about the flat and the blood stains. Porfiry didn’t have any real proof. If nothing new was found, they couldn’t convict him, even if they arrested him.
“Did you tell Porfiry I had been there?” Raskolnikov asked suddenly.
“Yes. The porters didn’t go, but I did.”
“Today?”
“I got there just before you, and I heard everything, how he questioned you.”
“Where?” Raskolnikov asked.
“In the next room. I was sitting there the whole time,” the man said.

The man explained how he went to Porfiry and told him everything, and Porfiry got very angry. He told the man to wait in the next room and locked him in until Nikolay arrived. After Raskolnikov left, Porfiry let him out and said he might call him again.
The man said Porfiry got rid of him before questioning Nikolay.
The man bowed again, touching the floor. “Forgive me for my evil thoughts,” he said.
“May God forgive you,” said Raskolnikov.
The man bowed again, turned, and left the room.
“It all goes both ways now,” Raskolnikov thought, feeling more confident.
“Now I’ll fight for it,” he said to himself as he went downstairs, feeling a little angry with himself for being scared before.

The morning after his talk with Dounia (Raskolnikov’s sister) and her mother, Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin woke up feeling upset. He finally had to admit that Dounia really did not want to marry him. This made him feel angry and sad. He looked at himself in the mirror to check if he was sick, but he looked healthy. For a moment, he told himself he could find another girl to marry, maybe even someone better. But soon he remembered how things really were, and that made him even more upset. His friend Andrey Semyonovitch Lebeziatnikov, who lived with him, smiled in a way that made Luzhin even angrier. Luzhin also got bad news about his legal work. He was annoyed that the man who owned the apartment he rented for his wedding would not give his money back, and the furniture store also refused to refund him.
Luzhin wondered if there was any chance Dounia would change her mind. He wished he could somehow get rid of Raskolnikov, who had made things worse for him.

Luzhin thought maybe he should have given Dounia and her family more gifts and money. He believed that if he had spent money on them, they would have felt bad about breaking up with him. He realized he had made a mistake.
Luzhin called himself a fool, but only in his mind.

When Luzhin went home, he was in a bad mood. He saw people getting ready for a funeral dinner at Katerina Ivanovna’s (Sonia’s stepmother). He heard he was invited, along with all the other people who lived in the building. Amalia Ivanovna, the landlady, was also invited and very happy to help. Luzhin found out that Raskolnikov would be there too, and this gave him an idea.

Luzhin did not really like Lebeziatnikov, but he stayed with him because he had heard Lebeziatnikov knew some important people in the city. Luzhin was afraid of being embarrassed or exposed by these “modern” groups, so he wanted to keep an eye on things.
Lebeziatnikov was a pale, thin man with light whiskers. He worked as a clerk and was proud to pay his rent on time. He liked new ideas, but he was not very smart.

Lately, Lebeziatnikov started to dislike Luzhin too. He noticed that Luzhin looked down on him and did not really respect him. Still, Luzhin liked it when Lebeziatnikov praised him for being “modern,” even if it was not true.
That morning, Luzhin counted some money at the table. Lebeziatnikov watched, pretending not to care, but really wishing he had money too.

Lebeziatnikov tried to talk about his favorite topic, making a “community” where everyone shared everything. But Luzhin was not interested and just made fun of him. Lebeziatnikov thought Luzhin was just sad about Dounia and wanted to cheer him up with his ideas.
Suddenly Luzhin asked about the party at Katerina Ivanovna’s place.
Lebeziatnikov said Luzhin was invited and reminded him they talked about it before.

Luzhin complained that Katerina Ivanovna was spending all the money she got from Raskolnikov on this party. He joked he did not need to go and only talked to her about maybe helping her get some money from the government.
Lebeziatnikov said he would not go either.
Luzhin teased Lebeziatnikov about fighting with Katerina Ivanovna.
Lebeziatnikov got upset and denied it.
Luzhin laughed and said Lebeziatnikov’s ideas about women were silly.
Lebeziatnikov said it was not true, he only protected himself when Katerina Ivanovna attacked him.
Luzhin kept laughing.
Lebeziatnikov explained his ideas about men and women being equal and said he was not going to the party because he did not like such old customs.
Luzhin asked if he’d go just to make fun of the dinner.
Lebeziatnikov said he would only “protest” to help people learn new ideas. He explained how some women he admired wrote honest letters when they left their husbands.
Luzhin asked if one woman, Terebyeva, had done this many times.
Lebeziatnikov said it did not matter if it was two times or fifteen; he liked protests.
Luzhin changed the subject and asked about the dead man’s daughter, Sonia.
Lebeziatnikov said he thought Sonia’s choices were normal for women in their situation and that in the future, things would be different.
Luzhin asked if Lebeziatnikov had gotten Sonia kicked out of her room.
Lebeziatnikov got angry.
He said that was not true and that he only wanted to help Sonia learn to stand up for herself.
Luzhin asked if he had invited Sonia to join his “community.”
Lebeziatnikov said he was trying to, but things would be different in the community.
Luzhin teased him.
Lebeziatnikov denied taking advantage of Sonia.
Luzhin kept laughing.
Lebeziatnikov insisted Sonia was very shy and proper with him.
Luzhin said Lebeziatnikov was trying to convince Sonia that being shy was silly.
Lebeziatnikov denied it, saying he respected her choices and only wanted her to be happy.
Luzhin suggested Lebeziatnikov should give Sonia a present.
Lebeziatnikov said Luzhin just did not understand and explained that Sonia was a good person who tried to learn new things.
Luzhin asked what “coming into the room” in the community meant.
Lebeziatnikov said they had discussed whether people could go into each other’s rooms at any time, and they decided yes.
Luzhin joked it could be awkward.
Lebeziatnikov was annoyed.
He said Luzhin always made things sound bad and that cleaning toilets was just as good as painting or writing if it helped people.
Luzhin laughed.
Lebeziatnikov said “honour” was an old-fashioned word, and only being useful mattered.
Luzhin laughed harder and finished counting his money. He left some of it on the table, happy to tease Lebeziatnikov.
Lebeziatnikov said Luzhin was in a bad mood because of his breakup.
Luzhin asked if Lebeziatnikov could bring Sonia in for a talk. He said Lebeziatnikov should stay in the room too.
Lebeziatnikov asked why.
Luzhin said he was leaving soon and wanted to talk to Sonia, but wanted Lebeziatnikov there so no one would think anything strange.
Lebeziatnikov agreed to help.
A few minutes later, Lebeziatnikov brought Sonia in. She looked very shy and nervous. Luzhin acted polite but also a little proud. He made Sonia sit down and told Lebeziatnikov to stay.
Luzhin whispered and asked if Raskolnikov was in the other room.
Lebeziatnikov said yes.
Luzhin asked Lebeziatnikov to stay in the room with him and Sonia, just in case.
Lebeziatnikov agreed.
Luzhin acted very serious and looked at Sonia, making her even more nervous.
Luzhin asked Sonia to tell Katerina Ivanovna (her stepmother) that he could not come to the dinner because he was busy.
He tried to sound friendly.
Sonia agreed quickly.
Luzhin thanked her and said he was sorry for missing the event.
Sonia said she would tell Katerina Ivanovna.
Sonia got up to leave.
Luzhin stopped her and said he had another reason for calling her in.
Sonia sat down again. She tried not to look at the money on the table, but she was embarrassed.
Luzhin said he had talked to Katerina Ivanovna yesterday and saw that she was having a hard time.
Sonia agreed.
Luzhin explained that Katerina Ivanovna was sick.
Sonia repeated what Luzhin said.
Luzhin asked if the whole family now depended on Sonia.
Sonia stood up and asked about the pension Luzhin had promised Katerina Ivanovna.
Luzhin said he never promised anything and that it was very unlikely they would get any help from the government.
Sonia said Katerina Ivanovna was just hopeful and kind, and she apologized for her.
Luzhin said he was not finished.
Sonia said she hadn’t heard what else he wanted.
Luzhin told her to sit again, and she did, feeling even more confused.
Luzhin said maybe they could collect money for Katerina Ivanovna by asking people to help, but he thought it was safer if Sonia managed the money instead of Katerina Ivanovna.
Sonia thanked him and said God would repay him.
Luzhin said he would talk more about it later, but warned Sonia not to give the money to Katerina Ivanovna herself. He wanted Sonia to handle it.
Sonia said Katerina Ivanovna was only having the party this once, but she would do whatever Luzhin thought was best.
Sonia started to cry.
Luzhin then gave Sonia a ten-rouble note, saying it was from him, but he did not want anyone to know.
Sonia turned red, quickly thanked him, and left the room feeling very upset and confused.
After Sonia left, Lebeziatnikov came over to Luzhin and shook his hand.
Lebeziatnikov said he saw what Luzhin did and thought it was kind, even though he didn’t really like private charity.
Luzhin mumbled that it was nothing.
Lebeziatnikov said he was surprised Luzhin could be so nice even after being dumped by Dounia. He said maybe it was good that Luzhin was not married and was still free.
Luzhin answered that he wanted legal marriage so he would not end up raising another man’s children.
Luzhin seemed to be thinking hard about something else.

Lebeziatnikov started talking about children and marriage. He said in the future, people would not be upset if their wife had another husband, and he would even help his wife find a lover to show he respected her.
Luzhin only snickered a little while listening. He was thinking about something else, and Lebeziatnikov noticed Luzhin looked excited and was rubbing his hands together.

Katerina Ivanovna (the wife of Marmeladov) decided to have a big dinner after Marmeladov’s funeral. She spent a lot of the money Raskolnikov gave her for this meal. She wanted to show everyone, especially the other lodgers and Amalia Ivanovna (the landlady), that Marmeladov was important and not to be looked down on. Katerina Ivanovna was poor and sick, and her mind was not very well, but she was proud and wanted to do things properly.

There was not much fancy food or drink at the dinner, but there was enough for everyone. There was vodka, rum, and some wine, plus rice with honey, pancakes, and a few other dishes. All the food was cooked in Amalia Ivanovna’s kitchen. A little Polish man, who also lived in the house, helped Katerina Ivanovna buy the food and run errands. At first, Katerina Ivanovna thought he was very helpful, but then she got tired of him because he kept bothering her. Katerina Ivanovna would praise people a lot at first, but if she got upset, she would quickly change her mind and be mean to them.

Amalia Ivanovna, the landlady, helped a lot with setting the table and making the food. She wore her best black dress and a cap with ribbons to welcome the guests. Katerina Ivanovna was annoyed by this, thinking Amalia Ivanovna was showing off and acting important just because she was the landlady. Katerina Ivanovna remembered how her father had once been a colonel and had big parties, and she didn’t like feeling lower than Amalia Ivanovna.

Katerina Ivanovna decided not to say anything mean to Amalia Ivanovna right away, but she felt angry inside. She was also upset that most of the important lodgers did not come to the funeral or the dinner, except for the little Pole. Only the poorest, silliest lodgers had shown up, and some of them were already drunk. Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin, who was supposed to be the most important guest, didn’t come. Katerina Ivanovna had told everyone how wonderful he was and how he would help her family, but he still didn’t show up.

Two other lodgers, a fancy lady and her grown-up daughter, didn’t come either. They had complained in the past about Katerina Ivanovna’s family making noise. Katerina Ivanovna wanted to prove to them that she was a real lady, so she invited them, but they didn’t come. Only a few strange, poor people came: the Pole, a dirty clerk, an old deaf man, and a retired clerk who was drunk and laughing too loudly.

One visitor even tried to come in a dressing gown instead of proper clothes, but Amalia Ivanovna and the Pole made him leave. The Pole brought two more Poles who were strangers. Katerina Ivanovna was very frustrated that all her hard work was wasted on these people. The children were not allowed at the table and had to eat in the corner, with Polenka (the oldest daughter) looking after the little ones.

Katerina Ivanovna tried to act very proud and important to the guests, even though she was upset. She looked at them sternly and told them to sit down. She blamed Amalia Ivanovna for the important people not coming and treated her coldly. Everyone finally sat down, but it was not a happy start.

Raskolnikov arrived just as everyone came back from the cemetery. Katerina Ivanovna was glad to see him because he was smart and going to be a professor. She made him sit next to her and started telling him, in a whisper, about how disappointed she was with the dinner, even though she was constantly coughing and worried about the food.

Katerina Ivanovna joked to Raskolnikov about Amalia Ivanovna, calling her an “owl” and laughing about her cap. She complained that the guests were silly and didn’t know Marmeladov. She made fun of them and told Raskolnikov to watch out for the landlady’s spoons in case someone stole them, laughing loudly.
Suddenly, Katerina Ivanovna started coughing very badly. She showed Raskolnikov her handkerchief with blood on it, but then kept talking to him quickly, her cheeks bright from fever.

Katerina Ivanovna told Raskolnikov she had tried very hard to invite the fancy lady and her daughter, but they hadn’t come. She wondered why Pyotr Petrovitch didn’t come either. Then Sonia (Katerina Ivanovna’s stepdaughter) came in, and Katerina Ivanovna told her to sit by Raskolnikov and eat. She also told the children to behave.

Sonia explained to Katerina Ivanovna that Pyotr Petrovitch was sorry he couldn’t come and would visit soon to talk about helping her. Sonia tried to say this in a very polite way to make Katerina Ivanovna feel better.
Sonia sat next to Raskolnikov but didn’t talk to him much. She looked worried and tried to make Katerina Ivanovna happy. Neither Sonia nor Katerina Ivanovna had proper black clothes for mourning.

Hearing Sonia’s message, Katerina Ivanovna felt proud. She whispered to Raskolnikov that it would have been strange for someone as important as Pyotr Petrovitch to come to such a poor dinner, even if he did care about her family.
She thanked Raskolnikov for coming, saying he must have done it out of friendship for her husband, Marmeladov.
Katerina Ivanovna tried to act like a good hostess, asking the old deaf man if he wanted more food or wine. He didn’t answer, and people laughed at him.

Katerina Ivanovna angrily told Amalia Ivanovna that her guests were not as good as the friends her father or husband would have had. The drunk commissariat clerk shouted that Marmeladov liked to drink.
“He was fond of drink!” the clerk yelled, drinking even more.

Katerina Ivanovna snapped that Marmeladov was kind and loved his family, and only drank because he was too trusting. She told Raskolnikov they had found a gingerbread rooster in his pocket, even when he was very drunk, because he was thinking of his children.
The clerk shouted about the rooster, but Katerina Ivanovna ignored him.
She sighed, lost in her thoughts.
She told Raskolnikov that people thought she was too strict with Marmeladov, but she really cared about him. She tried to be kind, but if she was soft, he would drink again.
The clerk shouted about Marmeladov getting his hair pulled, and Katerina Ivanovna said some people deserved a beating, but she wasn’t talking about her husband.
Katerina Ivanovna’s face turned red, and she was about to get very angry. Some of the guests were giggling and whispering, trying to make the drunk clerk act up even more.

Raskolnikov sat quietly, eating a little to be polite. He watched Sonia, who looked more and more upset, afraid things would end badly. Sonia knew the fancy ladies didn’t come because of her, and that made Katerina Ivanovna even more angry. Someone even passed Sonia a plate with two hearts and an arrow made out of bread, as a joke. Katerina Ivanovna called the person a “drunken ass” out loud.

Amalia Ivanovna, upset by Katerina Ivanovna’s attitude, tried to tell a story about “Karl from the chemist’s,” but it didn’t make sense and Katerina Ivanovna laughed at her. Amalia Ivanovna said her father from Berlin was very important, but Katerina Ivanovna just laughed more.

Feeling better, Katerina Ivanovna told Raskolnikov about her plan to open a school for girls when she got her pension. She showed him a special certificate that proved her father was a major. She said this would show everyone she came from a good family. The drunken guests passed the certificate around.
Katerina Ivanovna talked about how nice life would be in the new town, and how Sonia would help her with the school. Someone at the table laughed rudely.

Katerina Ivanovna ignored the laugh and started talking about how kind and smart Sonia was, hugging and kissing her. Sonia turned red, and Katerina Ivanovna began to cry, saying she was too upset and that it was time for tea.
Amalia Ivanovna, wanting to join in, said that in the new school, Katerina Ivanovna should make sure the girls’ laundry was clean and that they didn’t read novels at night.

Katerina Ivanovna snapped that Amalia Ivanovna didn’t know what she was talking about and should be quiet. Amalia Ivanovna got angry and said she only meant well, and that she had paid her gold for the lodgings a long time ago.

Katerina Ivanovna said that was a lie, because just yesterday Amalia Ivanovna had bothered her about rent while her husband was dead. Amalia Ivanovna said the fancy ladies didn’t come because Katerina Ivanovna wasn’t a real lady. Katerina Ivanovna called her a “slut” and said she couldn’t judge ladies. Amalia Ivanovna insisted her father was important and puffed out her cheeks, pretending to be him, which made everyone laugh and hope for a fight.
Katerina Ivanovna shouted that Amalia Ivanovna probably never had a father at all and was just a drunken Finn who used to be a cook.
Katerina Ivanovna said her own father really was a colonel, and Amalia Ivanovna’s father—if he existed—was just a milkman, and even her name was uncertain.

Amalia Ivanovna got very angry, hit the table, and yelled that she was Amalia Ivanovna, not Ludwigovna, and that her father was a burgomeister. Katerina Ivanovna stood up and threatened to tear off Amalia Ivanovna’s cap if she insulted her father. Amalia Ivanovna ran around, shouting that she was the landlady and Katerina Ivanovna should leave at once, then started grabbing the spoons. The children cried, Sonia tried to help, but when Amalia Ivanovna said something bad about Sonia’s past (“the yellow ticket”), Katerina Ivanovna pushed Sonia away and rushed at the landlady.
Just then, Pyotr Petrovitch Luzhin came in through the door, looking around at everyone with a serious face. Katerina Ivanovna hurried to him.

Katerina Ivanovna shouted, “Pyotr Petrovitch, help me! You must protect us. Tell this woman she can’t treat me this way. There are laws! I’ll go to the governor if I have to. Please, remember my father’s kindness—help these poor children.”

Pyotr Petrovitch (also called Luzhin) waved her away. “Excuse me, madam. I never knew your father. I don’t want to get in the middle of your arguments with Amalia Ivanovna (the landlady). I am here to talk about something important with your stepdaughter, Sofya Ivanovna (Sonia). Let me pass.”
Luzhin walked past Katerina Ivanovna and went over to Sonia.

Katerina Ivanovna stood there, shocked. She didn’t understand how Luzhin could say he didn’t know her father. She really believed he did, even if she had made it up. She was also surprised by Luzhin’s cold and serious tone. The room grew quiet. Everyone could tell something big was about to happen. Raskolnikov, who was standing by Sonia, moved aside. Luzhin ignored him. Lebeziatnikov showed up in the doorway, listening with curiosity.
