Luzhin spoke to everyone in the room. “Sorry to interrupt, but this is important. Amalia Ivanovna, please pay attention. Sofya Ivanovna,” he said to Sonia, “after your visit to my room, I found a hundred-rouble note missing. If you know anything about it, please say so now. If you tell the truth, I promise not to do anything else. But if not, I will have to take serious action.”
The room was silent. Not even the children cried. Sonia looked very pale and stared at Luzhin, unable to speak.
“Well, what do you say?” Luzhin asked, staring at her.
Sonia finally whispered, “I don’t know. I don’t know anything about it.”

Luzhin repeated, “You know nothing?” He waited a moment, then spoke more sternly. “Think about it, Sonia. I wouldn’t accuse you if I wasn’t sure. This morning I counted my money. I had several hundred-rouble notes on my table. You came in, at my invitation, to talk about helping Katerina Ivanovna. You thanked me, and I gave you ten roubles in front of Mr. Lebeziatnikov. I walked you to the door. After you left, I talked to Mr. Lebeziatnikov for ten minutes. When he left, I saw one of the hundred-rouble notes was missing. I cannot suspect Mr. Lebeziatnikov. I am sure I counted right. You seemed nervous and tried to leave quickly. That made me suspect you, even though I didn’t want to. I helped you, and you paid me back with this! But I am still your friend—think carefully, or I will have to be strict. What do you say?”
Sonia said, scared, “I didn’t take anything. You gave me ten roubles—here it is, take it.”
She took out her handkerchief, untied it, and handed Luzhin the ten-rouble note.
Luzhin asked, “And you don’t admit to taking the hundred roubles?”
Sonia looked around. Everyone stared at her with angry, cold eyes. She looked at Raskolnikov, who stood with his arms crossed.
Sonia cried out, “Oh God!”
Luzhin said softly, “Amalia Ivanovna, please call the house porter. We may need the police.”
“God have mercy! I knew she was the thief!” Amalia Ivanovna shouted.
Luzhin said, “You knew? Then you had a reason. Remember what you just said, in front of everyone.”
The room began buzzing with voices and everyone started moving.
Suddenly Katerina Ivanovna understood what was happening. She ran at Luzhin. “What! You accuse Sonia of stealing? You monsters!”
She hugged Sonia tightly.
“Sonia! Why did you take ten roubles from him? Give it to me! Give it here!”
She grabbed the note from Sonia and threw it at Luzhin’s face. It hit him and fell to the ground. Amalia Ivanovna picked it up. Luzhin got angry.
“Hold that mad woman!” Luzhin yelled.
More people came into the room, including two ladies.

Katerina Ivanovna screamed, “I’m not mad—you are! Sonia isn’t a thief. She would give away her last penny! Did you ever see such fools?” She turned to Amalia Ivanovna, “You, too? You say she’s a thief? She never left this room; she sat here beside Rodion Romanovitch (Raskolnikov). Search her! If you don’t find the money, you’ll answer for it! I’ll go to the Tsar himself! You thought Sonia would be quiet, but I won’t be!”
Katerina Ivanovna shook Luzhin and pulled him toward Sonia.
“Fine, search her!” she shouted. “Sonia, empty your pockets! See, her pocket is empty! Here’s her handkerchief! Look!”
Katerina Ivanovna turned Sonia’s pockets inside out. Suddenly, a piece of paper fluttered out and landed at Luzhin’s feet. He picked it up and showed everyone—it was a hundred-rouble note.
“Thief! Out of my house! Call the police!” yelled Amalia Ivanovna.
Everyone started shouting. Raskolnikov was silent, watching Sonia. Sonia stood still, shocked. Then she turned red, cried out, and covered her face.
“No, it wasn’t me! I didn’t take it! I know nothing about it!” Sonia wailed and ran to Katerina Ivanovna, who hugged her.

“Sonia, I don’t believe it! You see, I don’t! She would never steal. She would help anyone. She even got her yellow passport to help us when we were starving! Husband, do you see this? Defend her! Rodion Romanovitch, defend her! You all aren’t worth her little finger! Help her!”
Katerina Ivanovna’s crying made everyone feel sorry for her. Her sad, sick face and tears touched everyone. Even Luzhin seemed moved.

Luzhin said, “Madam, this isn’t your fault. No one blames you. You showed you had no idea by searching her. I feel sorry for you. Sonia, if you were driven by poverty, I could forgive you if you admitted it. Why didn’t you confess? Well, I will not carry this further. Let this be a lesson.”
Luzhin glanced at Raskolnikov, who glared back. Katerina Ivanovna kept hugging Sonia. The children hugged Sonia too. Polenka, not understanding, cried on Sonia’s shoulder.
Suddenly, a loud voice shouted from the doorway, “How terrible!”
“What a terrible thing!” said Lebeziatnikov, staring at Luzhin.
Luzhin was startled. Everyone noticed. Lebeziatnikov walked into the room.
“And you wanted me to be your witness?” he said to Luzhin.
“What do you mean?” muttered Luzhin.
“You are a liar!” Lebeziatnikov said angrily.
Raskolnikov watched him closely. The room was quiet. Luzhin seemed shocked.
“If you mean me...” Luzhin began, but was confused.
“I mean you! I heard everything. I waited to understand. I still don’t know why you did it.”
“What did I do? Stop saying riddles! Are you drunk?”
“You may drink, but I do not. I saw you give Sonia that hundred-rouble note. I can swear to it! When you said goodbye to her, you slipped it into her pocket. I saw it!”
“Are you crazy?” Luzhin shouted. “Sonia said I only gave her ten roubles. How could I have given her more?”
“I saw it,” Lebeziatnikov said. “You took a hundred-rouble note to give her ten roubles. You kept the note in your hand, and when you said goodbye, you put it in her pocket. I watched you.”
Luzhin turned pale.
“Lies!” he yelled. “You couldn’t see that from the window. You’re imagining things!”

“No, I saw everything. Even if I was far away, I saw you take the hundred-rouble note and slip it into her pocket. At first, I thought you were being kind. I even thought you wanted to surprise her. I was planning to tell Sonia about it, but I got busy and came here late. Now I know you did it on purpose!”
Lebeziatnikov finished, tired and sweaty. But everyone believed him because he sounded so sure. Luzhin saw things were going badly for him.
“What do your silly ideas have to do with me?” Luzhin shouted. “You are lying to get back at me because you don’t like my opinions!”
But no one agreed with Luzhin. People began to murmur against him.
“That’s nonsense!” cried Lebeziatnikov. “Call the police. I’ll swear I saw it. I only wonder why Luzhin would do something so mean.”
Raskolnikov stepped forward and said, “I can explain why he did it. And I’ll swear too.”
Raskolnikov looked calm and serious. Everyone could tell he knew something important.

Raskolnikov explained, “From the start, I suspected Luzhin was up to something. He used to be engaged to my sister, Avdotya Romanovna Raskolnikov, but we argued and I made him leave. After that, he sent a letter to my mother, trying to make her think I was giving money to Sonia, not Katerina Ivanovna, and saying bad things about Sonia. He wanted to turn my family against me. Last night, in front of everyone, I told him I gave the money for the funeral, not to Sonia. He was rude and had to leave. If he could prove Sonia was a thief, he would make my family think he was right about her and about me. He wanted revenge on me and to look good to my mother and sister. That’s why he did this.”
Raskolnikov spoke clearly and firmly. Everyone listened carefully, even though people interrupted sometimes.
“Yes! That’s it!” Lebeziatnikov said. “He asked me if you were here as soon as Sonia came in. He needed you to be here!”

Luzhin smiled angrily but said nothing. He was very pale and wanted to leave, but couldn’t. The room was noisy. Some people shouted at Luzhin, others called him names in Polish. Sonia stared at Raskolnikov, hoping he could help. Katerina Ivanovna was very tired. Amalia Ivanovna just looked confused.
Raskolnikov tried to speak again, but no one listened. Everyone crowded around Luzhin, shouting at him. Luzhin was not scared. He tried to act rude and strong.
Luzhin said, “Let me through! Don’t threaten me. You will not stop justice. The thief has been caught, and I will go to the police. The judges are not blind. Let me pass!”
“Don’t come back to my room!” Amalia Ivanovna shouted. “We are finished!”
Luzhin replied, “I told you I was leaving. You are a fool. See a doctor! Let me through!”

Luzhin pushed through the crowd. Someone threw a glass at him, but it hit Amalia Ivanovna instead. Luzhin left the house soon after. Sonia felt hurt and helpless. Even though people now knew she was innocent, she still felt sad and started crying. Soon she ran out of the room and went home. When the glass hit Amalia Ivanovna, she got angry and ran at Katerina Ivanovna.
“Out of my house! Right now!” shouted Amalia Ivanovna.
She started grabbing Katerina Ivanovna’s things and throwing them on the floor. Katerina Ivanovna, weak and tired, tried to fight back, but the landlady pushed her away.

Katerina Ivanovna cried, “After all this, you throw me and my children out! Where can we go? Is there no justice? I’ll find it! Polenka, stay with the children. Wait for me if you have to wait outside. I’ll find justice!”

Katerina Ivanovna put on her green shawl and ran out into the street, crying and shouting. Polenka held the little ones, trembling in the corner. Amalia Ivanovna kept yelling and throwing things. The other people in the house talked and argued, some even singing.
Raskolnikov thought, “Now it’s time for me to go. I wonder what Sonia will say now.”
And he set off to Sonia’s home.

Raskolnikov had helped Sonia when Luzhin tried to blame her, even though Raskolnikov felt very sad and scared inside. He was nervous because he knew he had to tell Sonia that he was the one who killed Lizaveta. He didn't want to, but he felt he had to. When he reached Sonia's room, he hesitated at the door, but then quickly opened it. Sonia was sitting at the table, but when she saw him, she stood up and came to meet him as if she'd been waiting.
“What would have happened to me without you?” Sonia said quickly when she saw Raskolnikov.

Raskolnikov sat down, and Sonia stood in front of him. He tried to talk, but his voice shook. He asked if she understood what Luzhin had said about her. Sonia looked upset and asked him not to talk like he did yesterday because things were already bad enough.

Sonia said she wanted to go back to Katerina Ivanovna’s, but she had waited for Raskolnikov. He told her that Amalia Ivanovna was making them leave and Katerina Ivanovna had run off to look for help. Sonia wanted to go after her, grabbing her cape, but Raskolnikov asked her to stay with him for a bit. He said Katerina Ivanovna would come to her if she needed to.

Sonia sat down, worried. Raskolnikov told her that Luzhin could have sent her to prison if he and Lebeziatnikov hadn’t helped. Sonia agreed softly. He said it was lucky they had been there by accident. He asked her what she would have done if she had gone to prison, but Sonia didn’t answer.

Raskolnikov then asked Sonia a strange question: what if she had to decide whether Luzhin or Katerina Ivanovna should live? Sonia was confused and didn’t want to answer. She said it wasn’t her place to judge who should live or die, and only God could decide that.

Sonia got upset and cried, thinking Raskolnikov just wanted to make her sad. Raskolnikov saw how much he was hurting her and said softly that he was sorry. He tried to smile, but he just put his face in his hands.

For a moment, he felt angry at Sonia, but when he looked at her, he saw how much she cared for him and the anger went away. He felt it was time to tell her the truth. He moved to sit on her bed, looking very pale.
Sonia was scared and asked what was wrong. Raskolnikov couldn’t speak. Sonia sat next to him and waited, watching him closely. Finally, he told her that he had come to tell her who killed Lizaveta.

Sonia started shaking. Raskolnikov said, “I have come to tell you.” Sonia asked if he really meant it and how he knew. He told her to guess. Sonia started to realize the truth and looked more and more afraid.

“Have you guessed?” he whispered. Sonia cried out and fell onto the bed, then quickly got up and grabbed his hands, hoping there was some mistake. But she saw it was true—Raskolnikov was the murderer.
He begged her to stop looking at him like that. Sonia jumped up, wringing her hands, then fell to her knees and hugged him, crying out, “What have you done to yourself?” She hugged him tightly.

Raskolnikov said, “You’re a strange girl, Sonia. You hug me even when I tell you this.” Sonia just cried, saying no one was as unhappy as him. Raskolnikov felt a kind feeling in his heart and even cried a little.

“You won’t leave me, Sonia?” he asked hopefully. Sonia promised she would never leave him and would follow him everywhere, even to Siberia. Raskolnikov said he might not want to go to Siberia yet, but Sonia just hugged him again.
Sonia tried to understand how Raskolnikov could have done such a thing. She asked if he did it because he was hungry or wanted to help his mother. Raskolnikov said no, that wasn’t the real reason.

Sonia was confused and asked if the money he gave to Katerina Ivanovna was from the crime. Raskolnikov said no, that money was from his mother. He explained that he didn’t even know if he took any money from the old woman, because he buried the things he took and didn’t look at them.

Sonia wondered why he said he did it to rob, but didn’t take anything. Raskolnikov said he wasn’t sure why, and started to talk strangely. Sonia wondered if he was mad, but then listened as Raskolnikov tried to explain.
He told Sonia, “If I had just killed because I was hungry, I would be happy now. But I didn’t. I asked you to come with me yesterday because you are all I have left. I just don’t want to be alone.”
Sonia squeezed his hand. Raskolnikov was upset and said he told her the truth because he couldn’t carry the burden alone. He wondered if Sonia could still love him.

“I have a bad heart, Sonia,” he said. “I came to you because I am a coward. Some people wouldn’t have come. But I had to speak, even if I don’t know how to start.” Sonia said it was good he came and that she would rather know.

Raskolnikov tried to explain why he did it. He said he wanted to be someone important, like Napoleon, and wondered if a great man would have done what he did. He thought maybe a great man would have killed the old woman without feeling bad, so he tried to do the same.
Sonia begged him to just tell things simply. Raskolnikov said he wanted to help his mother and sister, but he knew that killing was wrong. He got tired as he finished speaking.
Sonia said, “That’s not it, that can’t be the reason.” Raskolnikov agreed and said he was just talking nonsense. He started to get feverish and tired.

Suddenly, Raskolnikov said maybe he was just vain and angry. He explained how he had sat in his small room, doing nothing, thinking strange thoughts. He said he started thinking that only people who dared to do anything were important in the world, and he wanted to be one of them.
He told Sonia he wanted to dare to do something big, so he killed the old woman just to see if he could. Sonia cried out that he had turned away from God.

Raskolnikov said he knew it was wrong and the devil had led him. He had argued about it with himself for a long time. He said he wanted to find out if he was brave or just a coward, if he was a “louse” or a great man.

Sonia asked, “To kill? Do you mean you wanted the right to kill?” Raskolnikov got upset and said he just wanted to see if he could do it. He said he had killed himself, not just the old woman, because now he was full of pain.

Sonia cried out at his suffering. Raskolnikov asked, “What should I do now?” Sonia told him to go to a crossroads, bow to the ground, and tell everyone he was a murderer. She said then God would forgive him.
Raskolnikov asked if she meant he should give himself up and go to Siberia. Sonia said yes, he should suffer and pay for his crime. But Raskolnikov said he wouldn’t go.

Sonia cried, asking how he could live now or talk to his mother and sister. Raskolnikov said he hadn’t hurt them and that other people did bad things too. He didn’t want to give himself up just to be laughed at.

Sonia said it would be too much for him to bear. Raskolnikov thought maybe he could fight and keep living as he was. He told Sonia the police were after him, but he thought they had no real proof. He asked if Sonia would visit him in prison if he was arrested.
Sonia said she would. They sat together, both feeling sad and alone. Raskolnikov felt Sonia’s love but found it heavy and painful, even though he had hoped it would help.

He told Sonia maybe she shouldn’t visit him in prison. Sonia just cried. After a while, she asked if he had a cross. He said no. Sonia gave him a small cross made of wood that had once belonged to Lizaveta, saying they would suffer together.
Raskolnikov took the cross but said he’d wear it later, when it was time to face his suffering. Sonia agreed.
Just then, someone knocked at the door. It was Lebeziatnikov, asking if he could come in. Sonia rushed to the door, frightened.
Lebeziatnikov (a neighbor) came in looking worried. He told Sonia (Sofya Semyonovna) and Raskolnikov that Katerina Ivanovna, Sonia’s stepmother, had lost her mind. Sonia screamed in fear.

Lebeziatnikov explained that Katerina Ivanovna had gone to ask her late husband’s old boss for help, but was turned away and even threw something at him. Now she was shouting that everyone had abandoned her. She wanted to take the children into the street with a barrel-organ so they could sing and dance for money. She was making costumes for the children, teaching them songs, and beating them when they didn’t do well. She was very upset and wouldn’t listen to anyone.
Sonia quickly grabbed her things and ran out. Raskolnikov and Lebeziatnikov hurried after her.
“She really is mad,” Lebeziatnikov told Raskolnikov as they walked. “I tried to help, but she wouldn’t listen.”

Lebeziatnikov began talking about how in Paris, some people tried to cure madness with logical arguments, but Raskolnikov stopped listening. When they reached his house, Raskolnikov went inside and Lebeziatnikov left.
Raskolnikov sat alone in his small room, feeling more lonely than ever. He thought sadly about Sonia and how he might have made her life worse.
He decided, “I will stay alone, and Sonia shall not visit me in prison.” But after a while, he wondered if Siberia might be better for him.

Suddenly, his sister Dounia (Avdotya Romanovna) came in. She said she knew everything now, and didn’t blame him for staying away. She promised to care for their mother and told him to call on her if he ever needed help. As she left, Raskolnikov told her that Razumihin (Dmitri Prokofitch) was a good man. Dounia became worried, asking if this was a final goodbye, but Raskolnikov just said goodbye again.
He wanted to hug his sister goodbye but was too afraid. He wondered if Dounia or Sonia could handle such pain.
Raskolnikov went outside. He was sick and tired, but kept wandering the streets as night came. He felt miserable and hopeless.

Suddenly, Lebeziatnikov found him and said that Katerina Ivanovna had actually taken the children out into the street, just as she said she would. She was banging on a frying-pan, making the children dance, and a crowd was watching.

On the canal bank, a crowd had gathered. Katerina Ivanovna, wearing a torn hat and old dress, was making the children dance and sing. She shouted at them when they got things wrong, and sometimes at the people watching. The children were dressed up in funny costumes and looked frightened and sad. Sonia kept begging Katerina Ivanovna to go home, but she wouldn’t listen.

Katerina Ivanovna shouted that she wanted everyone to see how children from a good family were forced to beg. She hoped some important person would help them. She asked Raskolnikov to explain to Sonia that begging was the only way now. She tried to make the children sing and dance, but they kept crying.

Raskolnikov tried to talk her into going home, but Katerina Ivanovna only laughed sadly and said she would take care of the children herself now. She checked how much money Polenka had collected—it was barely anything. She argued with the children and tried to remember a good song for them to sing.

A policeman came and told them to stop making a disturbance. But a kind official gave Katerina Ivanovna some money, which made her happy for a moment. She tried to explain their story to the official and asked him to protect them. The policeman said they needed a license to perform in the street.
Katerina Ivanovna became upset, saying she had just buried her husband and didn’t need a license. The official gently said he would take her away from the crowd because she was ill.
Suddenly, Kolya and Lida, scared, ran away. Katerina Ivanovna chased after them, crying. Sonia and Polenka followed. Katerina Ivanovna fell down, and Sonia saw she was bleeding.
Raskolnikov, Lebeziatnikov, the official, and the policeman helped her. They saw the blood was coming from her chest, not a cut. The official said she was dying from her illness (consumption).

Sonia begged them to bring Katerina Ivanovna to her own room nearby. With help, they carried her there and laid her on the bed. The children and some neighbors came in too. Svidrigaïlov, another neighbor, appeared. Someone went to get a doctor, but it seemed too late.
Katerina Ivanovna woke up for a moment, asked for the children, and told Sonia she had ruined herself helping them. She said goodbye and wanted to die in peace.
She refused to see a priest, saying she had no money and no sins, and God would understand her suffering.
She started talking nonsense and remembering old songs. She became excited, tried to sing, but kept coughing and gasping.
Soon, Katerina Ivanovna became still and died. Sonia hugged her and cried. Polenka clung to her mother’s feet, sobbing. The younger children, still in costume, screamed in fear.
On the bed, Raskolnikov noticed Katerina Ivanovna’s certificate of merit from her husband’s work.
Lebeziatnikov told Raskolnikov, “She is dead.” Svidrigaïlov came over and said he wanted to talk.

Svidrigaïlov told Raskolnikov he would pay for Katerina Ivanovna’s funeral and put the children in a good orphanage. He promised to give money to each child when they grew up, so Sonia wouldn’t have to worry. He said this was how he would use Dounia’s ten thousand roubles.
Raskolnikov asked why Svidrigaïlov was helping. Svidrigaïlov said it was out of kindness and that Katerina Ivanovna was not a bad person. If he didn’t help, Polenka might end up in trouble too.

Raskolnikov was shocked because Svidrigaïlov used the same words Raskolnikov had once said to Sonia. He asked Svidrigaïlov how he knew. Svidrigaïlov explained he lived next door and could hear everything.
Svidrigaïlov laughed and said he was glad they had become friends and that Raskolnikov would see how helpful he could be.

Raskolnikov started to feel very strange. It was like he was surrounded by a thick fog and couldn’t find his way out. Sometimes he felt scared and nervous, other times he felt nothing at all, just empty. He couldn’t remember things clearly and often mixed up what happened. He wished he could stop worrying about the problems that made him feel so bad.

The person Raskolnikov worried about most was Svidrigaïlov. After Svidrigaïlov had said some scary things in Sonia’s room when Katerina Ivanovna died, Raskolnikov felt even more confused. Sometimes, when he was alone in the city or eating by himself, he would suddenly remember Svidrigaïlov and feel he should talk to him. Once, he thought they had planned to meet outside the city gates, but it wasn’t real. Another time, he woke up under some bushes and didn’t remember how he got there.
In the days after Katerina Ivanovna died, Raskolnikov met Svidrigaïlov a few times at Sonia’s place. They only spoke about ordinary things and didn’t talk about the important problem between them.

Katerina Ivanovna’s body was still in the coffin. Svidrigaïlov was organizing the funeral, and Sonia was helping. Svidrigaïlov told Raskolnikov that he had found good places for Katerina Ivanovna’s children to live, and that the money he gave helped a lot. He also said he would visit Raskolnikov soon because they needed to talk about something important.

This talk happened on the stairs. Svidrigaïlov looked closely at Raskolnikov and asked why he seemed so strange. He told Raskolnikov to cheer up and said, “What all men need is fresh air, fresh air... more than anything!”

Svidrigaïlov moved aside as the priest and his helper came up the stairs for the funeral service. Svidrigaïlov made sure the service was held twice a day. Raskolnikov went into Sonia’s room and watched the sad service. The children were kneeling by the coffin, and Polenka cried. Sonia was behind them, praying and crying softly.

Raskolnikov noticed Sonia hadn’t spoken to him in days. The room was sunny and filled with the smell of incense as the priest prayed. After the service, Raskolnikov went to Sonia. She took his hands and rested her head on his shoulder. Raskolnikov was surprised she was not angry or afraid of him. He thought she was being very kind.

Sonia didn’t say anything. Raskolnikov squeezed her hand and left, feeling very sad. He wanted to be alone, but even when he was by himself, he never felt peaceful. He walked far outside the city, but the quiet made him feel even more uneasy. Sometimes he went to busy places, like loud taverns, just to feel less alone. Once, while listening to singing in a tavern, he suddenly felt guilty, like he should be doing something else. He remembered Dounia and his mother and felt panicked. That night he woke up with a fever under some bushes and walked home. He slept for hours, and when he woke up, he felt a little better.
He remembered the funeral was happening that day and was glad he didn’t have to go. Nastasya brought him food, and he ate with a big appetite. He wondered why he had felt so panicked before.
Razumihin came in and saw Raskolnikov eating.
“Ah, he’s eating, so he’s not sick,” Razumihin said, sitting across from him.
Razumihin looked worried and serious.

“Listen,” Razumihin said. “I don’t care about your secrets, but I want to know if you are going crazy. People say you are, and I almost believe it, after how you’ve treated your mother and sister. Only someone mad could do that.”
“When did you see them last?” Raskolnikov asked.

“Just now,” said Razumihin. “Your mother has been sick since yesterday. She wanted to see you, so we all came here, but you weren’t home. She was sad and went back to bed with a fever. She thinks you only care about Sonia. I went to Sonia’s and saw the children crying and the coffin—no sign of you. So, I think you’re not actually with Sonia, and maybe you are just mad. But now I see you eating, maybe you’re not mad after all—just hiding a secret. I’ve come just to yell at you and feel better!”
“What are you going to do now?” Raskolnikov asked.
“It’s none of your business,” Razumihin said.
“You’re going to go drinking,” Raskolnikov guessed.
“How did you know?” Razumihin said, surprised.
“It’s pretty clear,” said Raskolnikov.
Razumihin sighed. “You’ve always been sensible, never crazy. You’re right, I’ll go drink. Goodbye!” He got up to leave.
“I talked to my sister, Dounia, about you the other day,” Raskolnikov said.
“About me? But when did you see her?” Razumihin asked, surprised.
“She came here and talked to me,” Raskolnikov replied.
“What did you say about me?” Razumihin asked.
“I told her you’re a good and honest man. I didn’t say you love her because she knows that already.”
“I trust you to take care of them, Razumihin,” said Raskolnikov. “I think Dounia may love you, too. So, decide for yourself if you still need to go drinking.”
Razumihin was touched. “Rodya! Well... But where are you going? Maybe I’ll find out your secret someday. But you are a good friend!”
“It’s good you don’t try to find out my secrets,” Raskolnikov said. “Just wait, you’ll know when the time comes. Someone told me we all need fresh air. I’m going to see what he meant.”
Razumihin stood thinking. He wondered if Raskolnikov was planning something important.
“So Dounia comes to see you, and you’re going to see a man who talks about fresh air. And Dounia got a letter today that upset her. It must all be connected,” Razumihin thought out loud.
“What letter?” Raskolnikov asked.
“Dounia got a letter today. It made her very upset. She even talked about maybe having to leave soon,” Razumihin said.
“She got a letter?” Raskolnikov asked.
“You didn’t know? Hmm…”
Razumihin said goodbye. “There was a time, brother, when I... Never mind, goodbye! I don’t need to drink now. That’s all over!”
He left, but then opened the door again and said, looking away:

“Oh, by the way, do you remember that murder—Porfiry’s case, the old woman? The murderer has confessed! It was one of the painters. He pretended he was innocent, but he tricked everyone. Now he has told everything.”
Raskolnikov asked quickly, “Who told you that, and why do you care?”
“Why not? Porfiry told me, and others too.”
“Porfiry?”
“Yes, Porfiry.”
“What did he say?” Raskolnikov asked, worried.
“He explained everything, in his own way,” Razumihin said.
“He explained it himself?”
“Yes. Goodbye! I’ll tell you more next time. I don’t need to drink now. I feel dizzy just talking to you! Goodbye, Rodya!”
Razumihin left.
After Razumihin left, Raskolnikov walked around his room, feeling like he could finally do something. He thought, “Yes, now I can try to escape from this mess. I can’t keep it all inside anymore.”

Svidrigaïlov was still a puzzle to him. Maybe there would be a struggle with Svidrigaïlov, but Porfiry was different. Porfiry had talked about the case with Razumihin, but Raskolnikov couldn’t believe Porfiry really thought the painter was guilty.
Raskolnikov put on his cap and left, thinking he needed to deal with Svidrigaïlov soon. He felt so angry, he thought he could hurt Porfiry or Svidrigaïlov.
“We shall see, we shall see,” he said to himself.
But as soon as he opened the door, he ran right into Porfiry in the hallway. Raskolnikov was surprised but not very afraid. He was ready for this moment.
“You didn’t expect a visitor, Rodion Romanovitch,” Porfiry said, laughing. “I was passing by and thought I’d stop in. Are you going out? I won’t stay long. Just let me have a cigarette.”
“Sit down, Porfiry Petrovitch,” said Raskolnikov, acting friendly.
Raskolnikov sat facing Porfiry, looking at him bravely. Porfiry lit a cigarette.
Raskolnikov wanted Porfiry to speak. He thought, “Come on, just say it.”

Porfiry Petrovitch (a police detective) lit a cigarette and sighed, “These cigarettes are so bad for me, but I just can’t stop! The doctor told me to quit, but what would I do instead? I don’t even drink! Everything in life is about what you compare it to, Rodion Romanovitch (that’s Raskolnikov’s full name), everything is relative!”

Porfiry continued, “I came to see you two days ago in the evening. I even came into this room because your door was open. I looked around, waited, but left without telling your servant. Don’t you lock your door?”
He smiled a little and said, “I’ve come to talk honestly with you, Rodion Romanovitch. I owe you an explanation.”

Porfiry looked sad and said, “Last time we met, things were very strange between us. Even the first time was odd. Maybe I wasn’t fair to you. Do you remember how upset we both were? We behaved badly, but we are supposed to be gentlemen.”

“Openness is better between us,” Porfiry said. “We can’t keep having all these suspicions and strange talks. Nikolay (a workman) stopped it, or things could have gotten worse. When you left, you probably saw the porters I called, but I hadn’t planned anything. Everything happened so suddenly. I thought, even if I missed something, I’d find another clue. I was hoping for some proof, just a little fact, because if someone is guilty, you can usually get something out of them. I was counting on your personality, Rodion Romanovitch. I thought maybe you’d just come out and tell me everything.”

“I want to explain how this whole misunderstanding started. I know I’ve made you suffer, Rodion Romanovitch. I’m not a monster. I understand it must be hard for a proud and strong person like you. I think you are a good person, even if I don’t agree with everything you believe. When I met you, I liked you. Maybe you didn’t like me, but I want to show you I’m not a bad person.”

Porfiry went on, “There were rumors. I won’t say where they came from, but they made me suspicious. It was just by chance. I was the first one to suspect you after the old woman’s murder (she was a pawnbroker). I also heard about how you acted at the office. It all added up. But, as people say, a hundred suspicions don’t make one proof. I even thought about your article in that journal; it showed you were bold and different. So I kept my eye on you. I searched your room when you were sick, but found nothing. We tried to get you to talk about the murder with Razumihin and Zametov, and you even said in a restaurant, ‘I killed her!’ That was very bold. But everything could be taken in two ways. So I waited for more proof, like the story about the bell-ringing and your trembling.”

“I was hoping for a small fact. When I heard about you walking with the workman who called you a murderer, and you didn’t even ask him why, I got excited. And your strange actions when you were sick made me suspect more.”

“So, can you blame me for acting the way I did? And then Nikolay confessed! But I never really believed him; it just didn’t make sense. Even when Nikolay explained things, I still thought he wasn’t the real murderer.”

“Nikolay is a strange, childlike man. He sings, tells stories, and sometimes doesn’t even know when he’s doing something wrong. He got scared and tried to hurt himself when he was blamed. In prison, he remembered his old teacher and began to think suffering was good. He’s not a criminal, just mixed up and easily led.”

“No, Rodion Romanovitch, Nikolay is not the murderer. This is a new kind of crime, where someone tries to follow a strange idea and ends up doing something terrible, like killing for a theory. The real murderer felt sick from what he did and thought he was better than others. That’s not Nikolay’s way.”
Raskolnikov whispered, “Then... who is the murderer?”
Porfiry leaned back and said softly, “You are, Rodion Romanovitch. You are the murderer.”
Raskolnikov jumped up, then sat back down, his face twitching.
Porfiry said kindly, “You misunderstood me. I came here to tell you everything openly.”
Raskolnikov whispered, like a scared child, “It wasn’t me.”
“No, it was you,” Porfiry answered firmly.
They sat in silence for a long time. Raskolnikov put his head in his hands.
Finally, Raskolnikov said angrily, “You’re using your old tricks again, Porfiry!”
Porfiry replied, “It doesn’t matter now. There’s no one else here. I’m not here to chase or arrest you. I’m sure you did it, even if you don’t confess.”
“Then why are you here? If you think I’m guilty, why not arrest me?” Raskolnikov asked.
“To arrest you right now wouldn’t help me,” Porfiry said.

“Even if I believe you did it, there’s not enough proof. If I arrested you, you could argue against it. All I have is what I think and feel, and that’s not enough. Besides, I came here for another reason.”
“I wanted to explain things to you, so you wouldn’t think I’m a monster. And, I want you to confess. It would be better for you and for me.”
Raskolnikov thought for a moment. “You say you only have feelings, but what if you’re wrong?”
Porfiry smiled. “No, I’m not wrong. I even have a small fact, something that proves it.”
“What fact?”
“I can’t tell you. But I have to arrest you soon. Think it over; it will be better for you if you confess.”
Raskolnikov laughed bitterly. “That’s silly. Even if I was guilty, why should I confess?”
“Maybe prison won’t be as easy as you think. But if you confess now, your punishment might be less. People will see you just made a terrible mistake. I promise to keep my word,” Porfiry said.
Raskolnikov stopped pretending and said quietly, “No. I don’t care about getting a lighter sentence.”
“That’s what I was afraid of,” Porfiry said sadly.
“Don’t give up on life!” Porfiry said. “You still have a lot ahead of you.”
“A lot of what?”
“Life! Maybe this is how you’ll find something good. It won’t last forever.”
Raskolnikov laughed, “The time will be shortened.”
“Are you scared of shame? Don’t be afraid to confess,” Porfiry said.
“Oh, stop it,” Raskolnikov muttered, upset.

Porfiry said, “You lost faith in your ideas, and you’re ashamed they didn’t work. But you’re not all bad. You went straight to the end. If you find faith or God, you’ll live. Suffering is sometimes good. Even Nikolay thinks so. Just go out and live, don’t be afraid. Maybe God saved you for something else.”
Raskolnikov asked, “When will you arrest me?”
“I’ll let you walk around for a day or two. Think about it and pray,” Porfiry answered.
“What if I run away?” Raskolnikov asked, smiling oddly.

“You won’t run away. You need a place to belong. Even if you did, you’d come back. If I put you in prison, you’d confess on your own after a while. Suffering is a big thing, Rodion Romanovitch. You’ll come to it,” Porfiry replied.
Raskolnikov stood up and grabbed his cap. Porfiry did the same.
Raskolnikov said, “Don’t think I confessed today. I just listened out of curiosity. I admitted nothing!”

Porfiry nodded, “I know. You’re shaking! Don’t worry. Just one thing: if anything happens, if you even think of ending your life, please leave a note about the stone. It would help. Goodbye, and I hope you make good choices!”
Porfiry left. Raskolnikov waited until he was sure Porfiry was gone, then hurried out too.

Raskolnikov hurried to see Svidrigaïlov (a man who seemed to have some power over him). He wasn’t sure why he needed to see him, but he couldn’t stop himself. On the way, he worried if Svidrigaïlov had gone to see Porfiry (the detective), but he decided he probably hadn’t. Still, he wondered if Svidrigaïlov might go later. These worries swirled in his mind, but he felt even more tired than anxious.

Raskolnikov wondered if it was even worth it to worry about Svidrigaïlov and his tricks. He was so tired of everything! But he kept going, thinking maybe Svidrigaïlov could help him somehow, or maybe he just needed to see him. He thought about Sonia (the kind girl who helped him) but was too afraid to see her now. Svidrigaïlov seemed like the only choice.

Raskolnikov didn’t trust Svidrigaïlov. People said he was cruel and sneaky. He was helping Katerina Ivanovna’s children, but who knew why? Maybe he had a secret plan. Worse, Raskolnikov was scared that Svidrigaïlov knew his secret and wanted to use it against his sister Dounia. What if Svidrigaïlov hurt her? Raskolnikov thought he might have to tell Dounia everything, or even turn himself in to protect her.
He decided he had to see Svidrigaïlov right away. If Svidrigaïlov was plotting against Dounia, he would stop him, even if it meant doing something terrible.
Raskolnikov was so tired and upset that he thought, “If he hurts Dounia, I’ll kill him.”

Suddenly, Raskolnikov stopped in the street, confused about where he was. He found himself near a noisy tavern. Looking up, he saw Svidrigaïlov at a window, smoking. Svidrigaïlov seemed to want to hide, but when he saw Raskolnikov watching, he smiled slyly and laughed loudly.
“Well, well, come in if you want me! I am here!” Svidrigaïlov called out.

Raskolnikov went inside and found Svidrigaïlov in a small room. There was a girl named Katia singing with a boy playing a hand organ. Svidrigaïlov told Katia to stop singing and paid her. She drank her wine, took her money, and left with the boy.
Svidrigaïlov seemed very comfortable in this dirty tavern room. He might spend whole days there.
Raskolnikov told Svidrigaïlov that he hadn’t meant to come this way, but just turned and saw him. It felt strange.
Svidrigaïlov joked, “Why don’t you say it’s a miracle?”
Raskolnikov said maybe it was just chance.
Svidrigaïlov laughed and said people are afraid to believe in miracles. He said he was curious about Raskolnikov because he had his own opinions.
Raskolnikov said Svidrigaïlov wanted to see him before he knew that. Svidrigaïlov said everyone has plans, and reminded Raskolnikov that he had told him about this tavern before.

Raskolnikov didn’t remember, but Svidrigaïlov said sometimes people do things without knowing. He watched Raskolnikov walking and talking to himself, and told him to be careful—someone besides him might be watching.
Raskolnikov asked if Svidrigaïlov knew he was being followed. Svidrigaïlov said no.
Raskolnikov asked why Svidrigaïlov tried to hide just now. Svidrigaïlov joked back, asking why Raskolnikov had pretended to sleep the other day. They both agreed they had their own reasons.
Raskolnikov looked closely at Svidrigaïlov. He had a strange, young-looking face, bright lips, blue eyes, and dressed very neatly.
Raskolnikov grew tired of talking in circles. He told Svidrigaïlov, “If you try to hurt my sister, I’ll stop you. If you have something to say, say it quickly.”
Svidrigaïlov asked why he was in such a hurry. Raskolnikov said everyone had their own plans.
Svidrigaïlov said he didn’t really want anything special, but liked watching interesting people, and that’s why he hung around Raskolnikov.
Svidrigaïlov said he was interested in Raskolnikov and also in Dounia, his sister. He joked that maybe he, too, was hoping to learn something new from Raskolnikov.

Raskolnikov asked what Svidrigaïlov could possibly gain from him. Svidrigaïlov said he was just bored, sitting in the tavern, eating bad food. He said he didn’t drink much, just a little champagne, and was about to go out. He thought maybe Raskolnikov would tell him something interesting.
Raskolnikov asked, “What are you, and why are you here?”
Svidrigaïlov answered, “I’m a gentleman. I was in the cavalry, then I came to Petersburg, got married, and lived in the country.”
Raskolnikov asked if he was a gambler. Svidrigaïlov said he was a poor gambler, more like a card-cheater.
Raskolnikov asked if he ever got beaten up. Svidrigaïlov said yes, and that he came to Petersburg for the women after his wife Marfa Petrovna died.

Svidrigaïlov didn’t feel bad about chasing after women, saying it was just what he liked. Raskolnikov said it was bad, like a sickness. Svidrigaïlov agreed it could be, but said everyone had something like that.
Raskolnikov asked if Svidrigaïlov could ever shoot himself. Svidrigaïlov quickly said no, he was afraid of death and didn’t want to talk about it. He said he was a little bit of a mystic.

Raskolnikov asked if Svidrigaïlov still saw Marfa Petrovna’s ghost. Svidrigaïlov said not in Petersburg and didn’t want to talk about it. He said he didn’t have much time and wished he could talk more.
Raskolnikov guessed Svidrigaïlov had a meeting with a woman. Svidrigaïlov admitted it, but said that wasn’t what he wanted to talk about.

Raskolnikov asked if Svidrigaïlov was bothered by all the bad things around him. Svidrigaïlov laughed at Raskolnikov for acting like a teacher. He called him an idealist and asked if he liked the writer Schiller.

Raskolnikov said Svidrigaïlov was a bragger. Svidrigaïlov laughed and said maybe he was, but he liked talking to someone interesting. He said something had made him excited, but he would keep quiet about it.
Raskolnikov felt uncomfortable and wanted to leave, thinking Svidrigaïlov was a very bad person.
Svidrigaïlov begged him to stay a little longer and have some tea. He offered to tell a story about how Dounia, Raskolnikov’s sister, once tried to help him.
Raskolnikov agreed, but hoped Svidrigaïlov would be respectful.
Svidrigaïlov promised to speak with respect, saying Dounia could only make him feel respect, even though he was a bad man.

Svidrigaïlov (a man who once knew Raskolnikov’s family) began to talk about his past. He said he owed a lot of money and had to stay in a prison for people with debts. Marfa Petrovna (his wife, who was older and not very educated) paid to get him out. She loved him very much, even though he told her he could not promise to always be faithful. They made an agreement: he would never leave her, would only be with other women if she knew about it, and would never fall in love with someone from their own social class. If he did fall in love, he had to tell her. Marfa Petrovna believed Svidrigaïlov could never truly love anyone, but she was very jealous. When Avdotya Romanovna (Raskolnikov’s sister, also called Dounia) came to work for them, Marfa Petrovna liked her a lot and told her all about her problems with Svidrigaïlov. Avdotya Romanovna learned many strange things about Svidrigaïlov from Marfa Petrovna. Svidrigaïlov said he was sorry for making Marfa Petrovna unhappy. When they argued, he stayed quiet, which made her calm down. But Marfa Petrovna did not like Dounia, even though she brought her into their house. Svidrigaïlov saw right away that Dounia was in danger being around him, so he tried not to talk to her. But she spoke to him first, and soon Marfa Petrovna was mad at him for not saying enough about Dounia. Marfa Petrovna told Dounia everything about Svidrigaïlov, even some bad rumors. Svidrigaïlov asked Raskolnikov if he had heard these tales.
Raskolnikov said, “I heard that Luzhin (another man who wanted to marry Dounia) said you caused a child’s death. Is that true?”
Svidrigaïlov got annoyed and said he didn’t want to talk about those stories.
Raskolnikov also mentioned hearing about a servant Svidrigaïlov treated badly.
Svidrigaïlov quickly said to stop talking about it.
Raskolnikov asked if it was the same servant whom Svidrigaïlov said had come back as a ghost.
Svidrigaïlov looked at Raskolnikov closely but stayed polite.

Svidrigaïlov said, “Yes, that’s right.” He joked about being interesting to people and thanked Marfa Petrovna for telling Dounia all these stories, because it made Dounia feel sorry for him. He said that when a girl feels sorry for someone, she wants to help him, and that can be very dangerous. Svidrigaïlov said he thought Dounia was the kind of person who would even suffer for others. He wished she had been born long ago, when people were heroes. He said Dounia was very good and very modest. Once, Dounia asked him to leave another girl, Parasha, alone because she was upset. Dounia tried to make Svidrigaïlov a better person, but he just pretended he wanted to change. He said it’s easier to flatter people than to tell the truth. He told about another time he flattered a lady and got her to like him, even though she tried to be good. He said he could have gotten Marfa Petrovna to give him all her money, but he did not. Svidrigaïlov admitted he started to have the same effect on Dounia, but he ruined it by acting badly and making her uncomfortable. They stopped talking, and he acted foolishly, making fun of Dounia’s efforts to help him. He even thought about giving her lots of money if she would run away with him. He was so obsessed that he would have done anything she asked! But instead, Marfa Petrovna tried to set up Dounia with Luzhin. Svidrigaïlov noticed Raskolnikov was paying close attention.
Svidrigaïlov banged his fist on the table. He was getting a little drunk. Raskolnikov noticed this and decided to ask more questions, feeling suspicious.
Raskolnikov said, “I’m sure you came to Petersburg because of my sister.”
Svidrigaïlov said, “No, I told you—she doesn’t even like me.”
Raskolnikov replied, “She definitely doesn’t, but that’s not the point.”
Svidrigaïlov grinned and said, “You think she doesn’t love me, but you can never be sure what happens between people. Are you sure Dounia really dislikes me?”
Raskolnikov said, “From the way you talk, I think you still have bad plans for Dounia.”
Svidrigaïlov acted surprised and asked if he had really said that.
Raskolnikov said he was showing it right now and asked what he was so afraid of.
Svidrigaïlov laughed and said he wasn’t afraid, but he realized he had drunk too much and was talking too much. He called for water.
He threw his champagne bottle out the window, and Philip (the servant) brought him water.
Svidrigaïlov said, “All this is nonsense. But I can end your doubts: I am getting married!”
Raskolnikov said, “You told me that before.”

Svidrigaïlov said he really had a fiancée now, and would show her to Raskolnikov if he had time. He explained that Madame Resslich (the woman he rented a room from) arranged the marriage. The girl’s family was poor. Her father was paralyzed, her mother was sensible, and they had other children to care for. The girl was almost sixteen. Svidrigaïlov said he was fifty, but no one cared about the age difference. He told how he met the family, talked to the parents, and became engaged the next day. He gave her many expensive gifts. The girl was shy and cried once, but soon promised to be a good wife. Svidrigaïlov thought she was like an angel and found the whole thing very exciting. He wanted to take Raskolnikov to meet her, but not right now.
Raskolnikov said, “You just like her because she is so much younger. Will you really marry her?”
Svidrigaïlov laughed and said everyone does things for themselves, and he admitted he was not a good man.
Raskolnikov pointed out that Svidrigaïlov had helped Katerina Ivanovna’s children, but said he understood Svidrigaïlov had his own reasons.

Svidrigaïlov said he liked children and told a story about going to a dance place when he first came to town. He saw a girl of thirteen dancing with older people and she started to cry. Everyone just laughed. Svidrigaïlov said he talked to her mother, offered help, and later helped the girl and her mother with money and lessons. He said he still visited them and offered to take Raskolnikov to meet them too.
Raskolnikov interrupted, telling Svidrigaïlov to stop telling such bad stories.
Svidrigaïlov just laughed and said he liked to shock Raskolnikov.
Raskolnikov muttered that he felt silly.
Svidrigaïlov laughed, called Philip to pay the bill, and got up.
He said, “I’m drunk. I’ve talked enough. It’s been fun.”
Raskolnikov stood up too and said, “It must be fun for someone like you to tell these stories. Especially with your new plans.”

Svidrigaïlov looked at Raskolnikov and said, “If you think about it, you’re a bit of a cynic too. You understand a lot. But that’s enough. I wish we could talk more, but I’ll be watching you. Wait a bit.”

Svidrigaïlov left the restaurant, and Raskolnikov followed. Svidrigaïlov was not as drunk now, but looked worried and excited. He was meaner to Raskolnikov, who noticed the change and decided to keep an eye on him.
They walked outside.
Svidrigaïlov said, “You go one way, I’ll go the other. Goodbye, maybe we’ll meet again.”
Then Svidrigaïlov walked away toward the Hay Market.
Raskolnikov (a young man) followed Svidrigaïlov (another man) down the street.
Svidrigaïlov turned and said, "Why are you following me?"
Raskolnikov answered, "I'm not going to let you out of my sight now."
Both men stared at each other, trying to act tough.
Raskolnikov said he knew Svidrigaïlov was still trying to bother his sister, Dounia. He had heard that Dounia got a letter that morning and didn’t trust Svidrigaïlov.
Svidrigaïlov threatened to call the police, but Raskolnikov said he didn’t care.

After a moment, Svidrigaïlov changed his attitude. He pretended to be friendly and joked about Raskolnikov being curious. He said he was just going home for money and then would go to the Islands for the evening.
Raskolnikov said he was going to Svidrigaïlov’s place to see Sofya Semyonovna (Sonia) to say sorry for missing the funeral.
Svidrigaïlov said Sonia wasn’t home. She had taken three children to visit a kind old lady. He told Raskolnikov that Sonia would be at the X. Hotel.
Raskolnikov said he would go anyway.
Svidrigaïlov didn’t care and said he wouldn’t go with Raskolnikov. When they arrived at the building, Svidrigaïlov teased Raskolnikov for being suspicious and said he was just being polite.
Raskolnikov accused Svidrigaïlov of listening at doors.
Svidrigaïlov laughed about it and started mocking Raskolnikov about his worries and his secret. He told Raskolnikov he should run away to America if he was so worried.
Raskolnikov, disgusted, said that wasn’t what he was thinking about.
Svidrigaïlov kept teasing him and talked about moral questions and even told Raskolnikov maybe he should shoot himself.
Raskolnikov said Svidrigaïlov was just trying to make him angry.

Svidrigaïlov led Raskolnikov to the stairs and showed him there was no one home. He talked about Sonia’s key and his landlady, Madame Resslich. He showed Raskolnikov some bonds, locked up his things, and got ready to leave for the Islands in a carriage. He offered Raskolnikov a ride, but Raskolnikov said no.
Svidrigaïlov got into the carriage, and Raskolnikov walked away, feeling disgusted with Svidrigaïlov. Raskolnikov didn’t see Svidrigaïlov get out of the cab and secretly walk away.
Raskolnikov was angry at himself for ever thinking Svidrigaïlov could help him.
Raskolnikov thought Svidrigaïlov was strange and was sure Svidrigaïlov would not stop bothering Dounia. But Raskolnikov was tired of thinking about it.
Alone, Raskolnikov walked deep in thought. He stopped on a bridge to look at the water. Suddenly his sister, Dounia, was near him.
Dounia saw her brother but he didn’t see her. She was worried and didn’t know if she should call to him. Then she noticed Svidrigaïlov sneaking nearby.
Svidrigaïlov tried to signal to Dounia to come to him without Raskolnikov seeing.
Dounia quietly walked past her brother and went to Svidrigaïlov.
Svidrigaïlov whispered that they should leave quickly. He didn’t want Raskolnikov to know they were meeting. He said Raskolnikov knew about his letter to Dounia and was suspicious.
Dounia said they were far enough away now, so he could speak.
Svidrigaïlov said he couldn’t talk out on the street, and that Sonia should hear too. He hinted he had a big secret about Raskolnikov. If Dounia didn’t come with him, he wouldn’t explain.
Dounia looked at Svidrigaïlov, not sure what to do.

Svidrigaïlov said there was nothing to fear, and they were almost at his house. He explained that Sonia lived next to him, and there were many rooms in the building. He tried to calm Dounia, but she was still scared.
Dounia said she was not afraid of him. Svidrigaïlov led her to Sonia’s room, but Sonia wasn’t home. He said she might be back soon and showed Dounia his rooms.
Svidrigaïlov showed Dounia two empty rooms next to his. He explained that he had used a chair to listen through the wall to Sonia and Raskolnikov talking.
Dounia was shocked that Svidrigaïlov had listened at the door.
Svidrigaïlov took Dounia back to his room. She gave him his letter and demanded to know if what he wrote about her brother was true. She said she didn’t believe it.
Svidrigaïlov asked why she came alone if she didn’t believe him. Dounia begged him to explain.
Svidrigaïlov said she was brave for coming by herself and asked what she thought of her brother.
Dounia wanted more proof than just seeing Raskolnikov.

Svidrigaïlov said he had heard Raskolnikov confess everything to Sonia. He told Dounia that Raskolnikov had killed an old pawnbroker woman and her sister, Lizaveta, with an axe. He said Raskolnikov stole money but hid it and never used it. Sonia knew the secret but would not tell anyone.
Dounia was shocked and couldn’t believe it. She said it was a lie.
Svidrigaïlov said Raskolnikov had stolen the money but was too afraid to use it.
Dounia couldn’t understand how her brother could steal or murder. She begged Svidrigaïlov to explain.

Svidrigaïlov said sometimes people do terrible things for strange reasons. He talked about Raskolnikov’s ideas about some people being above the law, like Napoleon. He said Raskolnikov thought he was special, but now he was suffering.
Dounia asked if Raskolnikov felt sorry for what he did.
Svidrigaïlov said everything was mixed up, and people sometimes had strange ideas. He said Russians often had big, confusing ideas.
Dounia said she had read Raskolnikov’s article about people who think they can do anything.
Svidrigaïlov was surprised and asked where she was going. Dounia said she wanted to see Sonia right away but felt faint.
Svidrigaïlov told Dounia that Sonia would not be back until late.
Dounia realized Svidrigaïlov had been lying to her and became very upset. She sat down, almost fainting.
Svidrigaïlov gave her water and said he could help Raskolnikov escape. He promised Raskolnikov could become a good man someday and that he would help him.
Dounia called Svidrigaïlov cruel and wanted to leave.
She tried to get out, but the door was locked. She asked why.
Svidrigaïlov said he was tired of talking and warned her not to do anything that would get her brother caught by the police. He said they should think together about how to save him.
Dounia asked if Raskolnikov could really be saved.

Svidrigaïlov said it was all up to Dounia. He became very emotional and said he loved her. He offered to help her brother escape if Dounia would love him back. He begged her, saying he would do anything for her.
Dounia was scared and tried to get away, but Svidrigaïlov locked the door and said no one else was home.
Dounia demanded the key, but Svidrigaïlov said he couldn’t find it.
Dounia became even more frightened and tried to protect herself with a table.
Svidrigaïlov told Dounia that no one would believe her if she accused him of anything, and she would be risking her brother’s safety.
Dounia called him a scoundrel. Svidrigaïlov said he would be her slave if she agreed to his plan.
Dounia suddenly pulled out a revolver and pointed it at him. Svidrigaïlov recognized it as his old gun and realized she knew how to use it.
Dounia said the revolver had belonged to Marfa Petrovna, Svidrigaïlov’s late wife, and warned him not to come closer or she would shoot.
Svidrigaïlov kept talking, and Dounia accused him of poisoning his wife.
Svidrigaïlov said maybe he had, but only because of Dounia.
Dounia said she had always hated him.
Svidrigaïlov teased her, but Dounia denied ever liking him.
Svidrigaïlov said he believed Dounia would really shoot, so he told her to go ahead.
Dounia aimed and fired. The bullet just grazed Svidrigaïlov’s head, making him bleed a little. He laughed.
Dounia was shocked and didn’t move.
Svidrigaïlov told her to shoot again. She tried, but the gun did not go off.
Svidrigaïlov said she could reload and fire again if she wanted.
Dounia saw he would not let her go and realized she would have to kill him to escape. Instead, she threw the gun away.
Svidrigaïlov was surprised. He walked over and gently put his arm around her. Dounia did not resist but looked at him sadly.
Dounia quietly asked him to let her go. Svidrigaïlov asked if she could ever love him. She shook her head.
"Never," Dounia said.
Svidrigaïlov seemed very sad. He turned to the window. After a moment, he took the key from his pocket and put it on the table.
He told Dounia to hurry. She grabbed the key, unlocked the door, and ran out.
Svidrigaïlov stood at the window for a while, looking sad and hopeless. He cleaned the blood from his head, found the revolver, and put it in his pocket. Then he took his hat and left.

That evening, Svidrigaïlov went from one rough place to another until late at night. He listened to Katia (a girl who sang in the streets) sing a silly song. He bought treats for Katia, the organ-grinder, some singers, the waiters, and two young clerks. Svidrigaïlov liked the clerks because both had funny crooked noses. The clerks took him to a small garden with just one skinny pine tree, three bushes, and a little café with tea and drinks. There were sad singers and a tired clown there. The clerks got into a fight with other clerks. Svidrigaïlov tried to help, but everyone was shouting. The problem was about a stolen teaspoon. Svidrigaïlov paid for the spoon and left the garden. He hadn’t had any wine, just tea. It was about six o’clock.
The evening was dark and stuffy. At ten o’clock, a storm came. Thunder crashed, rain poured down hard, and lightning flashed again and again.

Svidrigaïlov came home soaking wet. He locked himself in, took out his money, and tore up some papers. He put the money in his pocket. He thought about changing his clothes, but instead, he just grabbed his hat and left, not locking the door behind him. He went to see Sonia.
Sonia was at home with the four Kapernaumov children, giving them tea. When Svidrigaïlov came in, the children ran away, scared by his wet clothes.
Svidrigaïlov sat down and asked Sonia to sit with him. She was shy and quiet.

Svidrigaïlov told Sonia, “I might be leaving for America soon, so I came to settle some things. Your sisters and brother have money saved for them. Here are the receipts. And here are some bonds just for you—three thousand roubles. Keep this secret. You’ll need the money. Life is hard, but you don’t have to live the same way anymore.”
Sonia thanked him and tried to say more, but Svidrigaïlov stopped her.
Sonia said she was grateful, but she didn’t need the money because she could work.

Svidrigaïlov told her to keep it for herself. He said, “You might need it for Rodion Romanovitch (Raskolnikov). He could go to Siberia or worse. If he goes, you’ll follow him, right? You’ll need money for that. Also, you promised to pay Amalia Ivanovna. That was Katerina Ivanovna’s debt, not yours. Be careful about such things. If anyone asks about me visiting you, don’t say anything. Hide the money or give it to Razumihin to keep safe.”
Sonia stood up, worried and wanted to ask Svidrigaïlov a question, but didn’t know how.
She finally asked, “How can you go out now, in such rain?”
Svidrigaïlov just laughed and said, “I won’t let rain stop me from going to America! Goodbye, Sofya Semyonovna. Tell Razumihin I said hello.”
He left, and Sonia felt scared and confused.

Later that night, around eleven-thirty, Svidrigaïlov visited the parents of his fiancée. He was still soaking wet from the rain. At first the family was surprised, but Svidrigaïlov acted friendly. The mother started with odd questions like always, but Svidrigaïlov wanted to see his fiancée right away, even though she was already in bed. The girl came out to see him.

Svidrigaïlov told her he had to leave town for important business and gave her fifteen thousand roubles as a present. The family didn’t really understand why he gave so much money and why he came at midnight in the rain, but they were grateful. The mother whispered to keep the money secret and locked up safely. Everyone was excited, but the girl went to bed, feeling both surprised and sad.

At midnight, Svidrigaïlov crossed the bridge back to the city. The rain had stopped, but the wind was strong and cold. He looked at the dark river for a while, then kept walking, searching for a hotel he had seen before. At last, he found the wooden hotel called “Adrianople.” He went inside and asked a ragged man for a room. The man led him to a small, stuffy room under the stairs—it was the only one left.
Svidrigaïlov asked for tea and veal to eat, and nothing else.
He looked around his tiny room. The ceiling was so low he could hardly stand up. The bed was dirty, and the walls were covered in torn yellow paper.
Svidrigaïlov sat on the bed and listened to loud talking next door. Someone was yelling at another man.

Svidrigaïlov peeked through a crack in the wall. He saw a curly-haired man shouting at another man, calling him a beggar and saying he had taken care of him. The second man just sat and looked confused. There was a candle, some wine, and old tea on the table. Svidrigaïlov watched for a moment, then sat back down.

The ragged man brought his tea and veal. Svidrigaïlov drank the tea to warm up but felt sick and didn’t eat. He wrapped himself in the blanket and lay down. The room was smelly and noisy from the wind and mice. He started thinking about his life and all sorts of things, but soon blew out the candle and tried to sleep.
Svidrigaïlov couldn’t sleep. He thought of Dounia and how things might have been different. He remembered how he never really hated anyone, and wondered if that was a bad thing.

He started to doze off when he felt something run over his arm and leg. Scared, he jumped up, thinking it was a mouse. He saw a mouse run across the bed and tried to catch it, but it ran away. He was nervous and tried to sleep again.

He sat on the bed, wrapped in the blanket. His mind drifted to strange thoughts and dreams about flowers and a pretty garden. Then he dreamed of a girl lying in a coffin, surrounded by flowers. She had drowned herself because she was so sad.

Svidrigaïlov woke up, feeling cold. He opened the window and felt the wind and rain. He looked outside into the dark garden. He heard a cannon boom, which meant the river was flooding. He wondered about the time, and just then a clock struck three.
“It will be morning soon,” he thought. “I’ll go to the park now and find a big, wet bush.”
He put on his clothes and went to pay the ragged man for his room.

In the hallway, Svidrigaïlov found a little girl, about five years old, soaked and crying. She told him she ran away because her mother would beat her for breaking a cup. Svidrigaïlov took her to his room, dried her off, put her in bed, and covered her with a blanket. She fell asleep right away.

Svidrigaïlov looked at the sleeping girl. Her cheeks were red, as if she had a fever. Suddenly, her face seemed strange, and he thought she was pretending to sleep. She grinned at him in a way that scared him. He was shocked and shouted, but then he woke up. It had all been a dream.
He was back in bed, with daylight coming in.

“Just a nightmare,” he muttered. He felt tired and sore. It was almost five o’clock, and he had overslept. He got dressed, took out his revolver and a notebook. He wrote a few lines in the notebook, then sat thinking. Some flies landed on his food, and he tried to catch one, but soon stopped and left the room.

Outside, the city was covered in thick mist. Svidrigaïlov walked toward the river, thinking about his plan. The streets were empty and cold. He passed closed shops, a drunk man sleeping on the ground, and a tall tower. He decided this was the right place.
He walked to the big house with the tower. A sleepy guard named Achilles stood by the gate.
Achilles asked, “What do you want here?”
Svidrigaïlov replied, “Nothing, good morning.”
Achilles said, “This isn’t the place.”
“I’m going to foreign lands,” said Svidrigaïlov.
“To America,” he added.
Svidrigaïlov took out his revolver and readied it. Achilles looked surprised.
“Don’t do that here! This isn’t the place!” Achilles said, worried.
Svidrigaïlov answered, “It’s fine. Just tell people I was going to America.”
Svidrigaïlov put the gun to his head.
Achilles shouted, “You can’t do that here!”
Svidrigaïlov pulled the trigger.

That evening, around seven o’clock, Raskolnikov walked slowly to the place where his mother (Pulcheria Alexandrovna) and sister (Dounia) were staying. Razumihin had found this home for them. Raskolnikov was tired, and his clothes were dirty and wet from the rain. He felt unsure, but he had made up his mind to visit.

When Raskolnikov knocked, his mother opened the door. Dounia was not home, and even the servant was out. Pulcheria Alexandrovna was so happy and surprised to see her son. She took his hand and brought him inside, smiling and crying at the same time.
“Oh, Rodya (her nickname for Raskolnikov), I am so glad to see you! Don’t mind my tears. I cry easily since your father died. You look tired and muddy.”
“I was out in the rain yesterday, mother,” Raskolnikov said.

His mother quickly told him not to worry. She said she knew he was busy with important thoughts and plans. She was reading his article in a magazine, even though she didn’t understand everything. She guessed that his work was the reason he seemed so mysterious.
“Show me, mother,” Raskolnikov said, taking the magazine. He looked at his article, but reading it made him feel sad and upset, so he put it down.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna told him how proud she was of his smart ideas, and how she knew he would be famous one day. She remembered how his father had tried to get his own stories published but was not successful. She said she used to worry about Raskolnikov, but now she believed he would do great things.
“Is Dounia not at home, mother?”
“No, she’s out. Dmitri Prokofitch (Razumihin) comes to visit and always talks about you. Dounia loves you and me, but she keeps some secrets lately. Still, I am happy you came.”
Pulcheria Alexandrovna started to cry again.
She jumped up, saying she forgot to offer him coffee. But Raskolnikov told her not to bother, because he would be leaving soon and had something important to say.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna came closer, worried.
Raskolnikov asked, “Mother, will you always love me, no matter what happens or what you hear about me?”
“Rodya, how can you ask that? Of course, I will always love you! I wouldn’t believe anything bad people say.”
Raskolnikov told her he loved her and was glad they were alone. He said she might be unhappy soon, but she should always remember that he loves her more than anything.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna hugged him and cried softly.
She said she felt something bad was going to happen and had worried about him for many nights. She asked if Raskolnikov was going away.
“Yes,” he answered.
She begged to come with him, and said Dounia and Sofya Semyonovna (Sonia) could come too. She asked where he was going.
“Good-bye, mother,” Raskolnikov said.
“What, today?” she cried.
“I can’t stay. I must go.”
She asked again if she could go with him.
“No, but please pray for me,” he said.
She blessed him and made the sign of the cross. Both of them cried and hugged. She was not surprised by his strange behavior, because she had already felt something terrible was happening to her son.
Pulcheria Alexandrovna remembered when Raskolnikov was a little boy and used to comfort her. She asked again if he was leaving that day.
“No!” he said.
“You’ll come again?”
“Yes... I’ll come.”
“Is it far where you are going?”
“Very far.”
“Is there a good job waiting for you?”
“Whatever God decides. Just pray for me.” He got up to go, but his mother looked at him with fear.
“Enough, mother,” Raskolnikov said, wishing he hadn’t come.
“Will you come tomorrow?”
“I will, good-bye.” He left.

It was a warm, clear evening. Raskolnikov hurried back to his own room, wanting to finish everything before sunset and not meet anyone on the way. When he went inside, he saw Dounia waiting for him. She looked very sad, and he knew she understood everything.
“Should I come in or go away?” he asked.
Dounia said, “I was with Sofya Semyonovna (Sonia) all day. We were waiting for you.”
Raskolnikov sat down, feeling very weak and tired.
“I wish I could control myself, Dounia. I feel so tired.”
Dounia asked, “Where were you all night?”
“I don’t remember well. I walked by the river and thought about ending it all, but I couldn’t do it,” he whispered.
“Thank God you didn’t! Sonia and I were afraid you might hurt yourself.”
Raskolnikov said he had no hope, but he had just cried in his mother’s arms and asked her to pray for him. He didn’t understand his own feelings.
Dounia was shocked and asked if he had told their mother everything.
“No, but she understands a lot. Maybe I shouldn’t have gone. I don’t know. I’m not a good person, Dounia.”
“But you are brave enough to face the truth, aren’t you?” Dounia asked.
“Yes, I’m going now. I wanted to escape shame by drowning myself, but I decided to face it instead. It’s pride,” he said.
“Pride, Rodya.”
“You don’t think I was just afraid of the water, do you?” he asked with a strange smile.
“Oh, Rodya, please stop!” Dounia cried. They were silent for a while. Then Raskolnikov stood up.
“It’s time to go! I am going to give myself up. But I don’t know why.”
Dounia started to cry.
“You’re crying, but can you still hold my hand?”
“Did you ever doubt it?” Dounia hugged him.
“Isn’t it brave to take the punishment for what you’ve done?” she said, holding him close.

“Crime? What crime?” Raskolnikov said angrily. “I only killed a terrible old pawnbroker who hurt poor people. Was that really a crime? I only wanted to help people after that, but I failed. Now I am just giving up because I am weak, maybe even for my own benefit, like Porfiry said.”
“Brother, you shed blood,” Dounia cried.

“So do many people! Wars kill many, and people call them heroes. I only wanted to do good things after, but I couldn’t even finish the first step. Still, if I had succeeded, people would praise me. Now I am caught.”
“No, brother, don’t say that!”
“It just doesn’t look nice, that’s all. Why is killing in war better? I’ve never felt more sure that what I did wasn’t a real crime.”
But when he saw Dounia’s sad face, he remembered that he had made his mother and sister so unhappy.

“Dounia, if I am guilty, forgive me. Good-bye! Don’t follow me. Go to mother and stay with her. I left her worried and she needs you. Razumihin will help you. Don’t cry for me. I’ll try to be honest, even if I am a murderer. Maybe someday I’ll make you proud. Now, good-bye,” he finished quickly, seeing Dounia’s sad eyes. “Why are you crying? Don’t cry; this isn’t forever. Wait, I almost forgot!”
He took a little portrait from a book. It was of his landlady’s daughter, who had died. He looked at the face, kissed the picture, and gave it to Dounia.

“I used to talk to her about my ideas. She was against what I did, just like you. Now everything will change, but am I ready? They say I must suffer, but what’s the point? When I stood by the river this morning, I knew I was weak.”
At last, they both left the room. Dounia walked away, but after a while she turned to look at Raskolnikov. He was still there. He saw her looking and waved her away, then walked off.

“I am bad, I see that,” Raskolnikov thought. “Why do they love me if I don’t deserve it? If only I had been alone, none of this would have happened. Will I become humble and sad in prison after so many years? Is that what they want? But everyone has done wrong things, yet they would be angry if I didn’t get punished. I hate them all.”
He thought about how prison might change him and make him weak. He wondered why he was still going to give himself up, but he kept walking anyway.

When Raskolnikov went into Sonia’s room, it was getting dark. Sonia had been waiting for him all day, feeling very worried. Dounia (his sister) was with her. Dounia remembered Svidrigaïlov’s words, that Sonia knew Raskolnikov’s secret. The two girls became friends and cried together. Dounia felt better because she knew her brother would not be alone. She saw that Raskolnikov trusted Sonia and would stay with her. Sonia felt shy around Dounia because she thought Dounia was so kind and respectful.

After a while, Dounia left Sonia to wait for her brother in his room. Both girls were afraid Raskolnikov might hurt himself, but they tried to comfort each other. When they were alone again, Sonia remembered Svidrigaïlov saying Raskolnikov had two choices: to go to Siberia or something worse. She also knew Raskolnikov was proud and didn’t really believe in much.
The sun was setting. Sonia was sad and looked out the window at the blank wall. She started to think Raskolnikov was dead, but then he walked into the room.
Sonia cried out in happiness, but when she saw his face, she turned pale.
Raskolnikov smiled and said, “I have come for your cross, Sonia. You told me to go to the cross-roads. Why are you scared now that I’m really going?”
Sonia was surprised. He sounded strange, and she felt a shiver. She noticed he wouldn’t look at her.

Raskolnikov said he thought it was best to turn himself in, but he didn’t want all the people at the police office to stare and ask questions. He talked quickly and seemed upset. He asked for the crosses.
Raskolnikov was restless and couldn’t stand still. He talked with shaky hands.
Sonia took out two crosses, one wooden and one copper. She made the sign of the cross over herself and Raskolnikov, then put the wooden cross around his neck.

Raskolnikov laughed and said, “This is to show I’m taking up the cross. The wooden one is for me, and the copper one, which belonged to Lizaveta, you will wear. I remember now, I threw some things back on the old woman’s neck. But I’m forgetting what matters. I came to warn you, Sonia, that I’m going to turn myself in. That’s all. Why are you crying? Please don’t cry!”
He felt sad seeing Sonia cry and wondered why she cared so much about him.
Sonia quietly asked him to cross himself and say a prayer.
Raskolnikov agreed, though he wanted to say something else.
He crossed himself a few times. Sonia put on her green shawl. Raskolnikov noticed it was the same shawl Marmeladov had mentioned, but he didn’t say anything. He realized Sonia wanted to go with him.
“What are you doing? Where are you going? Stay here, I’ll go alone,” he said, feeling upset, and went to the door.
Sonia stood in the middle of the room. Raskolnikov hadn’t said good-bye. He left her there, feeling doubtful about what he was doing.
As he went down the stairs, he wondered if he was really doing the right thing and if he should turn back.
But he kept going. Then he remembered he didn’t say good-bye to Sonia. He stopped, thinking about it, and suddenly wondered why he had gone to see her at all.
He realized he hadn’t really needed to see Sonia. Maybe he just wanted to see someone who cared about him, or maybe he wanted her to feel sad for him. He felt ashamed and thought badly of himself.
Raskolnikov walked along the canal, almost at the police office. But when he reached the bridge, he turned and went to the busy Hay Market.

He looked at everything around him and tried to remember how things looked. He thought that soon he would be taken to prison and wondered how he would feel then. He saw a beggar woman with a baby and gave her his last coin.
He went into the crowded Hay Market. There was a drunk man dancing and falling down. Raskolnikov watched him, laughed a little, and then forgot about him.

Suddenly, he remembered what Sonia had told him: to go to the cross-roads, bow to the people, kiss the earth, and say, “I am a murderer.” He felt a rush of feelings and started to cry. He knelt down right there.
He bowed to the ground, kissed the dirty earth, stood up, and bowed again.
People around him laughed and joked about what he was doing.

The people’s laughter stopped Raskolnikov from saying out loud that he was a murderer. He got up quietly and walked toward the police office. He saw Sonia hiding behind a shack, following him. He knew then that Sonia would always stay with him, no matter what.
Raskolnikov went into the police building. He walked up to the third floor, feeling weak and nervous, but still moving forward.
He opened the office door. There were only a few people there. He walked in, thinking maybe he didn’t have to say anything after all.
He asked if anyone was there.
