Suddenly, a familiar voice called out. It was Ilya Petrovitch (the Explosive Lieutenant). Raskolnikov was surprised he was there.
Ilya Petrovitch greeted him kindly and talked a lot, asking what Raskolnikov wanted and talking about literature, his family, and other things.
Raskolnikov said his mother and sister had arrived.
Ilya Petrovitch said he had met Dounia and was sorry for being rude before. He asked if Raskolnikov was moving because of his family.
Raskolnikov said he was just looking for Zametov.
Ilya Petrovitch said Zametov was not there, and talked more about young men, literature, and his own life.
Raskolnikov listened, but most of the words sounded empty to him.
Suddenly, someone said from another room that Svidrigaïlov had shot himself.
Raskolnikov was shocked.
“Svidrigaïlov! Svidrigaïlov has shot himself!” he cried.
Ilya Petrovitch asked if he knew Svidrigaïlov.
Raskolnikov said yes, his sister had worked for him.
Ilya Petrovitch said Svidrigaïlov had died suddenly and left a note. He asked if Raskolnikov suspected anything.
Raskolnikov said he saw Svidrigaïlov yesterday, but didn’t know anything was wrong.
Raskolnikov felt like something heavy was pressing on him.
Ilya Petrovitch noticed he looked pale and offered him a seat and some water.
Raskolnikov said he needed to go and apologized for bothering him.
Ilya Petrovitch shook his hand and said it was always a pleasure to see him.

Raskolnikov left, feeling dizzy. He went down the stairs and out into the yard, where Sonia stood, looking very frightened. She looked at him with worry and pain. Raskolnikov stood still, smiled in a strange way, and then turned back into the police office.
Ilya Petrovitch was sitting at his desk with a peasant.
“Back again! Did you forget something?” Ilya Petrovitch asked.
Raskolnikov came closer, looking pale and scared. He tried to speak but could only make strange sounds.
Ilya Petrovitch told him to sit and brought him water.
Raskolnikov started to say, “It was I…”
He refused the water and, in a soft but clear voice, said, “It was I who killed the old pawnbroker woman and her sister Lizaveta with an axe and robbed them.”
Ilya Petrovitch was shocked. People ran over.
Raskolnikov repeated his confession.

Far away in Siberia, beside a wide, lonely river, there was a town with a fortress and a prison. Rodion Raskolnikov (a young man who had done something very wrong) had been in this prison for nine months. It had been almost a year and a half since he committed his crime.

At Raskolnikov’s trial, things were clear. He told the truth about what he did, step by step. He explained how he killed the old woman and Lizaveta, how he took the keys, what the chest looked like, and how he hid the money and jewelry under a stone. The judges were surprised he never used the money or even looked inside the purse. Some people thought he must have been sick in his mind when he did it. Dr. Zossimov and others said Raskolnikov had been very unhappy and not well at the time.
Raskolnikov did not try to defend himself. When people asked why he did it, he said it was because he was poor and wanted money. He said he felt sorry afterwards and confessed because of that.

The court was kinder than expected. They saw that Raskolnikov was poor, sick, and had not used the things he stole. Razumihin (his good friend) told the court that Raskolnikov had once helped a sick student and paid for his funeral. His landlady said Raskolnikov had saved two children from a fire. This helped make people think better of him.
So, the judge sent Raskolnikov to prison for eight years.

At the start of the trial, Raskolnikov’s mother, Pulcheria Alexandrovna, became ill. Dounia (his sister) and Razumihin took her away from the city to a quieter place so she could rest and they could watch over her.

When Dounia came back from seeing Raskolnikov, her mother was already sick and confused. Dounia and Razumihin told her a made-up story, saying Raskolnikov had gone away for work and would return with money and fame.

But Pulcheria Alexandrovna never asked much about Raskolnikov. She told her own story, saying he had many powerful enemies and had to hide, but would become great one day. She often read his article and spoke about his talents.

Dounia and Razumihin worried about her. She didn’t ask for letters from Raskolnikov anymore, even though she used to wait for them. Dounia thought her mother guessed something was wrong but was too afraid to ask.

Sometimes Pulcheria Alexandrovna asked questions that were hard to answer without talking about Raskolnikov. If she got strange answers, she became sad and quiet. She often talked about her son in odd ways. Dounia and Razumihin pretended to agree with her stories to keep her calm.

Five months after Raskolnikov confessed, he was sentenced. Razumihin and Sonia (a kind friend) visited him as much as they could. When it was time for Raskolnikov to leave, Dounia and Razumihin promised they would join him in Siberia one day. They all cried when they said goodbye.

Before leaving, Raskolnikov worried a lot about his mother. He barely spoke to Sonia, but she was getting ready to follow him to Siberia. At the last goodbye, Raskolnikov guessed his mother would not get better. He and Sonia left together.

Two months later, Dounia married Razumihin. It was a quiet, sad wedding, but Porfiry Petrovitch and Zossimov were there. Razumihin worked hard and studied at the university again, hoping they would all live together in Siberia one day. Until then, they counted on Sonia.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna was happy about Dounia’s marriage, but grew even more troubled. Razumihin tried to cheer her up by telling her about the good things Raskolnikov had done. She often talked to strangers about her son, his article, and his bravery. Dounia worried someone might remember the trial if they heard his name. Pulcheria Alexandrovna wanted to visit the family of the children Raskolnikov had saved from the fire.

Pulcheria Alexandrovna’s sadness got worse. One day, she said Rodya (her nickname for Raskolnikov) would soon come home, as he had promised to return in nine months. She got the room ready for him. But after a busy day, she became very sick and feverish. She died two weeks later, and in her last days, she said things that showed she knew more than people thought.

Raskolnikov did not know about his mother’s death for a long time. Sonia wrote letters to Dounia and Razumihin every month, telling them about Raskolnikov’s life in prison. Her letters were simple and full of facts about how he was doing.

At first, Dounia and Razumihin were sad reading the letters. Sonia wrote that Raskolnikov was quiet and kept to himself. When she finally told him about his mother, he did not seem very upset. He did his work, did not care much about food or comfort, and lived simply, not because he wanted to, but because he just didn’t pay attention.

Sonia’s visits became important to Raskolnikov, even though at first he was not kind to her. Later, he missed her when she couldn’t come. She saw him on holidays and sometimes at his work on the river or in the workshops.
Sonia also worked as a seamstress in the town and helped others, but she never told Raskolnikov that people were kinder to him because of her.
Later, Sonia wrote that Raskolnikov was getting sick and kept away from everyone. He became pale and was sent to the prison hospital.

Raskolnikov was ill for a long time, but it was not just because of prison. He was sad inside. He was not ashamed of his prison clothes or hard work, but he was hurt in his heart. He wished he could blame himself, but he mostly thought he was just unlucky.
He did not know what to live for. He wondered what would happen after eight years, and if he could ever be happy.
He wished he could feel truly sorry for what he did, but he did not.
He thought about his crime and did not see it as such a big mistake now.
He wondered why his idea was worse than others in the world.
He told himself he had broken the law, so he should be punished, but only because he had not succeeded.
He felt he was guilty just because he had failed and confessed.
He also wondered why he had not ended his own life, and why he had chosen to confess instead.
He did not understand that maybe, deep down, he was starting to change.
He looked at the other prisoners and saw how much they loved life, even after all their suffering. He was surprised by this.
Raskolnikov felt alone from the other prisoners. He was not like them, and they did not like him. Even people who had done worse things laughed at him.
Some said, “You are a gentleman. You shouldn’t have used an axe.”
One day at church, the prisoners got angry at him.
They shouted, “You don’t believe in God! You should be killed.”
Raskolnikov did not say anything. One man tried to attack him, but a guard stopped it.

Raskolnikov wondered why all the prisoners liked Sonia. She hardly met them, but they all respected her and called her “little mother.” She helped them with letters and small gifts. They were always happy to see her.

Raskolnikov was in the hospital from Lent until after Easter. While he was sick, he had a strange dream. He dreamed everyone in the world got a strange sickness that made them think only they were right. People argued, fought, and everything was destroyed. Only a few people were left to start the world over.

When he woke up, the dream bothered him for a long time. Spring came, and Sonia could only visit twice because it was hard to get permission. Sometimes she just stood in the hospital yard and looked at his window.

One day, when Raskolnikov was almost well, he saw Sonia waiting outside. He felt something strange in his heart. When he got out of the hospital, he learned Sonia was sick but not badly. She sent him a note saying she would visit soon. His heart beat fast as he read it.

On a sunny morning, Raskolnikov went to work by the river. He sat alone, looking at the water, lost in thought. Suddenly, Sonia came and sat beside him. She smiled, but was shy. This time, Raskolnikov took her hand and did not let go.
Suddenly, Raskolnikov fell at Sonia’s feet and cried. She was scared at first, but then she understood. She saw he loved her and was happy.
They could not speak, but their faces showed hope for a new life. They felt happy because of each other.
They knew they had to wait seven more years, but now they had hope. Raskolnikov felt like he was alive again. Sonia lived for him.
That night in bed, Raskolnikov thought about Sonia. He thought even the other prisoners looked at him differently now and were kinder. He felt things were changing.
He remembered how he had hurt Sonia before, but now he wanted to make it up to her. Everything that had happened—his crime, his prison—seemed far away. He just felt alive again.
Under his pillow was Sonia’s New Testament, the book she once read to him. He had been afraid she would push him to believe, but she never did. He had asked her for the book himself.
He wondered if he could believe what Sonia believed.
Sonia was sick again, but very happy. Seven years did not seem so long anymore. Raskolnikov did not know that a new life would not be easy, but he was ready to try.
This was the beginning of a new story—a story about Raskolnikov learning to live again. But this story, for now, is finished.
